title: Nervous system · Facial nerve lesion localisation

sections.heading: Facial nerve: upper versus lower motor neuron weakness
sections.html:
The facial nucleus in the pons has two functional parts. The part that drives the forehead and upper eyelid receives corticobulbar fibres from both motor cortices. The part that drives the lower face receives fibres mainly from the opposite cortex.

[[figure:s23e-fig0001]]

Localising the lesion

SiteFacial weaknessCompany it keeps
Motor cortex or internal capsule (upper motor neuron)Opposite lower face; forehead wrinkles normallyArm and hand weakness on the same side as the facial droop; aphasia if the dominant hemisphere
Pontine nucleus or fascicleWhole face on the same sideSame-side abducens palsy (the facial fibres loop around the abducens nucleus), opposite-side limb weakness
Cerebellopontine angleWhole face on the same sideHearing loss, tinnitus and imbalance (vestibulocochlear nerve), reduced corneal reflex (trigeminal)
Facial canal or after the stylomastoid foramenWhole face on the same sideDepends on the branches lost (below)

Branches inside the temporal bone

  • Greater petrosal nerve (leaves at the geniculate ganglion): parasympathetic to the lacrimal gland. A lesion at or above the ganglion gives a dry eye.
  • Nerve to stapedius: damps loud sound. Its loss makes ordinary sounds painfully loud on that side (hyperacusis).
  • Chorda tympani: taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and parasympathetic supply to the submandibular and sublingual glands.

A lesion at the stylomastoid foramen (for example, parotid tumour or surgery) spares all three and causes pure motor weakness.

Exam trap: a stroke patient with a droopy mouth who can still raise both eyebrows has a central lesion. Forehead involvement points to the nucleus or the nerve.
Pearl: the corneal reflex has a trigeminal afferent (V1) and a facial efferent. A facial nerve lesion abolishes the blink on the affected side whichever eye is touched, while the opposite eye still blinks.

title: Neurology · Acute facial weakness

sections.heading: Acute facial palsy: Bell palsy and its mimics
sections.html:
Bell palsy is an acute, idiopathic, unilateral lower motor neuron facial palsy that develops over hours to 3 days. Reactivated herpes simplex virus is the leading suspected cause. Patients often notice ear or mastoid ache, altered taste or loud-sound sensitivity on the same side.

Diagnosis

  • It is a clinical diagnosis: whole-hemiface weakness including the forehead, with no other neurological deficit.
  • Routine laboratory tests and imaging are not needed in a typical case.
  • Look for a cause when the picture is atypical, and image when weakness is gradual (over weeks), recurrent on the same side, or comes with other cranial nerve or limb signs.
MimicClueNext step
StrokeForehead spared; arm or speech involvedEmergency stroke pathway and brain imaging
Herpes zoster oticus (Ramsay Hunt syndrome)Painful vesicles in the ear canal or on the palate; hearing loss or vertigoCorticosteroid plus an antiviral
Lyme diseaseTick exposure in an endemic area; may be bilateral; erythema migransLyme serology; doxycycline if positive
Parotid or skull-base tumourSlow progression, a parotid mass, palsy of single branchesMRI with contrast
Otitis media or cholesteatomaEar discharge, conductive hearing lossOtoscopy, ENT referral, CT of the temporal bone

Management

  • Oral corticosteroid started within 72 hours of onset in patients aged 16 or older (for example, a 10-day course of prednisolone or prednisone). It improves the chance of full recovery.
  • An antiviral is not given on its own. Adding one to the steroid is optional in severe palsy, with little proven benefit.
  • Protect the eye: lubricating drops by day, ointment and taping the lid shut at night. Incomplete closure can lead to exposure keratitis and corneal ulceration.
  • Refer to a specialist if there is no recovery by 3 months, or for new or worsening neurological signs.

Prognosis. Most patients begin to improve within 3 weeks, and most recover fully. Complete paralysis at onset, older age and no improvement by 3 weeks predict a worse outcome. Aberrant regrowth can cause synkinesis (an eye that closes when the patient smiles) and lacrimation on chewing.

Exam trap: do not order MRI for a typical Bell palsy, and do not give an antiviral alone. Remember eye care: the most common preventable harm is to the cornea.

sections.heading: Meningitis: organisms, entry and the CSF
sections.html:
Meningitis is inflammation of the pia and arachnoid and the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) between them. Most bacteria reach the meninges through the blood after colonising the nasopharynx; fewer arrive by direct spread from a sinus, the middle ear, a skull fracture or a neurosurgical wound. Once in the subarachnoid space, where complement and antibody are scarce, bacteria multiply freely. Their cell-wall products trigger cytokine release (TNF-α, IL-1), which opens the blood–brain barrier, draws in neutrophils and causes vasogenic and cytotoxic oedema. Raised intracranial pressure, vasculitis of vessels crossing the subarachnoid space and blocked CSF outflow explain the strokes, seizures, hydrocephalus and cranial nerve palsies (especially sensorineural hearing loss) that follow.

Likely organisms by host

HostMost common bacteriaMicrobiology clue
Neonate (under 1 month)Group B streptococcus (Streptococcus agalactiae), Escherichia coli (K1 capsule), Listeria monocytogenesGBS: gram-positive cocci in chains; E. coli: gram-negative rods; Listeria: gram-positive rods with tumbling motility
Children and adultsStreptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidisPneumococcus: lancet-shaped gram-positive diplococci; meningococcus: gram-negative diplococci
Over 50 years, pregnancy, impaired cell-mediated immunityAdd ListeriaIntracellular organism; covered by ampicillin, not by cephalosporins
Unvaccinated infants and childrenHaemophilus influenzae type bPolyribosyl-ribitol phosphate capsule, the target of the conjugate vaccine
CSF shunt, neurosurgery, penetrating traumaStaphylococcus aureus, coagulase-negative staphylococci, gram-negative rodsBiofilm on hardware

Meningococcal disease is driven by lipooligosaccharide, an endotoxin shed in membrane blebs, which causes septic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation and the petechial or purpuric rash. Terminal complement deficiency (C5–C9) and asplenia predispose to recurrent Neisseria infection; eculizumab, which blocks C5, carries the same risk.

Reading the CSF

CauseOpening pressureCellsProteinGlucose
BacterialHighHundreds to thousands, mostly neutrophilsHighLow (CSF:serum ratio usually below 0.4)
Viral (for example enterovirus)Normal or mildly highTens to a few hundred, mostly lymphocytesNormal or mildly highNormal
TuberculousHighLymphocytesVery highLow
Fungal (cryptococcal)Often very highLymphocytes, may be few in advanced HIVHighLow or normal
Exam trap: early bacterial meningitis and partly treated meningitis can show lymphocytes. Low CSF glucose is the more reliable pointer to a bacterial, tuberculous or fungal cause.
Pearl: neonatal meningitis has few meningeal signs. Fever or low temperature, poor feeding, irritability and a bulging fontanelle are the clues.

sections.heading: Encephalitis, abscess, prions and infections of the immunocompromised brain
sections.html:
Encephalitis is infection or inflammation of the brain tissue itself, so altered behaviour, reduced consciousness, seizures and focal signs dominate, often with meningeal signs too.

Herpes simplex encephalitis

The most common cause of sporadic fatal viral encephalitis. In adults it is usually HSV-1. The virus has a strong preference for the medial temporal lobes and orbitofrontal cortex, causing haemorrhagic necrosis. Patients develop fever, headache, confusion, personality change, aphasia, olfactory or gustatory hallucinations and temporal-lobe seizures. CSF shows a lymphocytic pleocytosis, often with red cells, and HSV DNA by PCR confirms it. Acyclovir is a guanosine analogue that viral thymidine kinase phosphorylates; host kinases then make the triphosphate, which inhibits viral DNA polymerase and terminates the chain. It crystallises in renal tubules, so hydrate patients. Resistance arises from loss or alteration of viral thymidine kinase; foscarnet, which acts directly on the polymerase, is then used.

Brain abscess

  • Contiguous spread from sinusitis, otitis media, mastoiditis or dental infection: viridans streptococci (especially the S. anginosus group) and anaerobes. Frontal abscesses follow frontal sinus or dental disease; temporal lobe and cerebellar abscesses follow ear disease.
  • Haematogenous spread: endocarditis (S. aureus), lung abscess, and right-to-left shunts such as cyanotic congenital heart disease, which bypass pulmonary filtering. These abscesses are often multiple, at the grey–white junction.
  • Trauma or neurosurgery: S. aureus.

Imaging shows a ring-enhancing lesion with surrounding oedema and restricted diffusion in the centre. Fever is absent in many patients.

Prion disease

Prions are infectious proteins. The normal cell-surface prion protein (PrPC, mostly α-helical) is converted into a misfolded form (PrPSc) rich in β-pleated sheets that resists proteases and recruits more normal protein. Neurons die and vacuoles form in the neuropil (spongiform change) without inflammation. Sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease causes a rapidly progressive dementia over months with startle myoclonus, ataxia and akinetic mutism. Clues: cortical and basal ganglia diffusion restriction on MRI, periodic sharp-wave complexes on EEG, and a positive CSF RT-QuIC assay. Prions survive standard sterilisation, so iatrogenic spread through neurosurgical instruments, dura grafts and cadaveric growth hormone has occurred. Variant CJD is linked to bovine spongiform encephalopathy.

The immunocompromised brain (advanced HIV)

DiseaseOrganismTypical CD4 countImaging and tests
Cryptococcal meningitisCryptococcus neoformans, an encapsulated yeast with narrow-based buddingBelow 100/mm3Often normal imaging; very high opening pressure; cryptococcal antigen in CSF and serum
Cerebral toxoplasmosisToxoplasma gondii reactivationBelow 100/mm3Multiple ring-enhancing lesions at the grey–white junction and basal ganglia; positive serum IgG
Primary CNS lymphomaEBV-driven B-cell lymphomaBelow 50/mm3Usually a single enhancing periventricular mass; EBV DNA in CSF
Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathyJC polyomavirus infecting oligodendrocytesBelow 200/mm3, or with natalizumabNon-enhancing white matter lesions without mass effect; JC virus DNA in CSF

Neurosyphilis

Treponema pallidum invades the CNS early. Late forms include tabes dorsalis (degeneration of the dorsal roots and dorsal columns: lightning pains, loss of vibration and position sense, a positive Romberg sign, Charcot joints) and general paresis (a progressive dementia with personality change). The Argyll Robertson pupil is small and irregular, constricts to a near target but not to light.

Exam trap: PML is the one opportunistic HIV brain lesion that does not enhance and has no mass effect.

sections.heading: Demyelinating and autoimmune disorders of the CNS
sections.html:
CNS myelin is made by oligodendrocytes, each of which myelinates segments of many axons. Peripheral myelin comes from Schwann cells, so CNS demyelinating diseases spare peripheral nerves.

Multiple sclerosis

MS is an immune-mediated disease in which autoreactive CD4 T cells (Th1 and Th17), CD8 T cells and B cells cross the blood–brain barrier and destroy myelin and oligodendrocytes, with axonal loss that drives long-term disability. It is more common in women, usually starts between 20 and 40 years, and is linked to HLA-DRB1*15:01, low vitamin D, smoking and prior Epstein-Barr virus infection.

  • Plaques: sharply demarcated areas of demyelination with relative axonal sparing, in periventricular white matter (ovoid lesions perpendicular to the ventricles), juxtacortical and infratentorial regions and the spinal cord.
  • CSF: oligoclonal IgG bands not present in serum (intrathecal antibody synthesis), a raised IgG index, and at most a mild lymphocytic pleocytosis.
  • Classic findings: optic neuritis (painful monocular vision loss with a relative afferent pupillary defect); internuclear ophthalmoplegia from a lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus (the eye on the side of the lesion fails to adduct, and the abducting eye has nystagmus); partial myelitis with Lhermitte sign (an electric sensation down the spine on neck flexion); sensory symptoms; bladder urgency.
  • Uhthoff phenomenon: heat (a hot bath, exercise, fever) worsens symptoms because conduction in demyelinated axons fails at higher temperatures.

Diagnosis needs lesions disseminated in space and time, shown clinically or on MRI; CSF-specific oligoclonal bands can stand in for dissemination in time.

Disease-modifying drugs by mechanism

DrugMechanismKey adverse effects
Interferon-βShifts cytokines toward an anti-inflammatory profile; reduces T-cell entry into the CNSFlu-like symptoms, depression, raised transaminases, leukopenia
Glatiramer acetateRandom polymer resembling myelin basic protein; diverts T cells to a regulatory profileInjection-site reactions, transient flushing and chest tightness after injection
NatalizumabMonoclonal antibody to α4-integrin; blocks lymphocyte adhesion to VCAM-1 on brain endotheliumProgressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (risk highest with JC virus antibodies)
Ocrelizumab, ofatumumabAnti-CD20; depletes B cellsInfusion reactions, infections, hepatitis B reactivation
Fingolimod, siponimod, ozanimodSphingosine-1-phosphate receptor modulators; trap lymphocytes in lymph nodesFirst-dose bradycardia and AV block, macular oedema, infections
Dimethyl fumarateActivates the Nrf2 antioxidant pathwayFlushing, gastrointestinal upset, lymphopenia
TeriflunomideInhibits dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (pyrimidine synthesis in lymphocytes)Hepatotoxicity, teratogenicity
AlemtuzumabAnti-CD52; depletes T and B cellsSecondary autoimmunity: thyroid disease, immune thrombocytopenia, glomerulonephritis

Dalfampridine (4-aminopyridine) blocks potassium channels, which prolongs action potentials across demyelinated segments and can improve walking speed; it lowers the seizure threshold.

[[figure:s23e-fig0102]]

Other antibody-mediated and inflammatory disorders

DisorderTarget or mechanismDistinctive features
Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD)IgG against aquaporin-4, the water channel on astrocyte foot processes; complement-mediated astrocyte injurySevere optic neuritis, longitudinally extensive myelitis (3 or more segments), area postrema syndrome (intractable hiccups, nausea, vomiting)
MOG antibody-associated disease (MOGAD)IgG against myelin oligodendrocyte glycoproteinOften children; bilateral optic neuritis with disc swelling, ADEM-like illness
Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM)Post-infectious autoimmunity (molecular mimicry)Usually a child, days to weeks after an infection; encephalopathy plus multifocal deficits; usually monophasic
Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitisIgG against the GluN1 subunit, causing receptor internalisationYoung women; psychiatric symptoms, then seizures, orofacial dyskinesias, autonomic instability and hypoventilation; ovarian teratoma; can follow HSV encephalitis
NeurosarcoidosisNon-caseating granulomasCranial neuropathies (especially facial), basal meningitis, hypothalamic involvement
Exam trap: interferon-β, natalizumab and fingolimod help MS but can worsen NMOSD, so the distinction changes treatment.

sections.heading: Neural tube and forebrain malformations
sections.html:
The neural plate folds into the neural tube during the fourth week after fertilisation. Fusion begins in the cervical region and proceeds in both directions; the rostral (cranial) neuropore closes around day 25 and the caudal neuropore around day 27–28. Failure of closure leaves neural tissue in contact with amniotic fluid, so α-fetoprotein leaks out, raising maternal serum and amniotic fluid AFP, and acetylcholinesterase appears in amniotic fluid.

[[figure:s23e-fig0101]]
DefectWhat failedFeatures
AnencephalyRostral neuroporeAbsent forebrain and skull vault; lethal; polyhydramnios because the fetus does not swallow
EncephaloceleSkull defect, usually occipitalMeninges with or without brain herniate through the defect
Spina bifida occultaVertebral arch fusion onlySkin intact; a tuft of hair, dimple or lipoma over the lower spine; usually no deficit; normal AFP
MeningoceleArch; meninges herniateSac of meninges and CSF; cord in its normal place; few deficits
MyelomeningoceleCaudal neural tube and archCord and roots in the sac; leg weakness, sensory loss, neurogenic bladder and bowel, clubfoot; Chiari II and hydrocephalus

Risk factors: low maternal folate, antiseizure drugs that interfere with folate (valproate, carbamazepine), pregestational diabetes, obesity and maternal hyperthermia early in pregnancy. Folic acid supplementation before conception prevents most cases.

Posterior fossa malformations

MalformationAnatomyPresentation
Chiari ICerebellar tonsils extend more than about 5 mm below the foramen magnumOften found in adolescence or adulthood: occipital headache brought on by coughing or straining; may have a cervical syrinx
Chiari IIVermis, fourth ventricle and medulla displaced through the foramen magnumPresent at birth with lumbosacral myelomeningocele and obstructive hydrocephalus; stridor and swallowing problems from brainstem compression
Dandy-Walker malformationHypoplastic or absent cerebellar vermis, cystic enlargement of the fourth ventricle, enlarged posterior fossaHydrocephalus, developmental delay, ataxia

A syrinx in the central cervical cord first damages the spinothalamic fibres crossing in the anterior white commissure, causing loss of pain and temperature sensation over the shoulders and arms in a cape-like distribution, with touch and vibration preserved. Enlargement affects the anterior horns (wasting of the hand muscles) and lateral corticospinal tracts.

Holoprosencephaly

Failure of the forebrain (prosencephalon) to divide into two hemispheres, from defective sonic hedgehog signalling (SHH mutations, trisomy 13, maternal diabetes, prenatal alcohol, defects of cholesterol synthesis). The face mirrors the brain: hypotelorism, a single central incisor, cleft lip and palate, and, in the most severe form, cyclopia.

Pearl: lumbosacral myelomeningocele almost always comes with a Chiari II malformation, and most affected infants need CSF diversion for hydrocephalus.

sections.heading: Neurocutaneous syndromes and cerebral palsy
sections.html:
The neurocutaneous syndromes (phakomatoses) affect tissues derived from ectoderm, chiefly the skin, nervous system and eye. Most are inherited tumour-suppressor disorders: one germline mutation plus a second, somatic hit.

SyndromeGene and productSkin and eyeNervous system and other organs
Neurofibromatosis type 1 (autosomal dominant)NF1 (chromosome 17): neurofibromin, a GTPase-activating protein that switches off RasCafé-au-lait macules, axillary and inguinal freckling, Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas)Cutaneous and plexiform neurofibromas, optic pathway glioma, learning disability, scoliosis, pheochromocytoma, malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour
NF2-related schwannomatosis (autosomal dominant)NF2 (chromosome 22): merlin, a cytoskeletal tumour suppressorJuvenile posterior subcapsular cataractBilateral vestibular schwannomas, meningiomas, spinal ependymomas
Tuberous sclerosis complex (autosomal dominant)TSC1 (hamartin, chromosome 9) or TSC2 (tuberin, chromosome 16); the complex inhibits mTORHypomelanotic macules, facial angiofibromas, shagreen patch, ungual fibromas, retinal hamartomasCortical tubers, subependymal nodules and giant cell astrocytoma; infantile spasms and epilepsy; autism; cardiac rhabdomyoma; renal angiomyolipoma; lymphangioleiomyomatosis
Von Hippel-Lindau disease (autosomal dominant)VHL (chromosome 3): targets hypoxia-inducible factor for destructionRetinal haemangioblastomaCerebellar and spinal haemangioblastomas (may secrete erythropoietin), clear cell renal carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, pancreatic cysts
Sturge-Weber syndrome (sporadic)Somatic activating mutation of GNAQPort-wine stain in the ophthalmic (V1) distribution; glaucomaIpsilateral leptomeningeal capillary-venous malformation, cortical calcification, seizures, hemiparesis, intellectual disability

Loss of VHL protein lets HIF accumulate even with normal oxygen, so VEGF and erythropoietin are overproduced: hence the vascular tumours and secondary polycythaemia.

Cerebral palsy

Cerebral palsy is a group of non-progressive disorders of movement and posture caused by injury to the developing brain before, during or soon after birth. The motor picture can change as the child grows, but the lesion does not. Prematurity is the largest risk factor. In preterm infants the white matter beside the lateral ventricles is a watershed zone that is vulnerable to hypoxia-ischaemia and inflammation (periventricular leukomalacia). The corticospinal fibres to the legs run closest to the ventricles, so the result is spastic diplegia, with the legs affected more than the arms.

TypeLesionPicture
Spastic (most common)Corticospinal pathwaysUpper motor neuron signs: hypertonia, hyperreflexia, scissoring, toe walking; diplegia, hemiplegia or quadriplegia
DyskineticBasal ganglia (for example, bilirubin encephalopathy or acute near-total asphyxia at term)Athetosis, chorea, dystonia
AtaxicCerebellumHypotonia, poor balance, intention tremor
Exam trap: loss of skills that were already gained is not cerebral palsy. Regression points to a progressive metabolic, genetic or neurodegenerative disease.

sections.heading: Acute bacterial meningitis: the first hour
sections.html:
Suspect bacterial meningitis in anyone with fever and headache plus neck stiffness, altered mental status, a petechial rash or a seizure. The full triad of fever, neck stiffness and confusion is present in fewer than half of adults; almost all have at least two of headache, fever, neck stiffness and altered consciousness. Kernig and Brudzinski signs are specific but insensitive.

Sequence of care

  1. Blood cultures straight away.
  2. Lumbar puncture immediately if there is no reason to image first.
  3. Obtain CT of the head before the LP if any of these are present: immunocompromise, known CNS disease (mass, stroke, shunt), a seizure in the past week, papilledema, reduced level of consciousness or a focal neurological deficit.
  4. If CT is needed, or the LP will be delayed for any reason, give dexamethasone and empirical antibiotics first. Antibiotics given an hour or two before the LP rarely prevent identification of the organism by Gram stain, culture, antigen or PCR tests, and delay costs lives.

Empirical therapy

PatientRegimenReasoning
Under 1 monthAmpicillin plus cefotaxime (or ampicillin plus gentamicin)GBS, E. coli, Listeria; ceftriaxone is avoided in neonates
1 month to 50 yearsVancomycin plus ceftriaxone (or cefotaxime)Pneumococcus (including penicillin-resistant strains) and meningococcus
Over 50 years, pregnant, or impaired cell-mediated immunityVancomycin plus ceftriaxone plus ampicillinAdds Listeria cover
After neurosurgery, head trauma or with a shuntVancomycin plus an antipseudomonal β-lactam (cefepime, ceftazidime or meropenem)Staphylococci and hospital gram-negative rods

Dexamethasone is given just before or with the first antibiotic dose in adults with suspected bacterial meningitis (and in children with suspected H. influenzae type b). In adults it lowers mortality and neurological sequelae from pneumococcal meningitis; continue it only if pneumococcus is confirmed. It is not useful once antibiotics have been running for some time.

Public health and follow-up

  • Meningococcal disease: droplet precautions for the first 24 hours of therapy, notify public health, and give chemoprophylaxis to close contacts (household members, people who share sleeping quarters, anyone exposed to the patient's oral secretions, including staff who intubated without a mask). Options: a single oral dose of ciprofloxacin, a 2-day course of rifampin, or a single intramuscular dose of ceftriaxone (preferred in pregnancy).
  • Formal hearing testing after recovery, especially in children; sensorineural hearing loss is the most common lasting complication.
Exam trap: a question that offers "CT head" before antibiotics in a patient who needs imaging is testing whether you will let treatment wait. Cultures, dexamethasone and antibiotics come first.

sections.heading: Encephalitis and CNS infections in the immunocompromised
sections.html:
Encephalitis: treat herpes first

Fever with confusion, behaviour change, seizures or focal signs is encephalitis until proven otherwise. Start intravenous acyclovir as soon as the diagnosis is suspected, without waiting for CSF PCR or MRI. Then:

  • MRI (most sensitive imaging): T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the medial temporal lobes and insula, often asymmetric, suggests HSV.
  • CSF: lymphocytic pleocytosis, raised protein, normal glucose; red cells are common in HSV. HSV PCR is the diagnostic test; a negative result in the first 72 hours may be falsely negative, so repeat it if suspicion stays high.
  • EEG: temporal slowing or periodic lateralised discharges.

Continue acyclovir for 14–21 days in confirmed HSV encephalitis, keep the patient hydrated and watch renal function. Consider West Nile virus in late summer with flaccid weakness, and test for anti-NMDA receptor antibodies if symptoms relapse weeks after HSV encephalitis.

Brain abscess

Headache is the main symptom; fever and focal signs are each absent in many patients. MRI with contrast and diffusion-weighted imaging distinguishes abscess (restricted diffusion in the cavity) from necrotic tumour. Treatment combines neurosurgical aspiration or excision (which also gives the microbiology) with intravenous antibiotics for several weeks. A common empirical regimen for an abscess from a sinus, ear or dental source is a third-generation cephalosporin plus metronidazole, adding vancomycin after trauma or neurosurgery. Lumbar puncture adds little and risks herniation.

Advanced HIV

DiagnosisManagement
Cryptococcal meningitisInduction with amphotericin B (liposomal preferred) plus flucytosine, then fluconazole consolidation and maintenance. Lower raised intracranial pressure with repeated therapeutic lumbar punctures (not acetazolamide or steroids). Delay antiretroviral therapy for about 4–6 weeks to lower the risk of fatal immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome.
Cerebral toxoplasmosis (multiple ring-enhancing lesions, positive IgG)Start pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine plus leucovorin empirically. Repeat imaging after about 2 weeks; if lesions have not shrunk, biopsy to look for lymphoma. Primary prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole when CD4 is below 100/mm3 and Toxoplasma IgG is positive.
Primary CNS lymphoma (solitary periventricular lesion, EBV DNA in CSF)Stereotactic biopsy; high-dose methotrexate-based chemotherapy plus effective antiretroviral therapy. Avoid steroids before biopsy if possible because they can make the biopsy non-diagnostic.
Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathyNo specific antiviral. Restore immunity: start or optimise antiretroviral therapy; stop natalizumab and remove it with plasma exchange.

Neurosyphilis

Examine the CSF in any patient with syphilis and neurological, ocular or otic symptoms. A reactive CSF VDRL confirms it but is insensitive; a negative CSF FTA-ABS makes neurosyphilis unlikely. Treat with intravenous aqueous penicillin G for 10–14 days. Patients with penicillin allergy should be desensitised. Benzathine penicillin does not reach treponemicidal levels in the CSF.

Pearl: in cryptococcal meningitis the opening pressure is often above 25 cm H2O and drives much of the mortality. Draining CSF until the pressure halves (or normalises) relieves headache and saves vision.

sections.heading: Multiple sclerosis, NMOSD and autoimmune encephalitis: diagnosis and treatment
sections.html:
A first demyelinating event

Optic neuritis, partial myelitis or a brainstem syndrome in a young adult raises the question of MS. The key investigation is MRI of the brain (and often spinal cord) with gadolinium. Lesions in typical MS locations predict a high risk of a second attack and may already satisfy the criteria for dissemination in space; one enhancing and one non-enhancing lesion at the same time satisfy dissemination in time. CSF oligoclonal bands support the diagnosis. Check vitamin B12, and when the picture is atypical, test for AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG.

Relapse or pseudo-relapse?

A relapse is a new or worsening deficit lasting more than 24 hours, without fever or infection. A pseudo-relapse is a temporary return of old symptoms caused by heat, fever, infection (urinary tract infection is common) or metabolic stress. Look for and treat infection before giving steroids.

  • Disabling relapse: high-dose methylprednisolone (for example 1 g intravenously daily for 3–5 days; high-dose oral regimens are an alternative). This speeds recovery but does not change long-term disability.
  • Severe relapse that does not respond to steroids: plasma exchange.
  • Mild sensory relapse: steroids are optional.

Long-term disease modification

  • Start a disease-modifying therapy early in relapsing MS. Higher-efficacy agents (anti-CD20 antibodies, natalizumab) suit active disease.
  • Before anti-CD20 therapy, screen for hepatitis B (risk of reactivation) and update vaccines.
  • Before natalizumab, test for JC virus antibodies.
  • Primary progressive MS: ocrelizumab is the agent shown to slow disability progression.
  • Many disease-modifying drugs are avoided in pregnancy; plan pregnancy with the neurologist. Relapse rates fall during pregnancy and rise in the first months after delivery.

Symptom management

SymptomOptions
SpasticityStretching and physical therapy; baclofen or tizanidine; botulinum toxin for focal spasticity
Urgency with a small post-void residualAntimuscarinic (for example oxybutynin) or mirabegron; timed voiding
Incomplete emptying (large post-void residual)Clean intermittent self-catheterisation
Walking speedDalfampridine (avoid with a history of seizures or renal impairment)
Fatigue, depression, neuropathic painExercise and sleep hygiene; treat depression; gabapentinoids or duloxetine for pain

NMOSD

Suspect it with severe or bilateral optic neuritis, myelitis spanning 3 or more segments, or intractable hiccups and vomiting. Serum AQP4-IgG confirms it. Treat attacks with high-dose steroids and early plasma exchange. Prevent attacks with eculizumab or ravulizumab (complement C5 inhibitors; meningococcal vaccination first), inebilizumab (anti-CD19), satralizumab (anti-IL-6 receptor) or rituximab. Avoid interferon-β, natalizumab and fingolimod.

Autoimmune encephalitis

A young woman with new psychosis or agitation followed by seizures, abnormal movements, autonomic swings or reduced consciousness: send CSF and serum for anti-NMDA receptor antibodies (CSF is more sensitive), then image the pelvis (ultrasound or MRI) for an ovarian teratoma. First-line treatment is tumour removal plus immunotherapy with corticosteroids, IVIG or plasma exchange; rituximab or cyclophosphamide are used if these fail. Antipsychotics are poorly tolerated and can mimic or worsen catatonia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

Exam trap: a known MS patient with worse old symptoms and dysuria needs a urinalysis, not methylprednisolone.

sections.heading: Congenital CNS disorders: prevention, newborn care and follow-up
sections.html:
Preventing neural tube defects

  • Everyone who could become pregnant: 0.4–0.8 mg (400–800 µg) folic acid daily, starting at least 1 month before conception and continuing through the first trimester.
  • A previous pregnancy with a neural tube defect (or a parent with one): 4 mg daily, from at least 1 month before conception through the first trimester.
  • Before conception, review medicines: valproate carries the highest neural tube risk of the antiseizure drugs, and changing it should be planned before, not after, conception. Optimise glycaemic control in diabetes.

Prenatal detection

Second-trimester maternal serum AFP screening and the detailed anatomy ultrasound detect most open defects. Ultrasound signs of myelomeningocele include the "lemon" skull shape and the "banana" cerebellum of Chiari II. Prenatal (fetal) repair of myelomeningocele in selected pregnancies lowers the need for a shunt and improves motor outcome, at the cost of higher preterm birth and uterine scar risks. Planned caesarean delivery is common.

The newborn with an open myelomeningocele

  • Cover the defect with a sterile, saline-moistened, non-adherent dressing, nurse the infant prone or on the side, and avoid pressure on the sac.
  • Start broad-spectrum antibiotics if the sac is leaking; arrange surgical closure within about 48–72 hours.
  • Use latex-free equipment from birth: these children are at high risk of latex allergy.
  • Watch head circumference and ultrasound for hydrocephalus, which often needs a ventriculoperitoneal shunt or endoscopic third ventriculostomy.
  • Long term: clean intermittent catheterisation for neurogenic bladder (protects the kidneys), a bowel programme, orthopaedic care for clubfoot, hip and spine, and surveillance for a tethered cord (back pain, new weakness, worsening bladder control, scoliosis).

Shunt malfunction

Headache, vomiting, irritability, lethargy, a bulging fontanelle, rising head circumference or impaired upward gaze (sunsetting eyes) in a child with a shunt means shunt failure until proven otherwise. Arrange urgent imaging (rapid-sequence MRI or CT) with a shunt series of radiographs, and call neurosurgery. Fever adds shunt infection to the differential.

Chiari I in practice

MRI of the brain and cervical spine confirms tonsillar descent and shows any syrinx. Many incidental Chiari I malformations need no treatment. Refer for posterior fossa decompression when there are typical cough-induced headaches with a syrinx, brainstem signs or progressive deficits.

Cerebral palsy

Diagnose early from risk history, abnormal motor examination and MRI. Care is multidisciplinary: physical and occupational therapy, orthoses, and treatment of spasticity (oral baclofen or diazepam for generalised spasticity; botulinum toxin injections for focal spasticity; intrathecal baclofen or selective dorsal rhizotomy for severe cases). Screen regularly for hip displacement, scoliosis, epilepsy, feeding problems, poor growth, hearing and vision problems. In threatened preterm birth before 32 weeks, antenatal magnesium sulfate lowers the risk of cerebral palsy.

Surveillance in neurocutaneous syndromes

SyndromeKey surveillance or treatment
NF1Yearly eye examination in childhood (optic pathway glioma), blood pressure checks (renal artery stenosis, pheochromocytoma), developmental and scoliosis checks; MEK inhibitors for symptomatic plexiform neurofibromas
Tuberous sclerosisInfantile spasms: vigabatrin first line; mTOR inhibitors (everolimus) for subependymal giant cell astrocytoma and angiomyolipoma; renal imaging; echocardiography in infancy
Von Hippel-LindauRegular retinal examination, brain and spine MRI, abdominal imaging and plasma metanephrines
Sturge-WeberIntraocular pressure checks for glaucoma; seizure control; laser for the port-wine stain

title: Nervous system · Tumours of the nervous system

sections.heading: CNS tumours: where they arise and who gets them
sections.html:
Tumours inside the skull fall into three groups: metastases from a cancer elsewhere, primary benign tumours (most of them extra-axial, pressing on the brain from outside) and primary malignant tumours (most of them gliomas growing within the brain substance).

  • In adults, metastases outnumber all primary tumours. Among primary tumours, meningioma is the most common, and glioblastoma is the most common malignant one.
  • In children, brain tumours are the most common solid cancers. Pilocytic astrocytoma is the most common, and medulloblastoma is the most common malignant one.
[[figure:s23e-fig0201]]

Location follows age

Most adult primary tumours lie above the tentorium, in the cerebral hemispheres and meninges. Most childhood tumours lie in the posterior fossa (cerebellum, fourth ventricle, brainstem). Midline sellar and pineal tumours occur at both ages.

How they present

  • Raised intracranial pressure: headache that is worse on waking or lying down, vomiting, papilledema, and a sixth nerve palsy as a false localising sign. Posterior fossa tumours block the fourth ventricle early and cause obstructive hydrocephalus.
  • Seizures: most common with slow-growing cortical tumours such as oligodendroglioma and low-grade glioma.
  • Focal deficits that progress over weeks: hemiparesis, aphasia, visual field loss, personality change with frontal tumours.
  • Endocrine and visual syndromes with sellar tumours: bitemporal hemianopia from chiasm compression, hypopituitarism, growth failure in children.

Behaviour

FeatureWhat it means
Extra-axial (meningioma, schwannoma)Displaces rather than infiltrates brain; often curable by complete resection
Diffusely infiltrating (diffuse gliomas)Tumour cells extend well beyond the visible mass, so surgery cannot cure them
Spread through cerebrospinal fluidMedulloblastoma, ependymoma and germinoma seed the spinal leptomeninges ("drop metastases")
Spread outside the nervous systemRare for primary CNS tumours
Pearl: a "benign" tumour can still kill by location. A slow meningioma at the skull base or a pilocytic astrocytoma in the brainstem may be impossible to remove completely.

sections.heading: Benign CNS tumours: pathology and genetics
sections.html:
TumourCell of origin and siteHistology and markersAssociations

SchwannomaSchwann cells; vestibular division of CN VIII at the cerebellopontine angle, spinal nerve rootsCellular Antoni A areas with palisaded nuclei (Verocay bodies) and loose Antoni B areas; S-100 positiveBilateral vestibular schwannomas define NF2
NeurofibromaMixed Schwann cells, fibroblasts and perineurial cells within a nerveWavy spindle cells in a myxoid stroma; S-100 positive in partNF1; the plexiform type can become a malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour
Pilocytic astrocytomaAstrocytes; cerebellum, optic pathway, hypothalamus; childrenBipolar cells with hair-like processes, Rosenthal fibres, eosinophilic granular bodies; GFAP positive. Cyst with an enhancing mural noduleBRAF alterations; optic pathway gliomas in NF1
HemangioblastomaCerebellum, brainstem, spinal cord, retina; adultsThin-walled capillaries with lipid-laden stromal cells; cyst with mural nodulevon Hippel–Lindau disease; may secrete erythropoietin (polycythemia)
CraniopharyngiomaRemnants of Rathke pouch (oral ectoderm); suprasellarCalcified cystic tumour with cholesterol-rich fluid; squamous epithelium with "wet" keratinChildren (adamantinomatous type, CTNNB1) and older adults (papillary type, BRAF V600E)
Pituitary adenomaAnterior pituitary cells; sellaUniform cells; immunostains by hormone and transcription factorProlactinoma is the commonest functioning type; MEN1

The genetics behind them

  • NF1 (chromosome 17, neurofibromin): neurofibromin switches Ras off. Loss leaves Ras active. Café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, neurofibromas, iris Lisch nodules, optic pathway glioma, pheochromocytoma.
  • NF2 (chromosome 22, merlin): merlin links the membrane to the cytoskeleton and restrains growth. Bilateral vestibular schwannomas, meningiomas, ependymomas, juvenile cataract.
  • von Hippel–Lindau (chromosome 3p): the VHL protein tags hypoxia-inducible factor for destruction. Loss lets HIF drive VEGF and erythropoietin, giving vascular tumours: hemangioblastomas, clear cell renal carcinoma, pheochromocytoma.

Mass effect around the sella

A sellar or suprasellar mass that pushes up on the optic chiasm compresses the crossing nasal fibres and causes bitemporal hemianopia. A large nonfunctioning adenoma can modestly raise prolactin by compressing the stalk, which cuts off hypothalamic dopamine (the "stalk effect"). Very high prolactin, by contrast, means the tumour itself makes it.

Exam trap: the cyst-with-mural-nodule picture fits both pilocytic astrocytoma (a child) and hemangioblastoma (an adult, often with polycythemia or retinal lesions). Age and the associated findings decide.

sections.heading: Malignant primary CNS tumours: gliomas, embryonal tumours and lymphoma
sections.html:
Diffuse gliomas in adults: classified by molecular markers

The 2021 WHO classification (CNS5) defines adult diffuse gliomas first by IDH status, then by other markers. Histology alone no longer settles the diagnosis.

TumourDefining markersTypical picture
Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype (grade 4)IDH-wildtype, plus necrosis or microvascular proliferation, or TERT promoter mutation, EGFR amplification, or gain of chromosome 7 with loss of 10Older adults; ring-enhancing mass with central necrosis that may cross the corpus callosum ("butterfly"); pseudopalisading necrosis; GFAP positive
Astrocytoma, IDH-mutant (grades 2–4)IDH1 or IDH2 mutation, usually with ATRX loss and TP53 mutation; no 1p/19q codeletionYounger adults; slower course; better survival than glioblastoma
Oligodendroglioma, IDH-mutant and 1p/19q-codeleted (grades 2–3)IDH mutation and whole-arm 1p/19q codeletionFrontal lobe; seizures; calcification; round nuclei with clear halos and a delicate branching capillary network; the most chemosensitive glioma

Why IDH matters: mutant IDH makes 2-hydroxyglutarate. This oncometabolite inhibits enzymes that need α-ketoglutarate, including DNA and histone demethylases, so the genome becomes hypermethylated and cells stay undifferentiated. An IDH-wildtype diffuse astrocytic tumour in an adult that carries any of the molecular glioblastoma features is graded as glioblastoma, even without necrosis.

MGMT: temozolomide, an oral alkylating agent, adds methyl groups to guanine. The repair enzyme MGMT removes them. When the MGMT promoter is methylated (silenced), the tumour cannot repair the damage, responds better and the patient lives longer.

Tumours of childhood

TumourSitePathologyKey behaviour
MedulloblastomaCerebellar vermis, roof of the fourth ventricleEmbryonal; sheets of small round blue cells, Homer Wright rosettes; synaptophysin positiveTruncal ataxia, hydrocephalus; seeds the spinal leptomeninges through CSF; molecular groups (WNT, SHH, groups 3 and 4) guide prognosis
EpendymomaFloor of the fourth ventricle in children; spinal cord in adults (myxopapillary type at the filum terminale)Perivascular pseudorosettes (tumour cells around vessels with a fibrillary halo) and true ependymal rosettesHydrocephalus; outcome depends mainly on how completely it is removed
Diffuse midline glioma, H3 K27-alteredPons (formerly called diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma), thalamus, spinal cordInfiltrating glioma with altered histone H3Multiple cranial nerve palsies with long-tract signs; cannot be resected; median survival about a year

Primary CNS lymphoma

Almost always a diffuse large B-cell lymphoma confined to the brain, eyes, leptomeninges or cord. It clusters around vessels (angiocentric). Two settings:

  • Immunocompromised (advanced HIV with a CD4 count below about 50/mm³, transplant recipients): driven by Epstein–Barr virus. It can ring-enhance and mimic toxoplasmosis. EBV DNA in CSF supports it.
  • Immunocompetent older adults: deep periventricular, homogeneously enhancing mass(es); some patients also have vitreoretinal lymphoma.
Exam trap: corticosteroids make lymphoma cells die quickly, so a steroid given before biopsy can shrink the lesion and leave a nondiagnostic sample.

sections.heading: Metastases to the nervous system and paraneoplastic syndromes
sections.html:
Brain metastases

  • Common sources: lung cancer (the leading source), breast cancer, melanoma, renal cell carcinoma and colorectal cancer.
  • Route: arterial blood. Tumour emboli lodge at the gray–white matter junction, where arterioles narrow abruptly, and in arterial border zones.
  • Appearance: often multiple, round, well-circumscribed, ring- or solid-enhancing lesions with much more surrounding vasogenic edema than their size suggests.
  • Hemorrhage-prone metastases: melanoma, renal cell carcinoma, choriocarcinoma and thyroid carcinoma.

Spinal metastases and cord compression

Most spinal metastases start in the vertebral body and grow back into the epidural space. Breast, lung and prostate cancer and multiple myeloma lead the list. Prostate cancer reaches the spine through the valveless vertebral venous plexus and usually gives osteoblastic (sclerotic) lesions. The first symptom is almost always back pain, often worse when lying down and at night. Weakness, a sensory level and bladder dysfunction come later.

Leptomeningeal metastasis

Tumour cells spread through the subarachnoid space (breast and lung cancer, melanoma, leukemia and lymphoma). Symptoms appear at several levels at once: headache, several cranial nerve palsies, radicular pain and hydrocephalus.

Paraneoplastic neurologic syndromes

Here the tumour does not invade the nervous system. Instead it expresses a neural protein (an onconeural antigen), and the immune attack on the cancer also strikes neurons.

AntibodyUsual tumourSyndrome
Anti-Hu (ANNA-1)Small cell lung carcinomaEncephalomyelitis, sensory neuronopathy (dorsal root ganglia), limbic encephalitis
Anti-Yo (PCA-1)Ovarian and breast carcinomaSubacute cerebellar degeneration (Purkinje cell loss)
Anti-Ma2Testicular germ cell tumourLimbic, hypothalamic and brainstem encephalitis
Anti-NMDA receptorOvarian teratoma (young women), often no tumourPsychiatric onset, seizures, orofacial dyskinesias, autonomic instability, reduced consciousness
Anti-P/Q-type calcium channelSmall cell lung carcinomaLambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome
Pearl: antibodies against intracellular antigens (Hu, Yo, Ma2) are markers. Cytotoxic T cells cause the neuron loss, so immunotherapy helps little and treating the cancer is the priority. Antibodies against cell-surface targets (NMDA receptor, calcium channel) cause the disease themselves, and patients often recover with tumour removal and immunotherapy.
Exam trap: the paraneoplastic syndrome often appears before the cancer is known. A subacute, disabling cerebellar syndrome in a middle-aged woman with a normal MRI calls for a search for gynecologic or breast cancer.

title: Neurology · Brain and spinal tumours

sections.heading: Adult brain tumours: diagnosis and management
sections.html:
First steps

  • Imaging: MRI of the brain with and without gadolinium is the test of choice. Noncontrast CT is the first scan in an emergency (sudden deterioration, suspected hemorrhage or herniation).
  • Look for a primary cancer when the picture fits metastasis: CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis.
  • Tissue (biopsy or resection) gives the diagnosis, and molecular testing (IDH, 1p/19q, MGMT) is part of it.
  • Do not do a lumbar puncture in a patient with a mass and raised pressure before imaging. It can precipitate herniation.

Supportive care

  • Dexamethasone for symptomatic vasogenic edema. Taper to the lowest dose that works. Avoid it before biopsy when lymphoma is possible.
  • Antiseizure medication only after a seizure. Prophylaxis in a patient who has never had one is not recommended. Levetiracetam is preferred: it does not induce liver enzymes, so it does not interfere with chemotherapy or dexamethasone.
  • Venous thromboembolism is common in glioma; use mechanical and pharmacological prophylaxis around surgery.

Specific tumours

TumourManagement
GlioblastomaMaximal safe resection, then focal radiotherapy with concurrent and adjuvant temozolomide. Give Pneumocystis prophylaxis during the concurrent phase (lymphopenia plus steroids). Tumour-treating fields are an add-on option. Median survival is about 15–20 months.
IDH-mutant glioma (astrocytoma, oligodendroglioma)Maximal safe resection; then radiotherapy with chemotherapy for higher-risk or higher-grade disease. Selected grade 2 tumours can be watched or treated with an IDH inhibitor.
Primary CNS lymphomaStereotactic biopsy (not resection), ideally steroid-free; high-dose methotrexate–based chemotherapy; in HIV, also start antiretroviral therapy.
MeningiomaSmall, asymptomatic: serial MRI. Symptomatic or growing: surgical resection. Radiotherapy or radiosurgery for residual, recurrent or inoperable tumour.
Vestibular schwannomaSmall, little hearing loss: serial MRI and audiometry. Growing: stereotactic radiosurgery or microsurgery.
Prolactinoma (any size, even with field loss)Dopamine agonist (cabergoline) first; surgery if intolerant or resistant.
Nonfunctioning macroadenoma compressing the chiasmTranssphenoidal resection; check and replace pituitary hormones (cortisol before thyroid hormone).

Treatment-related problems

  • Pseudoprogression: in the first 12 weeks after chemoradiation, enhancement can increase because of treatment effect. If the patient is stable, continue therapy and repeat MRI rather than call it progression.
  • Pituitary apoplexy: sudden hemorrhage or infarction of an adenoma. Severe headache, ophthalmoplegia, visual loss and shock from acute adrenal insufficiency. Give stress-dose intravenous hydrocortisone first, then consider neurosurgical decompression.
  • Diabetes insipidus after pituitary surgery: high-volume dilute urine with rising sodium in the first days; treat with desmopressin and access to water.
Exam trap: a 3-cm sellar mass with prolactin only mildly raised is not a prolactinoma. It is a nonfunctioning adenoma with stalk effect, and a dopamine agonist will lower the prolactin without shrinking it.

furtherReading.label: StatPearls: Central Nervous System Lymphoma (NCBI Bookshelf)

sections.heading: Brain tumours in children
sections.html:
Brain tumours are the most common solid cancers of childhood and the leading cause of cancer death in children. Most arise in the posterior fossa.

Presentation

  • Morning headache and vomiting, irritability, declining school performance.
  • Ataxia: truncal (wide-based gait) from midline vermis tumours; limb ataxia from hemispheric tumours.
  • Infants: enlarging head circumference, a bulging fontanelle, loss of upward gaze ("setting sun" eyes).
  • Growth failure, delayed or precocious puberty, polyuria with sellar and hypothalamic tumours. Upgaze palsy with pineal region tumours.
  • Brainstem tumours: several cranial nerve palsies (often VI and VII) with ataxia and long-tract signs over weeks.

Image with MRI of the brain with and without gadolinium, under sedation if needed. A child with papilledema or focal signs needs imaging before any lumbar puncture.

Management by tumour

TumourManagement and outlook
Pilocytic astrocytomaGross total resection is usually curative. Chemotherapy or BRAF/MEK-targeted therapy for unresectable optic pathway or hypothalamic tumours.
MedulloblastomaStaging with MRI of the whole spine and CSF cytology; maximal safe resection, craniospinal radiotherapy (age 3 and older) and chemotherapy. Most children with standard-risk disease survive, often with neurocognitive and endocrine late effects.
EpendymomaGross total resection followed by focal radiotherapy; extent of resection is the strongest predictor of outcome.
Diffuse midline glioma (pons)Diagnosis by typical MRI ± biopsy; focal radiotherapy relieves symptoms for a while; survival is rarely beyond 2 years.
CraniopharyngiomaSurgery, often with radiotherapy. Lifelong follow-up for hypopituitarism, diabetes insipidus, visual loss and hypothalamic obesity.
Germinoma (pineal or suprasellar)Serum and CSF tumour markers (AFP, β-hCG); very sensitive to radiotherapy and chemotherapy.

Surveillance in tumour-predisposition syndromes

  • NF1: yearly eye examination in childhood to detect optic pathway glioma. Routine brain MRI in a child without symptoms is not recommended. Check blood pressure at every visit.
  • von Hippel–Lindau: scheduled eye examinations, MRI of the brain and spine, abdominal imaging and metanephrine testing from childhood.
Exam trap: a child with weeks of morning vomiting is often first labelled as having gastroenteritis or migraine. Ataxia, papilledema or a new head tilt changes the answer to MRI.

sections.heading: Brain metastases, spinal cord compression and leptomeningeal disease
sections.html:
Brain metastases

  • Diagnosis: MRI with gadolinium (more sensitive than CT for small and multiple lesions). With no known cancer, CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis finds the primary in most patients; biopsy the most accessible site.
  • Symptom control: dexamethasone for symptomatic edema (not needed for small asymptomatic lesions); antiseizure medication only after a seizure.
SituationUsual choice
One accessible symptomatic lesion, good performance status, controlled or treatable cancerSurgical resection, then stereotactic radiosurgery to the cavity
A limited number of small lesionsStereotactic radiosurgery alone (spares cognition compared with whole-brain radiotherapy)
Many lesionsWhole-brain radiotherapy with hippocampal avoidance and memantine, or CNS-active systemic therapy
Tumour with a targetable driver (e.g., EGFR, ALK) and small asymptomatic lesionsCNS-penetrant targeted therapy may come first, with close MRI follow-up
Poor performance status and uncontrolled cancerSupportive care (steroids, palliative care)

Metastatic spinal cord compression: an emergency

  1. Suspect it in any patient with cancer and new or worsening back pain, especially pain at night, on lying flat or with coughing.
  2. With neurological deficits, give dexamethasone at once.
  3. Get an urgent MRI of the whole spine with gadolinium; compression is often at more than one level.
  4. Definitive treatment: decompressive surgery followed by radiotherapy for suitable patients (spinal instability, a radioresistant tumour, a single level, reasonable life expectancy). Radiotherapy alone for radiosensitive tumours (myeloma, lymphoma, small cell cancer) in a stable spine, or for poor surgical candidates.

Function at the start of treatment predicts outcome: most patients who walk in walk out, and few who are paraplegic recover.

Leptomeningeal metastasis

  • Diagnosis: MRI of the brain and whole spine with gadolinium (leptomeningeal and nerve-root enhancement), then CSF cytology. Do the MRI first, because lumbar puncture can cause meningeal enhancement. CSF usually shows raised protein, sometimes low glucose and lymphocytes. One negative cytology does not exclude it; repeat with a large volume.
  • Treatment: palliative. Radiotherapy to symptomatic sites, systemic or intrathecal chemotherapy for selected patients, a shunt for hydrocephalus.

Paraneoplastic syndromes in practice

Send serum and CSF antibody panels and search for the tumour: CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis, then FDG-PET if negative. In anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis, image the pelvis for an ovarian teratoma. Treat with tumour removal plus first-line immunotherapy (corticosteroids, IVIG or plasma exchange), and escalate to rituximab if needed.

Exam trap: do not wait for the MRI to give dexamethasone to a patient with cancer, back pain and new leg weakness. Do not order plain radiographs as the main test; they miss epidural disease.

furtherReading.label: StatPearls: Palliative Radiation Therapy for Brain Metastases (NCBI Bookshelf)
