sections.heading: Cerebral arterial territories and the stroke syndromes they produce
sections.html:
Each large cerebral artery supplies a predictable piece of cortex and white matter, so the pattern of deficits localises an occlusion. The anterior circulation (internal carotid, anterior and middle cerebral arteries) supplies most of the frontal, parietal and lateral temporal lobes. The posterior circulation (vertebral, basilar and posterior cerebral arteries) supplies the brainstem, cerebellum, thalamus, occipital lobes and medial temporal lobes.

[[figure:s23e-fig0301]]

Cortical territories

ArteryRegion suppliedTypical deficits (left-hemisphere lesion)
Middle cerebral, stem (M1)Lateral convexity: face and arm motor and sensory cortex, language areas, plus deep branchesRight face and arm weakness and sensory loss more than leg; aphasia; eyes deviated toward the lesion (left); right homonymous field loss if the optic radiation is involved
Middle cerebral, superior divisionFrontal operculum, lateral motor stripExpressive (Broca-type) aphasia, right face and arm weakness
Middle cerebral, inferior divisionSuperior temporal and inferior parietal lobesReceptive (Wernicke-type) aphasia with fluent, meaningless speech; often little weakness
Anterior cerebralMedial frontal and parietal lobes, including the leg area of the motor and sensory stripsRight leg weakness and sensory loss; urinary incontinence; apathy and slowed initiation (abulia) when the medial frontal lobe is large
Posterior cerebralOccipital lobe, inferomedial temporal lobe, thalamusRight homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing; alexia without agraphia if the splenium is also damaged; memory loss if bilateral

Dominant versus nondominant. In most people the left hemisphere is dominant for language. A right (nondominant) middle cerebral lesion causes left-sided weakness with hemineglect: the patient ignores the left side of space and may deny the deficit (anosognosia).

Macular sparing in posterior cerebral infarcts reflects dual supply of the occipital pole, which receives collateral flow from the middle cerebral artery.

Deep and border-zone territories

  • Lenticulostriate arteries are small end-arteries from the middle cerebral stem. They supply the basal ganglia and internal capsule and are the usual site of lacunar infarcts and hypertensive hemorrhage.
  • Anterior choroidal artery (from the internal carotid) supplies the posterior limb of the internal capsule and part of the optic tract.
  • Watershed (border) zones lie between two cortical territories. A global fall in perfusion (cardiac arrest, profound hypotension) infarcts them first. The anterior/middle cerebral border zone produces weakness of the proximal arm and thigh with the hand and face spared.
Exam trap: leg weakness worse than arm weakness points to the anterior cerebral artery, not the middle cerebral. Arm and face worse than leg points to the middle cerebral.
Pearl: with a hemispheric lesion the eyes look toward the lesion (away from the weak side), because the frontal eye field that drives gaze to the opposite side is lost.

sections.heading: Brainstem and lacunar stroke syndromes
sections.html:
Brainstem strokes combine cranial nerve signs on the side of the lesion with long-tract signs on the opposite side of the body (crossed findings). Two questions localise them: which cranial nerve is involved (level) and whether the lesion is medial or lateral (which tracts).

[[figure:s23e-fig0302]]

Medial versus lateral rules

  • Medial structures: the corticospinal tract (pyramid, basis pontis, cerebral peduncle), the medial lemniscus (vibration and position sense) and the motor nuclei of cranial nerves III, IV, VI and XII. Supplied by paramedian branches (anterior spinal artery in the medulla, basilar paramedian branches in the pons).
  • Lateral structures: the spinothalamic tract, the spinal trigeminal nucleus, descending sympathetic fibres, vestibular nuclei, cerebellar connections and the nucleus ambiguus. Supplied by circumferential branches (vertebral artery and PICA in the medulla, AICA in the lower pons, superior cerebellar artery in the upper pons).
SyndromeUsual vesselSame side as lesionOpposite side
Lateral medullaryVertebral artery or PICALoss of pain and temperature on the face; Horner syndrome; limb ataxia; hoarseness and dysphagia (nucleus ambiguus); vertigo, nystagmusLoss of pain and temperature on the body
Medial medullaryAnterior spinal artery or vertebral paramedian branchesTongue weakness; the tongue deviates toward the lesionArm and leg weakness; loss of vibration and position sense
Lateral inferior pontineAICAFacial palsy; hearing loss and vertigo (labyrinthine artery); facial sensory loss; Horner; ataxiaLoss of pain and temperature on the body
Medial pontineBasilar paramedian branchesAbducens palsy (lower pons)Arm and leg weakness
Midbrain (ventral)Posterior cerebral penetrating branchesOculomotor palsy (eye down and out, ptosis, dilated pupil)Arm and leg weakness

Basilar artery occlusion infarcts the ventral pons on both sides. The patient may be locked in: awake and aware but quadriplegic and unable to speak, with only vertical eye movements and blinking preserved (the midbrain gaze centres are spared). Partial basilar ischemia can fluctuate for hours before it completes.

Lacunar infarcts

Lacunes are small (under about 15 mm) deep infarcts caused by occlusion of a single penetrating artery. Chronic hypertension and diabetes thicken these vessel walls (lipohyalinosis and microatheroma). There is no cortical sign: no aphasia, neglect, field cut or gaze deviation.

Lacunar syndromeTypical site
Pure motor hemiparesis (face, arm and leg equally)Posterior limb of the internal capsule or basis pontis
Pure sensory strokeVentral posterolateral thalamus
Ataxic hemiparesisBasis pontis or internal capsule
Dysarthria with a clumsy handBasis pontis or genu of the internal capsule
Sensorimotor strokeThalamus and adjacent internal capsule
Exam trap: in the lateral medullary syndrome the face and the body lose pain sense on opposite sides. The spinal trigeminal tract carries uncrossed facial fibres, whereas the spinothalamic tract has already crossed in the spinal cord.
Pearl: first decide the level from the cranial nerve sign (midbrain III and IV, pons V to VIII, medulla IX to XII), then decide medial versus lateral from which body tracts are involved.

sections.heading: Pathology of cerebral ischemia and hemorrhage
sections.html:
Ischemic injury

Neurons depend on a continuous supply of glucose and oxygen. Within minutes of ischemia ATP falls, ion pumps fail and neurons depolarise. Glutamate release overstimulates NMDA receptors, and calcium entry activates proteases, lipases and free-radical injury (excitotoxicity). A core of tissue dies quickly; the surrounding penumbra is underperfused but salvageable if flow is restored, which is the rationale for reperfusion therapy.

Time after infarctionMicroscopic change
12–24 hoursRed (eosinophilic) neurons: shrunken cell body, hypereosinophilic cytoplasm, pyknotic nucleus
About 1–3 daysNeutrophils enter
About 3–7 daysMicroglia and macrophages ingest myelin debris (lipid-laden macrophages)
1–2 weeks onwardReactive astrocytes and new vessels at the edge of the lesion
MonthsA fluid-filled cyst bounded by glial scar

Brain infarcts undergo liquefactive necrosis, unlike the coagulative necrosis of most other organs. An embolic infarct can bleed into itself after the clot breaks up and flow returns (hemorrhagic transformation).

Embolic versus thrombotic infarction

  • Cardioembolic: atrial fibrillation, recent myocardial infarction with a left ventricular thrombus, endocarditis, a prosthetic valve. Onset is abrupt and maximal; several territories may be involved.
  • Large-artery atherosclerosis: plaque at the carotid bifurcation or in the vertebrobasilar system causes artery-to-artery emboli or in-situ thrombosis. It is often preceded by transient attacks in the same territory, such as transient monocular blindness (amaurosis fugax) from emboli to the ophthalmic artery.
  • Paradoxical embolism: a venous clot crosses a patent foramen ovale.
  • Arterial dissection: a tear in the intima lets blood track into the wall. It is a leading cause of stroke under 50 years and may follow minor neck trauma.

Intracerebral hemorrhage

FeatureHypertensive hemorrhageCerebral amyloid angiopathy
VesselsSmall penetrating arteries with lipohyalinosis and tiny wall dilatations (Charcot–Bouchard microaneurysms)Beta-amyloid deposited in the walls of cortical and leptomeningeal vessels
LocationDeep: putamen (most common), thalamus, pons, cerebellumLobar (cortex and subcortical white matter)
PatientsLong-standing poorly controlled hypertensionOlder adults, often normotensive, recurrent hemorrhages, cognitive decline
CluesLipohyalinosis on histologyApple-green birefringence with Congo red stain; MRI shows many cortical microbleeds

Other causes: arteriovenous malformations (younger patients, seizures), anticoagulant therapy, sympathomimetic drugs such as cocaine and amphetamines, tumours, and coagulopathy.

Subarachnoid hemorrhage

Most nontraumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage comes from a ruptured saccular (berry) aneurysm. These develop at branch points of the circle of Willis, where the media is deficient. The most common site is the anterior communicating artery junction. Risk factors: hypertension, smoking, heavy alcohol use, a family history, autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, and connective tissue disorders such as Ehlers–Danlos (vascular type).

  • A posterior communicating artery aneurysm can compress the oculomotor nerve. The parasympathetic fibres lie on the outside of the nerve, so the pupil dilates early.
  • About 3–14 days after the bleed, vasospasm of arteries bathed in blood can cause delayed cerebral ischemia.
  • Blood in the subarachnoid space can block CSF absorption and cause hydrocephalus.
Exam trap: a lobar hemorrhage in an older normotensive person suggests amyloid angiopathy; a putaminal hemorrhage suggests hypertension.

sections.heading: Consciousness, coma and hypoxic-ischemic brain injury
sections.html:
Arousal depends on the ascending reticular activating system: neurons in the tegmentum of the upper pons and midbrain project through the thalamus to the cortex, aided by cholinergic, noradrenergic, serotonergic, histaminergic and orexin (hypocretin) pathways. Awareness depends on the cerebral hemispheres. Coma therefore needs either damage to the upper brainstem tegmentum or thalamus, or diffuse dysfunction of both hemispheres (metabolic, toxic, anoxic or widespread structural injury). A one-sided hemispheric lesion does not cause coma unless it compresses the brainstem.

States of impaired consciousness

StateEyes open and sleep–wake cyclesAwarenessUsual lesion
ComaNoNoneUpper brainstem or both hemispheres
Unresponsive wakefulness (vegetative state)YesNone: reflex responses onlyDiffuse cortical or thalamic injury with a working brainstem
Minimally conscious stateYesInconsistent but reproducible signs (follows a command, tracks with the eyes)Less severe diffuse injury
Locked-in syndromeYesFullVentral pons (basilar occlusion) or severe peripheral paralysis
Death by neurologic criteriaNoNone; no brainstem reflexes or breathingIrreversible loss of all brain function

Brainstem signs used to localise coma

  • Pupils: small reactive pupils suggest a metabolic cause or opioids; pinpoint pupils with coma and quadriplegia suggest a pontine lesion (sympathetic pathways are interrupted); a single fixed dilated pupil suggests oculomotor compression by uncal herniation; midposition fixed pupils suggest midbrain damage.
  • Oculocephalic reflex: in a comatose patient with an intact brainstem the eyes move opposite to a head turn and seem to stay fixed in space.
  • Cold caloric test: with an intact brainstem but nonfunctioning cortex, cold water in one ear makes both eyes drift slowly toward that ear with no corrective fast phase. An awake person instead develops nystagmus with the fast phase away from the cold ear. No movement means the brainstem pathway is lost.
  • Breathing: the drive to breathe comes from medullary centres; central chemoreceptors on the ventral medulla sense the hydrogen ion concentration of CSF, which follows arterial carbon dioxide.

Hypoxic-ischemic injury

Global loss of perfusion (cardiac arrest) or oxygen damages the most metabolically active and glutamate-sensitive neurons first:

  • pyramidal neurons of the hippocampus, CA1 sector;
  • cerebellar Purkinje cells;
  • neocortical pyramidal neurons in layers 3, 5 and 6, which gives a band-like (laminar) necrosis;
  • the striatum, especially in neonates;
  • arterial border zones, when the cause is low perfusion pressure rather than low oxygen content.

The brainstem is relatively resistant, which is why a patient may recover sleep–wake cycles and brainstem reflexes without awareness.

Exam trap: a locked-in patient is fully aware. Always test vertical eye movement and blinking to command before calling a patient unresponsive.

sections.heading: Head trauma: skull, hematomas and diffuse axonal injury
sections.html:
The brain is cushioned by CSF and tethered by vessels and nerves. Trauma injures it through direct impact (contusion under the blow and on the opposite side, coup–contrecoup) and through rotational acceleration (shearing).

Extra-axial hematomas

FeatureEpidural hematomaSubdural hematoma
SpaceBetween the skull and the duraBetween the dura and the arachnoid
Usual vesselMiddle meningeal artery, torn by a fracture of the squamous temporal bone near the pterionBridging veins running from the cortex to the dural sinuses
WhoYoung adults after a blow to the side of the headOlder adults with brain atrophy (stretched veins), people with heavy alcohol use, anticoagulated patients, infants with abusive head trauma
CourseBrief loss of consciousness, a lucid interval, then rapid decline as arterial bleeding expandsAcute after severe trauma, or chronic: weeks of headache, confusion or falls after a minor bump
CT shapeBiconvex (lens-shaped); does not cross suture lines because the dura is tightly attached at suturesCrescent-shaped; crosses suture lines but not the midline (falx)

On CT, blood is bright (hyperdense) when acute and becomes isodense and then dark (hypodense) over about 1–3 weeks. Chronic subdural hematomas can rebleed from fragile membranes and show mixed density.

Parenchymal injury

  • Contusions are bruises of the cortex, most often on the frontal poles and the anterior temporal lobes, where the brain strikes the bony ridges of the skull base.
  • Diffuse axonal injury follows rotational acceleration and deceleration, as in high-speed motor vehicle collisions. Axons shear at the grey–white junction, in the corpus callosum and in the dorsolateral brainstem. CT may look nearly normal despite deep coma; MRI shows small hemorrhages. Microscopy shows axonal swellings (spheroids), which stain for beta-amyloid precursor protein within hours.
  • Concussion is a transient disturbance of brain function after trauma, without a structural lesion on standard imaging. It reflects ion flux, glutamate release and an energy mismatch rather than cell death.

Skull fractures

Signs of a basilar skull fracture: bruising behind the ear (mastoid ecchymosis), bruising around both eyes, blood behind the tympanic membrane, and CSF leak from the nose or ear. A depressed fracture may need surgical elevation.

Exam trap: the lucid interval is classic for epidural hematoma but is absent in many patients. Decide on CT shape: lens means epidural, crescent means subdural.

sections.heading: Intracranial pressure, herniation and hydrocephalus
sections.html:
The skull is a rigid box holding brain, blood and CSF. When one component grows (a hematoma, edema, a tumour, trapped CSF), the others must shrink to keep pressure normal: CSF moves into the spinal sac and venous blood leaves. Once this reserve is used up, a small extra volume causes a steep rise in intracranial pressure (ICP).

Cerebral perfusion pressure = mean arterial pressure − ICP. Normal autoregulation keeps cerebral blood flow steady across a wide range of perfusion pressures by adjusting arteriolar tone. Arterial carbon dioxide is a powerful regulator: hypercapnia dilates cerebral arterioles and raises blood volume and ICP; hypocapnia constricts them.

Signs of raised ICP: headache worse lying down or on waking, vomiting, papilledema, an abducens palsy (a false localising sign from stretching of the long nerve), and falling consciousness. The Cushing reflex (hypertension, bradycardia and irregular breathing) is a late sign of brainstem compression.

[[figure:s23e-fig0303]]

Herniation syndromes

TypeWhat movesStructures compressed and signs
SubfalcineCingulate gyrus under the falxAnterior cerebral artery: infarction with weakness of the opposite leg
Uncal (lateral transtentorial)Medial temporal lobe over the tentorial edgeSame-side oculomotor nerve: fixed dilated pupil, then ptosis and a down-and-out eye. Posterior cerebral artery: occipital infarct. Opposite cerebral peduncle pushed against the tentorium: weakness on the same side as the mass (a false localising sign). Midbrain hemorrhages (Duret hemorrhages) from stretched perforating arteries.
Central (downward transtentorial)Diencephalon and midbrain through the tentorial notchSmall then midposition pupils, falling consciousness, decorticate then decerebrate posturing
TonsillarCerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnumMedulla: respiratory and cardiovascular arrest. Lumbar puncture in a patient with a posterior fossa or large supratentorial mass can provoke it.

CSF circulation and hydrocephalus

The choroid plexus secretes about 500 mL of CSF a day. CSF flows from the lateral ventricles through the foramina of Monro, the third ventricle, the cerebral aqueduct and the fourth ventricle, exits through its foramina into the subarachnoid space, and is absorbed mainly through the arachnoid granulations into the venous sinuses. Carbonic anhydrase in the choroid plexus supports secretion.

  • Obstructive (noncommunicating): flow is blocked within the ventricles, for example aqueductal stenosis, a colloid cyst at the foramen of Monro, or a posterior fossa tumour. Ventricles upstream of the block enlarge.
  • Communicating: CSF reaches the subarachnoid space but is not absorbed, for example after meningitis or subarachnoid hemorrhage scars the arachnoid granulations. All ventricles enlarge.
  • Normal pressure hydrocephalus: a communicating hydrocephalus of older adults with intermittently raised pressure. The triad is a wide-based, shuffling, magnetic gait, urinary urgency and incontinence, and cognitive slowing. Stretching of periventricular fibres to the legs and bladder explains the first two.
  • Ex vacuo enlargement: ventricles enlarge because brain tissue is lost (Alzheimer disease, chronic alcohol use); pressure is normal and this is not true hydrocephalus.

Idiopathic intracranial hypertension

Raised ICP with no mass, no hydrocephalus and normal CSF composition. It typically affects women of reproductive age with obesity or recent weight gain. Some drugs are associated: tetracyclines, high-dose vitamin A and other retinoids, and growth hormone. Headache, pulsatile tinnitus, brief visual obscurations and papilledema are typical, and untreated papilledema can cause permanent visual loss. Acetazolamide, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, lowers CSF production.

Exam trap: hyperventilation lowers ICP within minutes by constricting cerebral vessels, but prolonged hypocapnia can cause ischemia. It is a short bridge, not a treatment.

title: Neurology · Stroke, coma and head injury

sections.heading: Acute ischemic stroke: the first hours
sections.html:
Treat suspected stroke as an emergency in which every minute counts. The key times are when the patient was last known well (not when symptoms were found) and the time to imaging and treatment.

Immediate assessment

  1. Airway, breathing and circulation; check the fingerstick glucose at once, because hypoglycemia can mimic stroke.
  2. Grade severity with a standard scale such as the NIH Stroke Scale.
  3. Noncontrast head CT to exclude hemorrhage. Early ischemic changes are often absent. CT angiography of the head and neck is done at the same visit when the patient might be a candidate for thrombectomy, and should not delay thrombolysis.
  4. Ask about anticoagulants, recent surgery, bleeding and prior hemorrhage. Do not wait for coagulation results before thrombolysis unless a bleeding disorder or anticoagulant use is suspected.

Intravenous thrombolysis

  • Give an intravenous thrombolytic, alteplase or tenecteplase, to eligible adults with a disabling deficit who can be treated within 4.5 hours of last known well.
  • Blood pressure must be lowered below 185/110 mm Hg before treatment (for example, labetalol or nicardipine) and kept below 180/105 mm Hg for the next 24 hours.
  • Important exclusions: hemorrhage on CT, a large established infarct, recent intracranial hemorrhage, head trauma or stroke within 3 months, intracranial neoplasm or recent intracranial or spinal surgery, active internal bleeding, platelets below 100,000/mm³, INR above 1.7, and therapeutic anticoagulation with a direct oral anticoagulant in the last 48 hours.
  • The main risk is symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage. New headache, vomiting or worsening during or after the infusion means: stop the infusion, scan, and reverse the drug.
  • No antiplatelet or anticoagulant drug is given for 24 hours after thrombolysis, until imaging excludes hemorrhage.

Endovascular thrombectomy

Mechanical clot retrieval improves outcomes in large-vessel occlusion of the anterior circulation (internal carotid or proximal middle cerebral artery). It is standard within 6 hours of last known well, and in selected patients up to 24 hours when imaging shows a small core with salvageable tissue. Thrombectomy is also used for basilar occlusion. Eligible patients receive thrombolysis and thrombectomy; one does not replace the other.

When thrombolysis is not given

  • Allow permissive hypertension: treat only if blood pressure exceeds about 220/120 mm Hg, because the penumbra depends on perfusion pressure.
  • Start aspirin within 24–48 hours once hemorrhage is excluded.
  • Keep glucose roughly 140–180 mg/dL, treat fever, screen swallowing before oral intake, and prevent venous thromboembolism with intermittent pneumatic compression.

Complications to anticipate

Large middle cerebral infarcts swell over 2–5 days (malignant edema) and can herniate; decompressive hemicraniectomy saves lives in selected patients. Cerebellar infarcts can swell and compress the fourth ventricle and brainstem, needing surgical decompression. Aspiration pneumonia is common.

Exam trap: do not lower blood pressure aggressively in a stroke patient who is not receiving thrombolysis. Do not give heparin for acute ischemic stroke to improve outcome.

furtherReading.label: StatPearls: Acute Stroke: Evaluation and Management (NCBI Bookshelf)

sections.heading: Transient ischemic attack and secondary prevention of stroke
sections.html:
A transient ischemic attack (TIA) is a brief episode of focal neurological dysfunction caused by ischemia, without infarction on imaging. Symptoms usually last minutes. The risk of stroke is highest in the first 48 hours, so a TIA needs urgent workup, ideally within a day.

Workup of TIA and ischemic stroke

  • Brain MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging (shows small infarcts) or CT.
  • Vessel imaging of the head and neck: CT angiography, MR angiography or carotid duplex ultrasound.
  • ECG and cardiac rhythm monitoring for atrial fibrillation, with prolonged monitoring when no cause is found.
  • Echocardiography for a cardiac source (thrombus, valve disease, patent foramen ovale).
  • Blood tests: complete blood count, glucose and hemoglobin A1c, lipids.

Risk scores such as ABCD2 (age, blood pressure, clinical features, duration, diabetes) help to judge short-term risk; a score of 4 or more marks a high-risk TIA.

Antithrombotic therapy

SituationPreferred therapy
Minor noncardioembolic stroke (low NIH Stroke Scale score) or high-risk TIA, seen earlyAspirin plus clopidogrel started within 24 hours and continued for about 21 days, then a single antiplatelet drug long term
Other noncardioembolic ischemic stroke or TIAA single antiplatelet drug: aspirin, clopidogrel, or aspirin with extended-release dipyridamole
Atrial fibrillationAn oral anticoagulant, preferably a direct oral anticoagulant (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, dabigatran); warfarin if there is a mechanical valve or moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis. Start within days for most strokes, later for large infarcts.

Dual antiplatelet therapy is time-limited: beyond the first weeks, the bleeding risk outweighs the benefit.

Carotid stenosis

  • Symptomatic internal carotid stenosis of 70–99% (TIA, amaurosis fugax or nondisabling stroke in that territory): carotid endarterectomy, ideally within 2 weeks of the event. Stenting is an alternative in selected patients.
  • Symptomatic 50–69% stenosis: endarterectomy can be considered, depending on patient factors.
  • Stenosis below 50% and complete occlusion: medical therapy only.
  • Asymptomatic stenosis: intensive medical therapy is the foundation; revascularisation is reserved for selected patients.

Risk-factor control

  • Blood pressure target below about 130/80 mm Hg for most patients, started once the acute phase has passed.
  • High-intensity statin, aiming for LDL cholesterol below 70 mg/dL; add ezetimibe if needed.
  • Diabetes control, smoking cessation, exercise, a Mediterranean-style diet, and limiting alcohol.
  • Patent foramen ovale closure for adults up to about 60 years with an embolic-appearing stroke and no other cause.
Exam trap: an acute stroke with atrial fibrillation does not need heparin while waiting; give aspirin until it is safe to start the oral anticoagulant.

sections.heading: Hemorrhagic stroke, cerebral venous thrombosis and arterial dissection
sections.html:
Intracerebral hemorrhage

Sudden focal deficit with headache, vomiting and falling consciousness suggests hemorrhage, but only imaging separates it from infarction. Noncontrast CT shows acute blood as bright. The hematoma often grows during the first hours, which drives early worsening.

  • Blood pressure: in patients with a systolic pressure of about 150–220 mm Hg, lowering it promptly to around 140 mm Hg is reasonable; avoid driving it below about 130 mm Hg.
  • Reverse anticoagulation at once:
    • warfarin: four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate plus intravenous vitamin K (prothrombin complex works faster than plasma);
    • dabigatran: idarucizumab;
    • factor Xa inhibitors (apixaban, rivaroxaban): andexanet alfa or four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate;
    • unfractionated heparin: protamine.
  • Do not give platelet transfusions to patients taking antiplatelet drugs unless they need surgery. Do not give prophylactic antiseizure drugs or glucocorticoids.
  • Surgery: urgent evacuation for a cerebellar hemorrhage with neurological decline, brainstem compression or hydrocephalus; external ventricular drainage for hydrocephalus.
  • CT or MR angiography in younger patients and in lobar or unusual hemorrhages, to look for a vascular malformation or aneurysm.

Aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage

Classic history: a sudden thunderclap headache that reaches maximal intensity within a minute, often described as the worst ever, with vomiting, neck stiffness, a brief loss of consciousness or a seizure. Some patients have a smaller warning (sentinel) bleed days earlier.

  1. Noncontrast CT first. Its sensitivity is very high in the first 6 hours and falls after that.
  2. If CT is negative but suspicion remains (particularly beyond 6 hours), do a lumbar puncture: xanthochromia (yellow CSF from hemoglobin breakdown) or red cells that do not clear from tube 1 to tube 4 support hemorrhage.
  3. CT angiography to find the aneurysm; catheter angiography when CT angiography is unclear.

Management in a neurocritical care unit:

  • Secure the aneurysm early, by endovascular coiling or surgical clipping, to prevent rebleeding, which carries a high mortality and is most likely in the first day.
  • Until it is secured, keep systolic blood pressure moderately controlled (for example, below about 160 mm Hg) and reverse any anticoagulant.
  • Oral nimodipine for 21 days improves outcome by reducing delayed cerebral ischemia.
  • Maintain normal blood volume; do not fluid-restrict. Hyponatremia is common (from cerebral salt wasting or SIADH) and is corrected with saline.
  • Watch for delayed cerebral ischemia from vasospasm (about days 3–14: new deficit or falling consciousness), acute hydrocephalus (external ventricular drain), seizures and cardiac dysfunction.

Cerebral venous thrombosis

Thrombosis of the dural sinuses or cortical veins. Risk factors: pregnancy and the postpartum period, estrogen-containing contraceptives, inherited and acquired thrombophilias, cancer, dehydration and local infection. It presents with headache (often progressive), signs of raised ICP such as papilledema, seizures and focal deficits; venous infarcts are often hemorrhagic and do not follow arterial territories. Diagnose with MR venography or CT venography. Treat with anticoagulation (low-molecular-weight or unfractionated heparin) even when there is a hemorrhagic venous infarct, followed by an oral anticoagulant for months.

Cervical artery dissection

Neck or face pain and headache with ischemic symptoms in a younger adult, sometimes after neck trauma or chiropractic manipulation. Carotid dissection can cause a partial Horner syndrome (ptosis and miosis) on the same side. Vertebral dissection causes posterior neck pain with brainstem or cerebellar signs. Diagnose with CT or MR angiography. Give antithrombotic therapy: antiplatelet and anticoagulant drugs give similar results. Thrombolysis is still given to eligible patients with an acute stroke.

Exam trap: a negative CT more than 6 hours after a thunderclap headache does not exclude subarachnoid hemorrhage. The next step is lumbar puncture, not discharge.

furtherReading.label: StatPearls: Cerebral Venous Sinus Thrombosis (NCBI Bookshelf)

sections.heading: The unresponsive patient, recovery after cardiac arrest and death by neurologic criteria
sections.html:
First minutes with a comatose patient

  1. Airway, breathing, circulation. Intubate to protect the airway when the Glasgow Coma Scale score is 8 or less or airway reflexes are poor. Immobilise the cervical spine if trauma is possible.
  2. Fingerstick glucose; give intravenous dextrose for hypoglycemia. Give thiamine alongside dextrose when alcohol use disorder or malnutrition is possible; do not delay glucose to do so.
  3. Naloxone when the picture suggests opioids: small pupils and slow, shallow breathing.
  4. Noncontrast head CT for a structural cause: hemorrhage, a large infarct, a mass or hydrocephalus.
  5. Laboratory tests: electrolytes including sodium and calcium, renal and liver function, blood gas, toxicology, ammonia, thyroid function and cultures as indicated. Lumbar puncture if CNS infection is possible and imaging shows no contraindication; do not delay antibiotics.
  6. EEG when nonconvulsive status epilepticus is possible (fluctuating consciousness, subtle twitching, or no explanation for coma).

The Glasgow Coma Scale sums eye opening (1–4), the best verbal response (1–5) and the best motor response (1–6); scores run from 3 to 15.

Psychogenic unresponsiveness

Clues: the eyes are held shut and resist opening, the raised hand falls away from the face, and cold caloric testing produces nystagmus, which shows the cortex is awake. Avoid labelling it until organic causes are excluded.

After cardiac arrest

  • Comatose survivors need temperature control: actively prevent fever for at least the first 72 hours.
  • Avoid hypotension and hypoxemia, and treat seizures.
  • Do not decide prognosis early. Prognosis is assessed no sooner than about 72 hours after the arrest (after sedation has cleared and normothermia is reached), using several tests together: examination (pupillary and corneal reflexes, motor response), EEG, somatosensory evoked potentials, neuron-specific enolase and MRI. No single sign decides it.

Death by neurologic criteria (brain death)

Brain death is the irreversible loss of all brain function, including the brainstem. A person who meets the criteria is legally dead in the United States. The 2023 adult and pediatric consensus guideline sets out the process:

  • Prerequisites: a known catastrophic cause that explains the findings; enough time since the injury (at least 24 hours after hypoxic-ischemic injury from cardiac arrest); exclusion of confounders: core temperature at least 36 °C, adequate blood pressure, no sedating or paralysing drugs still acting, and no severe metabolic or endocrine disturbance.
  • Examination: coma with no response to noxious stimuli above the spinal cord; absent pupillary, corneal, oculocephalic, oculovestibular (cold caloric), gag and cough reflexes.
  • Apnea test: no breathing effort while arterial carbon dioxide rises to at least 60 mm Hg and at least 20 mm Hg above baseline, with acidemia.
  • Ancillary tests (for example, a test of cerebral blood flow) are used only when part of the examination or the apnea test cannot be completed or interpreted. They do not replace the examination.

Spinal reflexes, such as triple flexion of the legs or a plantar response, can persist and are compatible with brain death. Family consent is not needed to determine death, but the family should be told clearly and kindly. Organ donation is discussed separately by the organ procurement organisation.

Exam trap: a hypothermic or recently sedated patient cannot be examined for brain death yet. Correct the confounder first.

sections.heading: Traumatic brain injury: emergency care, hematomas and concussion
sections.html:
Initial care

  • Trauma primary survey; protect the cervical spine. Grade severity with the Glasgow Coma Scale: 13–15 mild, 9–12 moderate, 3–8 severe.
  • Prevent secondary injury: even one episode of hypotension or hypoxia worsens outcome. Intubate for a score of 8 or less.
  • Noncontrast head CT for moderate and severe injury. In mild injury, validated decision rules select patients for CT: a low or falling coma score, suspected open, depressed or basilar skull fracture, repeated vomiting, older age, a dangerous mechanism, or amnesia for events before the impact. Patients taking anticoagulants or with a bleeding disorder need CT even after a minor injury.
  • Glucocorticoids are harmful in traumatic brain injury and are not given.
  • In severe injury, a short course of an antiseizure drug lowers the risk of early seizures in the first week.

Hematomas

LesionManagement
Epidural hematomaUrgent craniotomy and evacuation when it is large, causes midline shift, or the patient is deteriorating; small ones in alert patients can be watched with repeat CT
Acute subdural hematomaCraniotomy when thick, causing shift, or with neurological decline; otherwise close observation. Reverse anticoagulation.
Chronic subdural hematomaSymptomatic collections are drained through burr holes; small ones without symptoms can be observed. Review the need for antithrombotic drugs.

Concussion

Symptoms after a blow or jolt: headache, dizziness, confusion, amnesia, nausea, light and noise sensitivity, slowed thinking, irritability and sleep change. Loss of consciousness is not required.

  • An athlete with a suspected concussion is removed from play and does not return the same day, even if symptoms settle quickly.
  • CT is needed only for red flags: worsening headache, repeated vomiting, focal deficits, seizure, falling consciousness, or anticoagulation.
  • After a short period of relative rest (about 1–2 days), light activity that does not worsen symptoms is encouraged; long strict rest in a dark room delays recovery.
  • Return to school comes first, then a graded, stepwise return to sport, moving to the next step only when symptom-free, with medical clearance before full contact.
  • A second injury before recovery can cause severe brain swelling in young people (second impact syndrome). Symptoms lasting beyond about 4 weeks call for specialist assessment.

Disorders after brain injury

  • Central diabetes insipidus from pituitary stalk or hypothalamic injury: large volumes of dilute urine with rising serum sodium; treat with desmopressin.
  • SIADH: hyponatremia with concentrated urine in a euvolemic patient.
  • Post-traumatic epilepsy, chronic headache, mood disorders and cognitive change.
Exam trap: an older adult on an anticoagulant who bumps the head needs a CT even with a normal examination, and may need a repeat scan for delayed bleeding.

sections.heading: Managing raised intracranial pressure; idiopathic intracranial hypertension and normal pressure hydrocephalus
sections.html:
Raised ICP in the critically ill

Recognise it from a falling level of consciousness, a new dilated pupil, posturing, or the Cushing reflex (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing). Treat in steps while arranging definitive treatment of the cause:

  1. General measures: head of the bed at about 30°, head midline with no tight collar (venous drainage), normal temperature, normal sodium or above, treat pain and agitation, avoid hypotension and hypoxia.
  2. Hyperosmolar therapy: hypertonic saline or mannitol draws water out of the brain. Mannitol is an osmotic diuretic, so watch volume status and serum osmolality.
  3. CSF drainage through an external ventricular drain, which also measures ICP.
  4. Brief hyperventilation (target arterial carbon dioxide about 30–35 mm Hg) only as a bridge for impending herniation.
  5. Refractory cases: deeper sedation, barbiturate coma, and decompressive craniectomy.
  6. Treat the cause: evacuate a hematoma, resect or debulk a mass, give dexamethasone for vasogenic edema around a tumour or abscess (not for trauma or stroke).

Do not treat the hypertension of the Cushing reflex with antihypertensives: it maintains cerebral perfusion. Do not do a lumbar puncture when a mass or herniation is suspected.

Idiopathic intracranial hypertension

  • Who: typically women of reproductive age with obesity or recent weight gain; some cases follow tetracyclines, retinoids, high-dose vitamin A or growth hormone.
  • Symptoms: daily headache, pulsatile tinnitus, brief visual greying when standing, double vision from an abducens palsy. Papilledema is the key sign.
  • Diagnosis: first MRI of the brain with MR venography to exclude a mass, hydrocephalus and venous sinus thrombosis (MRI may show an empty sella or flattened globes). Then lumbar puncture in the lateral decubitus position: opening pressure above 250 mm H₂O in adults (normal 70–180 mm H₂O) with normal CSF cell count, protein and glucose.
  • Treatment: weight loss and stopping a causative drug, plus acetazolamide. Formal visual field testing is the key follow-up measure. Rapid or severe visual loss needs urgent surgery: optic nerve sheath fenestration, CSF shunting or venous sinus stenting.

Normal pressure hydrocephalus

  • Who and what: an older adult with a gait disorder (broad-based, slow, feet that seem stuck to the floor), urinary urgency or incontinence, and cognitive slowing, usually with the gait problem first.
  • Imaging: ventricles enlarged out of proportion to sulcal widening.
  • Next step: a high-volume lumbar puncture (tap test) or lumbar drain with gait assessment before and after; improvement predicts benefit from a shunt.
  • Treatment: a ventriculoperitoneal shunt. Gait responds best; cognition responds least.
Exam trap: in suspected idiopathic intracranial hypertension do imaging before the lumbar puncture, and in normal pressure hydrocephalus remember that the tap test, not a drug, is the next step.

furtherReading.label: StatPearls: Idiopathic Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NCBI Bookshelf)

title: Nervous system · Spinal cord, cranial and peripheral nerves, pain pathways

sections.heading: Spinal cord tracts and the classic cord lesion syndromes
sections.html:
Three long tracts explain almost every spinal cord localisation question. Learn where each one crosses, because that decides whether a deficit appears on the same side as the lesion or the opposite side.

TractCarriesFirst synapse / crossingSide of deficit below a one-sided cord lesion

Lateral corticospinal tractVoluntary movementCrosses in the pyramidal decussation of the caudal medulla; synapses on ventral horn motor neuronsSame side (upper motor neuron signs)

Lesion patterns

SyndromeStructures hitFindingsTypical cause

Pearl: nitrous oxide inactivates the cobalamin cofactor, so a recreational user can develop subacute combined degeneration with a normal serum B12. Elevated methylmalonic acid and homocysteine reveal the functional deficiency.
Exam trap: after a hemisection the pain and temperature loss is on the side opposite the weak leg. Students often put all deficits on one side.

The spinothalamic tract is laminated with sacral fibres outermost. A lesion that expands from the centre of the cord can therefore spare perineal sensation (sacral sparing), while an extrinsic compression affects the sacral fibres early.

sections.heading: Roots, conus medullaris and cauda equina; spinal cord autonomic physiology
sections.html:
The adult spinal cord ends as the conus medullaris at about the L1–L2 vertebral level. Below it, the lumbar and sacral roots run down the lumbar cistern as the cauda equina. A lumbar puncture at L3–L4 or L4–L5 therefore enters subarachnoid space that holds only roots, which slide away from the needle. The needle passes skin, supraspinous and interspinous ligaments, ligamentum flavum, epidural space, dura and arachnoid.

In the cervical spine a root exits above the vertebra of the same number, so a C5–C6 disc compresses C6. In the lumbar spine, a typical posterolateral disc herniation compresses the root that exits one level lower: an L4–L5 herniation affects L5.

Conus versus cauda equina

Bladder and bowelEarlyLater
Motor signsMixed upper and lower motor neuron; ankle jerks may be lost, knee jerks keptLower motor neuron only: flaccid, areflexic, asymmetric

Autonomic effects of a high cord injury

  • Spinal shock: right after injury, flaccid paralysis and absent reflexes below the lesion. Over days to weeks, reflexes return and become brisk with spasticity.
  • Neurogenic shock: injury above about T6 cuts the descending drive to sympathetic neurons in the thoracolumbar cord. Vasodilation lowers blood pressure, and unopposed vagal tone slows the heart, so hypotension comes with bradycardia and warm skin.
  • Autonomic dysreflexia: in a chronic injury at or above T6, a stimulus below the lesion (full bladder, impacted stool, pressure sore) triggers a spinal sympathetic reflex. Splanchnic vessels constrict and blood pressure surges. Baroreceptors sense it and raise vagal output (bradycardia) and cause vasodilation above the lesion (flushing, sweating, headache), but the inhibitory signals cannot descend past the injury.
Exam trap: neurogenic shock causes bradycardia; hemorrhagic shock causes tachycardia. A trauma patient can have both, so look for the cord level.

sections.html:
NerveMusclesPalsyAnatomical points
Oculomotor (III)Medial, superior and inferior recti; inferior oblique; levator palpebrae; parasympathetic fibres to the sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscleEye down and out, ptosis; a dilated, poorly reactive pupil if the parasympathetic fibres are involvedNucleus in the midbrain; the nerve leaves between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries and runs next to the posterior communicating artery

Long, thin course: vulnerable to head trauma
Abducens (VI)Lateral rectusHorizontal diplopia worse at distance and toward the affected side; eye turned inLong course up the clivus: can be stretched by raised intracranial pressure, a false localising sign. Its nucleus sits under the facial colliculus with the facial nerve fibres looping over it

Two kinds of oculomotor palsy

The pupillomotor fibres travel in the outer layer of the oculomotor nerve, close to its blood supply from the surface. A compressing lesion, such as an aneurysm of the posterior communicating artery or a herniating uncus, presses from outside, so the pupil is dilated early. Diabetic or hypertensive microvascular ischaemia damages the core of the nerve, the watershed of the small vessels that supply it, so the pupil is usually spared. The ischaemic palsy is often painful and tends to recover within about 3 months.

Cavernous sinus

The cavernous sinus on each side of the sella holds the internal carotid artery with its sympathetic plexus. The oculomotor and trochlear nerves and the ophthalmic (V1) and maxillary (V2) divisions of the trigeminal nerve lie in its lateral wall. The abducens nerve runs through the sinus beside the artery, so an aneurysm of the cavernous carotid often affects it first. A cavernous sinus lesion combines ophthalmoplegia with numbness of the forehead or cheek and sometimes a Horner syndrome; the mandibular division (V3) is spared because it leaves through the foramen ovale below the sinus.

Pearl: the facial veins and pterygoid plexus drain to the cavernous sinus without effective valves, so infections of the central face or sphenoid sinus can spread there (septic cavernous sinus thrombosis).
Exam trap: a pupil-involving third nerve palsy is an aneurysm until proved otherwise; do not attribute it to diabetes.

sections.heading: Trigeminal and lower cranial nerves; brainstem nuclei and foramina
sections.html:
Trigeminal nerve (V)

  • Sensation of the face, scalp to the vertex, cornea, nasal and oral mucosa, anterior two-thirds of the tongue (general sensation) and most of the dura.
  • The mandibular division (V3) also carries motor fibres to the muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, pterygoids), tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini.
  • Exits: V1 through the superior orbital fissure, V2 through the foramen rotundum, V3 through the foramen ovale.
  • A lower motor neuron lesion of V3 makes the jaw deviate toward the weak side on opening, because the opposite lateral pterygoid pushes the jaw across.

Glossopharyngeal (IX), vagus (X), accessory (XI) and hypoglossal (XII)

NerveMain functionsLesion sign

The recurrent laryngeal nerves supply all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except the cricothyroid. The left nerve hooks under the aortic arch, so a thoracic aortic aneurysm, a mass in the aortopulmonary window or an enlarged left atrium can cause hoarseness. Both nerves are at risk in thyroid surgery.

Brainstem nuclei

Motor nuclei lie close to the midline; sensory nuclei lie more laterally. Level matters: III and IV in the midbrain; V (motor), VI, VII and VIII in the pons; IX, X, XI (in part) and XII in the medulla. A lesion that involves a cranial nerve nucleus on one side and the descending corticospinal fibres gives a crossed picture: cranial nerve signs on the side of the lesion and limb weakness on the other side.

Exam trap: the uvula moves away from a vagus lesion but the tongue moves toward a hypoglossal lesion. Both point at the weak muscle being overpowered by the healthy side.

NerveTypical injuryDeficit

Pearl: foot drop with weak inversion or weak hip abduction is an L5 root problem, not a fibular nerve problem.

Patterns of peripheral nerve disease

  • Length-dependent (distal symmetric) polyneuropathy: the longest axons fail first, so symptoms start in the toes and rise to the shins before the fingers are involved, giving a stocking-and-glove pattern. Ankle jerks are lost early. Causes: diabetes (the most common), alcohol, vitamin B12 deficiency, hypothyroidism, chronic kidney disease, chemotherapy (vincristine, platinum drugs, taxanes), isoniazid without pyridoxine, HIV, paraproteins and amyloid.
  • Mononeuropathy: one nerve, from compression or entrapment.
  • Mononeuritis multiplex: separate named nerves fail one after another, often painfully, on different sides. It suggests ischaemia of the vasa nervorum from vasculitis (polyarteritis nodosa, ANCA-associated vasculitis, cryoglobulinaemia), and sometimes diabetes, leprosy or sarcoidosis.
  • Demyelinating versus axonal: nerve conduction studies separate them. Demyelination slows conduction and causes conduction block; axonal loss reduces the amplitude of the response with near-normal speed.

Hereditary neuropathy. Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A, the most common form, is a demyelinating neuropathy caused by duplication of the PMP22 gene and is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait. It presents in childhood or adolescence with high arches, hammer toes, distal leg wasting and foot drop, with little sensory complaint.

Diabetic neuropathy results from chronic hyperglycaemia: glucose shunted through the polyol pathway (aldose reductase → sorbitol), advanced glycation end products, oxidative stress and microvascular disease of the nerve. Small fibres (pain, temperature) and large fibres (vibration, position) are both affected, which puts the insensate foot at risk of ulcers and Charcot joints.

sections.heading: Pain pathways and the pharmacology of neuropathic pain
sections.html:
From receptor to cortex

  1. Transduction: free nerve endings respond to heat (TRPV1 channels, also opened by capsaicin), cold, pressure and chemicals released by injured tissue (bradykinin, prostaglandins, H+, ATP). Prostaglandin E2 sensitises the endings; this is where NSAIDs act.
  2. First-order fibres: thinly myelinated A-delta fibres carry fast, sharp, well-localised first pain; unmyelinated C fibres carry slow, burning, poorly localised second pain. Cell bodies are in the dorsal root ganglia (trigeminal ganglion for the face).
  3. Dorsal horn: the fibres release glutamate and substance P onto second-order neurons in the superficial laminae. These axons cross in the anterior white commissure and ascend as the spinothalamic tract to the ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus of the thalamus; facial pain travels via the spinal trigeminal nucleus to the ventral posteromedial (VPM) nucleus. Thalamic neurons project to the somatosensory cortex, while parallel paths to the insula and anterior cingulate add the unpleasantness.
  4. Modulation: large A-beta touch fibres excite inhibitory interneurons in the dorsal horn (the basis of rubbing a bump). Descending fibres from the periaqueductal grey relay through the rostral ventromedial medulla and locus coeruleus, releasing serotonin, noradrenaline and endogenous opioids onto the dorsal horn.

Why neuropathic pain behaves differently

After nerve injury, damaged axons and their ganglion cells express extra sodium channels and fire on their own (ectopic discharge). Repeated input strengthens dorsal horn synapses through NMDA receptors (central sensitisation), so light touch is felt as pain (allodynia) and painful stimuli hurt more (hyperalgesia). Lost inhibition from interneurons adds to it. After amputation, reorganisation of the somatosensory map and neuroma formation in the stump drive phantom limb pain; mirror therapy aims to correct the mismatch between motor intent and visual feedback.

Drugs by mechanism

DrugMechanismNotable adverse effects
Carbamazepine, oxcarbazepineStabilise voltage-gated sodium channels in the inactivated stateHyponatraemia, rash including SJS/TEN (HLA-B*15:02), agranulocytosis and aplastic anaemia, liver injury, CYP3A4 induction, neural tube defects
Gabapentin, pregabalinBind the α2δ subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels, reducing transmitter releaseSedation, dizziness, oedema, weight gain; renally cleared, so reduce the dose in kidney disease
Duloxetine, venlafaxine (SNRIs)Block serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake, strengthening descending inhibitionNausea, raised blood pressure, serotonin syndrome with other serotonergic drugs
Amitriptyline, nortriptyline (TCAs)Reuptake blockade as above, plus sodium channel blockadeAnticholinergic effects, orthostasis, QRS widening and arrhythmia in overdose
Lidocaine (topical)Sodium channel blockade in superficial nerve endingsLocal skin reaction; little systemic absorption
Capsaicin (high-strength patch)Activates TRPV1; sustained calcium entry defunctionalises the nociceptor terminalsBurning during application

Named central and peripheral pain syndromes

  • Thalamic pain (Dejerine–Roussy syndrome): weeks to months after a stroke in the VPL/VPM thalamus, burning pain and allodynia appear in the half of the body that lost sensation.
  • Complex regional pain syndrome: type I follows a fracture, surgery or immobilisation without a definable nerve lesion; type II follows a known peripheral nerve injury.
  • Trigeminal neuralgia: compression of the trigeminal root entry zone by a looping artery (often the superior cerebellar artery) causes focal demyelination and ephaptic, paroxysmal firing.

sections.heading: Spinal emergencies: cord compression, epidural abscess and cauda equina syndrome
sections.html:
Three conditions share one rule: back pain plus a new neurological deficit needs MRI the same day, because function lost before decompression is often not regained.

Red flags in back or neck pain

  • History of cancer, unexplained weight loss, pain that is worse lying down or at night (malignancy)
  • Fever, injection drug use, recent bacteraemia, spinal procedure, immunosuppression, diabetes, haemodialysis (infection)
  • Urinary retention or overflow incontinence, saddle numbness, reduced anal tone, bilateral or progressive leg weakness (cauda equina or cord)
  • Significant trauma, osteoporosis or long-term glucocorticoid use (fracture)
Malignant cord compressionSpinal epidural abscessCauda equina syndrome
SettingKnown or occult cancer (lung, breast, prostate, kidney, myeloma); thoracic spine most oftenFever (not always), injection drug use, diabetes, recent procedure or bacteraemia; Staphylococcus aureus in most casesLarge central disc herniation, tumour, abscess, haematoma after a spinal procedure
Early signsProgressive back pain, often worse when lying flat; later leg weakness, a sensory level, sphincter lossFocal spinal pain and tenderness, then radicular pain, weakness and paralysisBilateral sciatica, saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention, lax anal sphincter
ImagingMRI of the whole spine (multiple levels are common)MRI with gadolinium of the whole spine; blood cultures; ESR and CRP are usually highEmergency MRI of the lumbosacral spine
TreatmentHigh-dose dexamethasone at once when deficits are present, then radiotherapy and/or surgical decompressionEmpiric IV antibiotics covering MRSA and gram-negative rods (for example, vancomycin plus a third- or fourth-generation cephalosporin) once cultures are drawn, and urgent surgical drainage when there is a deficitUrgent surgical decompression
Exam trap: do not perform a lumbar puncture when an epidural abscess is suspected: it adds nothing and can seed the subarachnoid space. Plain radiographs are normal early in all three conditions and must not delay MRI. If MRI is contraindicated, CT myelography is the alternative.
Pearl: a post-void residual volume is a quick bedside test. Painless retention of several hundred millilitres in a patient with sciatica is cauda equina syndrome until imaging says otherwise.

sections.heading: Spinal cord injury, cervical myelopathy and transverse myelitis
sections.html:
Acute traumatic spinal cord injury

  • Immobilise the spine and manage airway, breathing and circulation first. Lesions at C3–C5 threaten the phrenic nerve and breathing; watch vital capacity.
  • Neurogenic shock (injury above about T6): hypotension with bradycardia and warm, dry skin. Exclude bleeding first; then give fluids and a vasopressor. Norepinephrine is preferred when there is bradycardia because it adds β1 support; a pure α-agonist such as phenylephrine can slow the heart further. Many centres aim for a mean arterial pressure of about 85–90 mm Hg for the first days to protect cord perfusion. Atropine or pacing treats symptomatic bradycardia.
  • High-dose methylprednisolone is not routinely recommended: its benefit is doubtful and its harms (infection, bleeding, hyperglycaemia) are real.
  • CT of the spine is the first imaging test in trauma; MRI defines cord and ligament injury.

Incomplete cord syndromes at the bedside

SyndromeClue in the historyClue on examination
Central cordOlder adult, fall onto the face (hyperextension), often no fractureArms and hands much weaker than legs
Anterior cordAortic surgery or dissection, flexion injuryParalysis and lost pain and temperature, but vibration and position sense intact
Brown-SéquardStab or gunshot woundOne weak leg; the other leg has lost pain and temperature

Autonomic dysreflexia (chronic injury at or above T6)

Sudden severe hypertension, pounding headache, flushing and sweating above the lesion, often with bradycardia. Management in order: sit the patient up and loosen tight clothing; find and remove the trigger, most often a blocked or absent urinary catheter or bladder distension, then stool impaction; if systolic pressure stays high (about 150 mm Hg or more), give a fast, short-acting antihypertensive such as topical nitrate or nifedipine (avoid nitrates after a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor).

Degenerative cervical myelopathy

The most common cause of spinal cord dysfunction in older adults. Spondylotic narrowing of the canal causes clumsy hands, trouble with buttons and handwriting, unsteady gait, and sometimes urinary urgency or electric sensations down the back on neck flexion (Lhermitte sign). Examination shows brisk reflexes below the level, Hoffmann sign, upgoing toes and often wasting of hand muscles at the compressed level. MRI of the cervical spine confirms it. Moderate, severe or progressive myelopathy is treated with surgical decompression; mild, stable cases may be watched closely. Check vitamin B12 and copper when the picture is atypical, because they cause a similar myelopathy.

Transverse myelitis

Inflammation across one or more cord segments causing bilateral weakness, a sensory level and bladder dysfunction that peak over hours to days. Work-up: MRI of the spine and brain with gadolinium (first exclude a compressive lesion), CSF examination, and serum aquaporin-4 IgG and MOG IgG. A lesion spanning three or more vertebral segments (longitudinally extensive) points to neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (aquaporin-4 antibody) or MOG antibody disease; short, partial lesions suggest multiple sclerosis. Acute treatment is high-dose IV methylprednisolone, with plasma exchange for a poor response.

Exam trap: in neurogenic shock the pulse is slow; a trauma patient with hypotension and tachycardia is bleeding until proved otherwise.

sections.heading: Radiculopathy: sciatica and cervical root pain
sections.html:
Radiculopathy is pain, numbness or weakness in the territory of one nerve root, usually from a disc herniation or a narrowed foramen. Pain radiates below the knee (sciatica) or into the arm and is worse with coughing or straining. The straight-leg raise test reproduces leg pain between about 30° and 70° in lumbar radiculopathy; pain in the affected leg when the other leg is raised is less sensitive but more specific. In the neck, extending and rotating the head toward the painful side can reproduce arm pain.

Management without red flags

  • Most cases improve within 6 weeks. Do not image in the first 6 weeks unless there are red flags or a severe or progressive motor deficit.
  • Stay active rather than bed rest; heat; NSAIDs for pain (check kidney function, bleeding and cardiovascular risk); a short course of a muscle relaxant may help acute muscle spasm. Opioids have no advantage for most patients.
  • Physical therapy once the acute pain settles.
  • MRI is for red flags, a progressive or severe motor deficit, or persistent disabling symptoms after about 6 weeks in a patient who would consider an epidural steroid injection or surgery.
  • Surgery (for example, microdiscectomy) speeds relief of persistent sciatica but gives results similar to conservative care at 1–2 years; it is urgent only for cauda equina syndrome or a progressive deficit.

sections.heading: Double vision and other cranial neuropathies: what to do next
sections.html:
Step 1: monocular or binocular?

Ask the patient to cover each eye. Double vision that persists with one eye covered (monocular) comes from the eye itself: refractive error, cataract, corneal or lens problems. It needs an eye examination, not brain imaging. Double vision that disappears with either eye covered (binocular) means misalignment of the eyes: a cranial nerve, the neuromuscular junction, an extraocular muscle or the orbit.

An isolated, pupil-sparing third, fourth or sixth nerve palsy in an older patient with diabetes or hypertension is usually microvascular and improves within about 3 months. Many clinicians still obtain MRI, because compressive and inflammatory lesions can mimic it, and any palsy that worsens, involves the pupil later or fails to recover needs imaging.

Lower cranial nerves in clinical practice

  • Hoarseness lasting more than about 4 weeks, or sooner in a smoker, needs laryngoscopy. A paralysed left vocal fold without a surgical explanation calls for CT from the skull base to the chest, looking for a lung or mediastinal tumour, or an aortic aneurysm, along the course of the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
  • Surgical nerve injuries: lymph node biopsy in the posterior triangle of the neck can cut the spinal accessory nerve (shoulder droop, weak shrug, trouble lifting the arm overhead). Carotid endarterectomy can stretch the hypoglossal nerve (tongue deviates toward the operated side) or the vagus and recurrent laryngeal nerves (hoarseness). Thyroidectomy risks the recurrent and superior laryngeal nerves.

sections.heading: Entrapment neuropathies and plexus injuries in practice
sections.html:
Carpal tunnel syndrome

  • Presentation: tingling and pain in the thumb, index and middle fingers, worst at night or when driving or holding a phone; shaking the hand relieves it. Later, weakness of thumb abduction and thenar wasting.
  • Look for associations: pregnancy, hypothyroidism, diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, acromegaly, obesity, long-term haemodialysis and amyloidosis. Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome can precede transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis by years.
  • Diagnosis: clinical; nerve conduction studies confirm it, grade its severity and are advised before surgery.
  • Treatment: a neutral-position wrist splint at night and activity change first; a corticosteroid injection into the carpal tunnel for short-term relief. Surgical release for thenar weakness or wasting, severe findings on conduction studies, or failure of conservative care. Carpal tunnel syndrome of pregnancy usually resolves after delivery, so splinting is preferred.

Ulnar neuropathy at the elbow

Numbness of the little and ring fingers, weak pinch and clumsy fine movement. First-line care is avoiding pressure on the elbow and prolonged elbow flexion, with a padded splint holding the elbow fairly straight at night. Surgery (decompression with or without transposition) is for weakness, wasting or failure of conservative care.

Other common entrapments

  • Common fibular neuropathy: foot drop after weight loss, leg crossing, long squatting or a tight cast. Remove the cause, use an ankle-foot orthosis, and expect recovery over weeks to months. Image or perform conduction studies if it does not recover or the cause is unclear.
  • Meralgia paresthetica: burning numbness over the anterolateral thigh with normal strength and reflexes. Reassure; loosen belts and tight clothing and encourage weight loss. Most cases settle.
  • Radial neuropathy at the spiral groove after sleeping with the arm draped over a chair: wrist splint and recovery over weeks. Wrist drop after a humeral shaft fracture is usually a neurapraxia and is watched rather than explored.

Brachial plexus injuries

Newborn plexus palsy (most often C5–C6) is managed with gentle range-of-motion exercises to prevent contracture; most infants recover in the first months. Lack of recovery of biceps function by about 3–6 months prompts referral for possible nerve surgery. In adults, a lower-trunk plexopathy with Horner syndrome in a smoker suggests an apical lung (Pancoast) tumour; get chest imaging.

sections.heading: Polyneuropathy: work-up, diabetic foot care and vasculitic neuropathy
sections.html:
Distal symmetric polyneuropathy

Numbness, tingling or burning starting in both feet, lost ankle jerks, reduced vibration and pinprick sensation in a stocking pattern. The highest-yield initial blood tests are:

  • fasting glucose or HbA1c (an oral glucose tolerance test finds more cases of impaired glucose metabolism);
  • vitamin B12, with methylmalonic acid if the level is borderline;
  • serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation (monoclonal gammopathy, myeloma, amyloid);
  • often TSH, kidney and liver tests and a complete blood count.

Nerve conduction studies help when the pattern is asymmetric, motor-predominant, rapidly progressive or demyelinating. Nerve biopsy is reserved for suspected vasculitis, amyloid or other treatable infiltrative disease.

Diabetic neuropathy: screening and foot protection

  • Screen people with type 2 diabetes at diagnosis, and people with type 1 diabetes 5 years after diagnosis, then every year: history plus a 10-g monofilament test and at least one other test (pinprick, temperature or vibration with a 128-Hz tuning fork).
  • Patients with loss of protective sensation need education on daily foot inspection, proper footwear and podiatry follow-up.
  • Better glucose control helps prevent neuropathy in type 1 diabetes and slows it, more modestly, in type 2.

Mononeuritis multiplex

Sudden, often painful failure of separate nerves (for example, wrist drop followed weeks later by foot drop on the other side) is a vasculitic neuropathy until proved otherwise. Check ESR and CRP, kidney function and urinalysis, ANCA, hepatitis B and C serology, cryoglobulins, complement, HIV and glucose. Conduction studies show patchy axonal loss and guide the choice of nerve to biopsy. A combined nerve and muscle biopsy (often sural nerve) confirms vasculitis. Polyarteritis nodosa classically spares the lungs, is ANCA-negative and can be associated with hepatitis B; it causes hypertension, kidney ischaemia, abdominal pain and livedo. Treatment of systemic vasculitis is high-dose glucocorticoids with cyclophosphamide or rituximab; hepatitis B-associated disease also needs antiviral therapy.

Exam trap: a serum protein electrophoresis without immunofixation can miss a small monoclonal protein. And B12 deficiency can coexist with diabetes, especially in patients taking metformin for years.

sections.heading: Managing neuropathic pain: trigeminal neuralgia, postherpetic neuralgia, CRPS and painful diabetic neuropathy
sections.html:
Trigeminal neuralgia

  • Diagnosis: seconds-long, electric-shock pains in the maxillary or mandibular division, set off by light touch, chewing, talking or a cold breeze, with pain-free intervals. The neurological examination is normal in the classic form.
  • MRI of the brain (with attention to the trigeminal nerve) is advised for every patient to look for a compressing vessel or a secondary cause. Suspect multiple sclerosis or a tumour when the patient is young, the pain is bilateral, or there is sensory loss.
  • First-line: carbamazepine, or oxcarbazepine, which is often better tolerated. Test for HLA-B*15:02 before carbamazepine in patients with ancestry from regions where the allele is common (for example, much of East and Southeast Asia). Monitor sodium and blood counts.
  • Refractory or intolerant: microvascular decompression for a fit patient with neurovascular compression on MRI (the most durable relief); percutaneous ablative procedures or stereotactic radiosurgery for older or higher-risk patients. Opioids do not help.

Postherpetic neuralgia

  • Pain in the dermatome of a shingles rash that lasts 3 months or more after the rash. The risk rises with age and with severe acute pain or rash.
  • Prevention: recombinant zoster vaccine, 2 doses 2–6 months apart, for adults aged 50 or older and for immunocompromised adults aged 19 or older, including those who have already had shingles.
  • Treatment: topical lidocaine for localised pain, especially in older adults; gabapentin or pregabalin; tricyclic antidepressants (nortriptyline is better tolerated than amitriptyline); high-strength capsaicin patch. Avoid tricyclics in older adults with cardiac disease, urinary retention, glaucoma or falls.

Painful diabetic neuropathy

First-line choices are a gabapentinoid (pregabalin or gabapentin), an SNRI (duloxetine) or a tricyclic, chosen by comorbidity: duloxetine suits a patient with depression but should be avoided with severe kidney impairment; gabapentinoids need dose reduction in kidney disease; tricyclics are poorly tolerated in older adults. Combine drugs of different classes if one gives partial relief. Avoid long-term opioids, including tramadol, as routine therapy.

Complex regional pain syndrome

Weeks after a fracture, sprain or surgery (classically a distal radius fracture), the limb develops pain out of proportion to the injury with allodynia, swelling, colour and temperature differences, sweating changes, and later stiffness and trophic skin, hair and nail changes. Diagnosis is clinical (Budapest criteria); a three-phase bone scan can support it. The cornerstone of treatment is early, graded physical and occupational therapy to restore use, with pain control and psychological support; options for persistent cases include a short glucocorticoid course, bisphosphonates, neuropathic agents and sympathetic nerve blocks. Prolonged immobilisation makes it worse.

Central post-stroke pain and phantom limb pain

Central post-stroke pain responds poorly to simple analgesics and opioids; amitriptyline and lamotrigine are commonly used. Phantom limb pain is treated with neuropathic agents, physical therapy and techniques such as mirror therapy.

sections.heading: Neurodegenerative dementias: pathology, genetics and drugs
sections.html:
Dementia (major neurocognitive disorder) is an acquired decline in one or more cognitive domains that is large enough to take away independence in daily activities. Mild cognitive impairment is a measurable decline with daily function still intact; a share of patients progress to dementia each year, while others stay stable.

Alzheimer disease

  • Amyloid cascade. Amyloid precursor protein (APP) is a membrane protein. When it is cut first by beta-secretase and then by gamma-secretase, it releases amyloid-beta peptides (especially the 42-residue form), which aggregate into extracellular neuritic plaques and deposit in vessel walls (cerebral amyloid angiopathy, a cause of lobar hemorrhage in older adults).
  • Tau. Hyperphosphorylated tau detaches from microtubules and forms intracellular neurofibrillary tangles. Tangle burden tracks cognitive decline more closely than plaque burden.
  • Where. Damage starts in the entorhinal cortex and hippocampus (so new memories fail first), then spreads to temporal and parietal association cortex. Loss of cholinergic neurons in the nucleus basalis of Meynert lowers cortical acetylcholine, which is the rationale for cholinesterase inhibitors.
  • Genes. Late-onset disease: the APOE e4 allele (chromosome 19) raises risk in a dose-dependent way, and e2 lowers it; neither is diagnostic. Early-onset familial disease: autosomal dominant mutations in APP (chromosome 21), PSEN1 (chromosome 14) or PSEN2 (chromosome 1). Adults with Down syndrome carry three copies of APP and usually develop Alzheimer pathology by middle age.
Drug classExamplesMechanismKey adverse effects
Cholinesterase inhibitorsdonepezil, rivastigmine, galantamineBlock acetylcholinesterase, so more acetylcholine stays in the synapseNausea, vomiting, diarrhea, weight loss, vivid dreams; bradycardia and syncope (muscarinic effect on the SA and AV nodes)
NMDA antagonistmemantineUncompetitive, voltage-dependent block of the NMDA receptor channel, limiting excess calcium entryDizziness, headache, confusion; usually well tolerated
Anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodieslecanemab, donanemabBind aggregated amyloid-beta and promote its clearanceAmyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA): vasogenic edema (ARIA-E) and microhemorrhage or siderosis (ARIA-H); infusion reactions
Pearl: ARIA risk is highest in APOE e4 homozygotes, which is why genotype counseling and MRI monitoring accompany anti-amyloid therapy. These antibodies are for mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia with proven amyloid pathology only.

Other neurodegenerative dementias

DiseaseLeading clinical picturePathology
Frontotemporal dementiaOnset often in the 50s or 60s; personality change, disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, compulsions, sweet cravings, or a progressive language disorder; memory and visuospatial skills relatively spared earlyFrontal and anterior temporal atrophy; tau inclusions (including round Pick bodies) or TDP-43 inclusions. A C9orf72 repeat expansion links familial FTD with ALS.
Dementia with Lewy bodiesFluctuating attention, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations, REM sleep behavior disorder, parkinsonism; dementia comes before or within a year of the motor signsAlpha-synuclein Lewy bodies in cortical and brainstem neurons
Parkinson disease dementiaDementia that begins a year or more after established Parkinson diseaseAlpha-synuclein, spreading from brainstem to cortex
Vascular cognitive impairmentStepwise or patchy decline, slowed thinking and executive dysfunction, focal signs, vascular risk factorsMultiple infarcts or diffuse small-vessel white matter disease
Prion diseaseDementia progressing over weeks to months with myoclonus and ataxiaSpongiform change from misfolded beta-sheet prion protein
Exam trap: in dementia with Lewy bodies, first-generation antipsychotics can cause severe rigidity, confusion and even a neuroleptic malignant-like state. A hallucinating older adult with fluctuating cognition and dream enactment should not get haloperidol.

sections.heading: Amnestic syndromes: Wernicke-Korsakoff and transient global amnesia
sections.html:
Forming new declarative memories depends on a circuit that runs from the hippocampus through the fornix to the mammillary bodies, then to the anterior and medial dorsal thalamic nuclei and the cingulate cortex. Damage anywhere on this loop, on both sides, produces anterograde amnesia with relatively preserved attention and older memories.

Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency

  • Biochemistry. Thiamine pyrophosphate is the cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase and transketolase. Without it, neurons with high glucose turnover cannot make enough ATP, and lactate rises. Red-cell transketolase activity is a functional test of thiamine status.
  • Who. Alcohol use disorder, hyperemesis, starvation and refeeding, bariatric surgery, long dialysis or parenteral nutrition without vitamins.
  • Wernicke encephalopathy (acute): confusion, eye movement abnormalities (nystagmus, lateral rectus palsy, gaze palsies) and gait ataxia. All three together are present in only a minority, so the threshold to treat is low. Lesions sit around the third and fourth ventricles and aqueduct: mammillary bodies, medial thalamus, periaqueductal gray.
  • Korsakoff syndrome (chronic): severe anterograde and some retrograde amnesia with confabulation and lack of insight; mammillary body atrophy and medial dorsal thalamic damage.
Exam trap: giving glucose to a thiamine-depleted patient speeds pyruvate formation without the cofactor to handle it, and can precipitate or worsen Wernicke encephalopathy. Give thiamine first or at the same time, but never withhold glucose from a hypoglycemic patient.

Transient global amnesia

A sudden, isolated loss of the ability to form new memories in a middle-aged or older adult, often after strenuous exertion, cold water immersion, emotional stress or a Valsalva-like effort. The patient is alert, knows who they are, performs complex tasks, and asks the same questions again and again. It resolves within 24 hours, leaving a gap only for the episode. Diffusion MRI may show small, temporary hippocampal dots. It recurs rarely and is not a stroke risk marker.

FeatureTransient global amnesiaDissociative amnesiaFocal seizure
Personal identityPreservedOften lostPreserved
DurationHours (under 24)Hours to monthsMinutes, often recurrent
BehaviourRepetitive questioningLinked to a psychological stressorAutomatisms, impaired awareness

sections.heading: Motor neuron disease and the neuromuscular junction
sections.html:
Motor neuron disease

  • Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) destroys both upper motor neurons (cortex and lateral corticospinal tracts) and lower motor neurons (anterior horn cells and motor nuclei of the brainstem). Expect weakness with atrophy and fasciculations alongside spasticity, brisk reflexes and extensor plantar responses, usually starting asymmetrically in a limb or in bulbar muscles. Sensation, eye movements and sphincters are spared. Most cases are sporadic; known genes include C9orf72 (the most common), SOD1 and TARDBP. TDP-43 inclusions are found in most cases. Drugs: riluzole (reduces glutamate release; modest survival benefit), edaravone (free-radical scavenger), and tofersen, an antisense oligonucleotide that lowers SOD1 protein in SOD1 carriers.
  • Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is autosomal recessive loss of SMN1 (chromosome 5q), which kills anterior horn cells. Infants have symmetric proximal weakness, hypotonia, absent reflexes, tongue fasciculations and a bell-shaped chest, with normal alertness. A back-up gene, SMN2, mostly skips exon 7 and makes little working protein; more SMN2 copies mean milder disease. Therapies: nusinersen (intrathecal antisense oligonucleotide that makes SMN2 keep exon 7), risdiplam (oral small molecule with the same splicing goal), and onasemnogene abeparvovec (one-time AAV9 vector that delivers a working SMN1 copy). Newborn screening allows treatment before symptoms.

Neuromuscular junction disorders

[[figure:s23e-fig0501]]
Myasthenia gravisLambert-Eaton syndromeBotulism
TargetPostsynaptic: antibodies to the nicotinic ACh receptor (most), MuSK or LRP4Presynaptic: antibodies to P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channelsPresynaptic: toxin protease cleaves SNARE proteins, so vesicles cannot fuse
Typical patientYoung woman or older man; thymus abnormal in many (hyperplasia, or thymoma in a minority)Older smoker; over half have small cell lung cancerHome-canned food, injection drug use, wound; infants from ingested spores
PatternFatigable ptosis and diplopia, bulbar and proximal weakness; worse with use and late in the dayProximal leg weakness, dry mouth, erectile dysfunction; strength and reflexes briefly improve after effortDescending symmetric paralysis from cranial nerves down; dilated, sluggish pupils; alert, afebrile, no sensory loss
