Drug cluePyridostigmine (cholinesterase inhibitor) helpsAmifampridine (blocks potassium channels, prolonging the presynaptic action potential)Antitoxin; human botulism immune globulin in infants
Pearl: aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, macrolides, magnesium, beta-blockers and immune checkpoint inhibitors can unmask or worsen myasthenia gravis.

sections.heading: Muscular dystrophies, inflammatory myopathies and immune neuropathies
sections.html:
Dystrophinopathies

Dystrophin links the actin cytoskeleton of a muscle fibre to the extracellular matrix through the dystroglycan complex. Without it, the sarcolemma tears during contraction, the fibre necroses, and muscle is gradually replaced by fat and fibrous tissue. The gene is on Xp21 and is very large, so new mutations are common (about one-third of cases).

DuchenneBecker
MutationUsually a deletion that shifts the reading frame; little or no dystrophinUsually an in-frame deletion; shorter, partly functional dystrophin
OnsetToddler: late walking, frequent falls, waddling gait, Gowers manoeuvre (climbing up the thighs to stand)Later childhood or adolescence; slower course
CourseWheelchair in early teens without treatment; scoliosis, respiratory failure, dilated cardiomyopathyWalking into adulthood; cardiomyopathy may dominate

Both cause enlarged calves (fibrofatty pseudohypertrophy) and a very high creatine kinase. Diagnosis is by deletion/duplication testing of the dystrophin gene, with sequencing if that is negative. Glucocorticoids slow the decline; exon-skipping oligonucleotides help boys with specific deletions; cardiac and respiratory surveillance are lifelong.

Myotonic dystrophy type 1

Autosomal dominant expansion of a CTG repeat in the untranslated region of DMPK (chromosome 19). The expanded RNA sequesters splicing regulators, so many proteins are mis-spliced. Features: myotonia (slow relaxation of grip), distal and facial weakness with ptosis and a long, thin face, frontal balding, cataracts, cardiac conduction block, insulin resistance and testicular atrophy. Repeats tend to grow when passed on, especially from the mother, who can have a severely hypotonic newborn (congenital form).

Inflammatory myopathies (neurological view)

  • Dermatomyositis and polymyositis: symmetric proximal weakness over weeks to months, raised creatine kinase; skin signs in dermatomyositis; screen adults for malignancy.
  • Inclusion body myositis: men over 50, slowly progressive and asymmetric weakness of finger flexors and quadriceps, rimmed vacuoles on biopsy, poor response to immunosuppression.

Immune neuropathies

Guillain-Barré syndrome follows an infection by days to weeks (classically Campylobacter jejuni). Antibodies made against microbial lipooligosaccharide cross-react with peripheral nerve gangliosides (molecular mimicry). The demyelinating form shows conduction slowing and block; the axonal motor form is linked to anti-GM1 antibodies; the Miller Fisher variant (ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia) to anti-GQ1b. CSF shows high protein with a normal cell count. Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy progresses or relapses beyond 8 weeks and, unlike Guillain-Barré syndrome, responds to corticosteroids.

Exam trap: a boy with calf enlargement and weakness is not "muscular". Large calves with a very high creatine kinase mean fat and fibrous replacement, not hypertrophy.

sections.heading: Basal ganglia circuits and movement disorders
sections.html:
The basal ganglia do not start movement; they select it. Cortex excites the striatum (caudate and putamen). Two GABAergic output routes from the striatum then set how strongly the internal globus pallidus and substantia nigra pars reticulata inhibit the motor thalamus.

[[figure:s23e-fig0502]]
  • Direct pathway (D1 receptors, Gs-coupled): striatum inhibits the internal pallidum, so the thalamus is released and movement is facilitated.
  • Indirect pathway (D2 receptors, Gi-coupled): striatum inhibits the external pallidum, which then stops inhibiting the subthalamic nucleus; the subthalamic nucleus excites the internal pallidum, which brakes the thalamus.
  • Dopamine from the substantia nigra pars compacta excites the direct pathway and inhibits the indirect pathway. Both effects promote movement.
DisorderCircuit changeResult
Parkinson diseaseLoss of nigral dopamine neurons; direct pathway underactive, indirect overactiveToo much pallidal braking: bradykinesia, rigidity, rest tremor
Huntington diseaseEarly loss of striatal neurons that project to the external pallidum (indirect pathway)Too little braking: chorea
HemiballismusLesion of the subthalamic nucleus (often a small stroke)Violent flinging of the opposite limbs

Parkinson disease

Pigmented dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta die, and survivors carry Lewy bodies: eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions of aggregated alpha-synuclein. Symptoms appear once most striatal dopamine is gone. Non-motor features (loss of smell, constipation, REM sleep behaviour disorder, depression) can precede the motor signs by years. MPTP, a contaminant of illicit opioid synthesis, is converted by MAO-B to a toxin that destroys these neurons.

DrugMechanismTeaching point
Levodopa with carbidopaLevodopa crosses the blood-brain barrier and is turned into dopamine; carbidopa blocks peripheral DOPA decarboxylase and does not enter the brainMost effective drug; nausea and hypotension are reduced by carbidopa; long-term motor fluctuations and dyskinesia
Dopamine agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotine)Stimulate D2/D3 receptors directlyImpulse control disorders (gambling, shopping, hypersexuality), sleep attacks, hallucinations, leg edema
MAO-B inhibitors (selegiline, rasagiline, safinamide)Slow dopamine breakdown in the brainMild effect; interaction risk with serotonergic drugs
COMT inhibitors (entacapone, opicapone)Block peripheral levodopa breakdown, prolonging each doseFor "wearing off"; tolcapone can injure the liver
AmantadineNMDA antagonism, plus dopamine releaseReduces levodopa-induced dyskinesia; livedo reticularis, ankle edema
Antimuscarinics (trihexyphenidyl, benztropine)Rebalance striatal acetylcholine against low dopamineTremor in younger patients; confusion and retention in older adults

Other movement disorders

  • Huntington disease: autosomal dominant CAG repeat expansion in HTT (chromosome 4). Longer repeats mean earlier onset; repeats expand most during spermatogenesis, so anticipation is typical after paternal transmission. Chorea, psychiatric disease (depression, irritability, suicide) and dementia; caudate atrophy enlarges the frontal horns. VMAT2 inhibitors (tetrabenazine, deutetrabenazine, valbenazine) deplete presynaptic dopamine to reduce chorea.
  • Essential tremor: bilateral action and postural tremor of hands, head or voice, often familial, often better after alcohol.
  • Wilson disease: autosomal recessive loss of ATP7B, the hepatocyte copper-transporting ATPase that loads ceruloplasmin and excretes copper into bile. Copper deposits in the putamen and other basal ganglia (tremor, dysarthria, dystonia, parkinsonism, psychiatric change) and in Descemet membrane (Kayser-Fleischer rings).
  • Tourette syndrome: multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic for over a year, starting before 18; often with ADHD or OCD.
Exam trap: tremor at rest that improves with movement points to Parkinson disease; tremor that appears when holding a posture or reaching points to essential tremor or a cerebellar cause.

sections.heading: Metabolic, storage and mitochondrial disorders of the nervous system
sections.html:
Acquired metabolic encephalopathies

  • Hepatic encephalopathy. Gut-derived ammonia escapes a failing or bypassed liver. In the brain, astrocytes clear ammonia by making glutamine (glutamine synthetase); glutamine builds up and the astrocytes swell. Inflammation and increased GABAergic tone add to the effect. Clinical picture: inattention and day-night reversal progressing to stupor, with asterixis (flapping tremor from brief lapses of posture). Lactulose is broken down by colonic bacteria into acids; in the acidic colon, ammonia (NH3) becomes ammonium (NH4+), which cannot be absorbed and leaves in stool. Rifaximin reduces ammonia-producing gut bacteria.
  • Uremic encephalopathy: confusion, asterixis, myoclonus and seizures in advanced kidney failure; it is reversed by dialysis.
  • Sodium. Falling serum sodium moves water into brain cells (headache, vomiting, confusion, seizures). Over about 48 hours the brain adapts by exporting osmolytes. If chronic hyponatremia is then corrected too fast, the adapted cells shrink and oligodendrocytes are injured: osmotic demyelination of the central pons and sometimes other regions. Days after correction the patient develops dysarthria, dysphagia and spastic quadriparesis, up to a locked-in state.
  • Hypoglycemia causes confusion, seizures and even focal deficits that mimic stroke; always check glucose.

Vitamin-related myelopathies and neuropathies

DeficiencyNeurologyLab clue
Vitamin B12 (cobalamin)Subacute combined degeneration: dorsal columns (lost vibration and position sense, positive Romberg) plus lateral corticospinal tracts (spasticity, extensor plantars), peripheral neuropathy, cognitive changeMethylmalonic acid and homocysteine both high; anemia may be absent
FolateAnemia without the combined degeneration pictureHomocysteine high, methylmalonic acid normal
CopperA myeloneuropathy that looks like B12 deficiency, often with anemia and neutropeniaLow serum copper and ceruloplasmin; follows gastric surgery or excess zinc
ThiamineWernicke-Korsakoff; dry beriberi (sensorimotor neuropathy)Low red-cell transketolase activity
Pearl: nitrous oxide oxidises the cobalt in cobalamin and inactivates it. Recreational use, or anaesthesia in someone with low stores, can trigger subacute combined degeneration.

Inherited storage and peroxisomal disorders

Disease (inheritance)Missing enzyme or proteinAccumulatesNeurological hallmarks
Tay-Sachs (AR)Hexosaminidase AGM2 gangliosideInfant regression, exaggerated startle, macular cherry-red spot, no organomegaly
Niemann-Pick type A (AR)SphingomyelinaseSphingomyelinRegression and cherry-red spot with hepatosplenomegaly; foam cells
Krabbe (AR)GalactocerebrosidaseGalactocerebroside and toxic psychosineIrritability, spasticity, optic atrophy, peripheral neuropathy; globoid cells
Metachromatic leukodystrophy (AR)Arylsulfatase ASulfatidesCentral and peripheral demyelination: gait disorder, ataxia, cognitive decline
X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (XR)ABCD1, a peroxisomal membrane transporterVery-long-chain fatty acidsBoys with school and behaviour decline and adrenal insufficiency; posterior white matter disease

Mitochondrial encephalomyopathies

Mitochondrial DNA comes from the mother, and each cell carries a mixture of normal and mutant copies (heteroplasmy), so severity varies within a family. MELAS (most often the m.3243A>G tRNA mutation) causes stroke-like episodes that do not follow arterial territories, lactic acidosis, seizures, short stature, hearing loss and diabetes. MERRF causes myoclonic epilepsy. Muscle biopsy shows ragged red fibres: clumps of abnormal mitochondria under the sarcolemma on modified Gomori trichrome stain.

sections.heading: Cognitive decline: evaluation and management of dementia
sections.html:
Step 1: is it dementia, delirium or depression?

DementiaDeliriumDepression with cognitive symptoms
OnsetMonths to yearsHours to daysWeeks to months, often after a loss
AttentionNormal earlyImpaired, fluctuatingPoor effort
Typical answerTries, makes errors, covers gapsDisorganised"I don't know"
ActionWork-up belowFind and treat the causeTreat the depression, then reassess cognition

Work-up

  • History from an informant, medication review (anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, opioids, sedating antihistamines), alcohol use, hearing and vision, mood screen, and a functional assessment (finances, medications, driving).
  • Brief cognitive test (for example, MoCA or Mini-Cog) and a neurological examination.
  • Labs: complete blood count, metabolic panel with calcium and glucose, vitamin B12 and TSH. Syphilis and HIV testing when there are risk factors.
  • Structural brain imaging (MRI or CT) once, to look for tumour, subdural hematoma, stroke burden or hydrocephalus.
  • Biomarkers (amyloid PET, CSF amyloid and tau, validated blood tests) are used when the result changes management, such as eligibility for anti-amyloid therapy, or for atypical or early-onset cases. APOE genotyping is not a diagnostic test.

Treatable mimics

  • Normal pressure hydrocephalus: gait first (wide-based, slow, feet that seem stuck to the floor), then urinary urgency or incontinence, then cognitive slowing. Ventricles are enlarged out of proportion to sulcal atrophy. A large-volume lumbar tap with a before-and-after gait test predicts who will improve with a ventriculoperitoneal shunt.
  • Hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, depression, medication effects, chronic subdural hematoma, sleep apnea.

Management

  • Cholinesterase inhibitor for mild to severe Alzheimer disease, dementia with Lewy bodies and Parkinson disease dementia; add or use memantine for moderate to severe Alzheimer disease. Check heart rate and ask about syncope.
  • Anti-amyloid antibodies (lecanemab, donanemab) only for mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia due to Alzheimer disease with amyloid confirmed by PET or CSF. Before starting: a recent brain MRI (exclude more than a few microhemorrhages, prior intracerebral hemorrhage or superficial siderosis), APOE genotype counseling, and review of anticoagulant use. Scheduled MRIs during the first months detect ARIA, which is usually silent but can cause headache, confusion or seizures.
  • Behavioural and psychological symptoms: look first for pain, constipation, urinary retention, infection, hunger, noise or a new drug. Use routines, daylight, activity and caregiver techniques. Antipsychotics increase mortality and stroke in older adults with dementia and are reserved for severe, dangerous psychosis or agitation, at the lowest dose for the shortest time.
  • Safety and planning: driving and firearms, wandering, financial exploitation, advance directives and a health care proxy while the patient still has capacity, caregiver support and respite.
Exam trap: do not start an antipsychotic or a benzodiazepine as the first response to evening agitation in a nursing home resident. Look for a cause and use non-drug measures first.

sections.heading: Acute and progressive neuromuscular weakness: diagnosis and management
sections.html:
First question: is breathing threatened?

Neuromuscular respiratory failure can develop with a normal oxygen saturation until late. Follow forced vital capacity (FVC) and negative inspiratory force (NIF) at the bedside. Intubate electively when FVC falls below about 20 mL/kg, NIF is weaker than about −30 cm H2O, values are falling quickly, or the patient cannot handle secretions. Rising PaCO2 is a late sign.

Guillain-Barré syndrome

  • Progressive, roughly symmetric weakness over days (maximal by about 4 weeks), reduced or absent reflexes, distal tingling and often back pain. Autonomic instability (tachycardia, bradycardia, swings in blood pressure) can be fatal.
  • Diagnosis is clinical, supported by lumbar puncture (high protein with a normal white cell count; protein may be normal in the first week) and nerve conduction studies.
  • Treat non-ambulatory patients (or those getting worse) within about 2 weeks with IVIG or plasma exchange; they are equally effective, and giving one after the other adds nothing. Corticosteroids do not help. Admit to a monitored bed, check FVC and NIF frequently, give thromboprophylaxis and manage pain.
  • A CSF white count well above normal suggests another diagnosis (HIV, Lyme disease, lymphoma, poliomyelitis-like illness).

Myasthenia gravis

  • Confirm with acetylcholine receptor antibodies (MuSK antibodies if negative); electrodiagnostic tests (repetitive stimulation, single-fibre EMG) for seronegative cases. Image the chest (CT or MRI) for thymoma.
  • Symptomatic: pyridostigmine (muscarinic side effects: cramps, diarrhea, sweating). Immunotherapy: prednisone, then steroid-sparing agents (azathioprine, mycophenolate); for refractory generalized disease, complement inhibitors or FcRn blockers. Thymectomy for any thymoma, and for generalized acetylcholine-receptor-positive disease in younger adults.
  • Myasthenic crisis (often after infection, surgery or a provoking drug): ICU, airway protection when FVC or NIF fall or secretions pool, then IVIG or plasma exchange, with corticosteroids started or continued. Remove provoking drugs.

Other causes

DisorderKey action
Lambert-Eaton syndromeSearch for small cell lung cancer (CT chest, repeated if negative); amifampridine for symptoms
Adult botulismNotify public health and give equine antitoxin early, without waiting for confirmation; support breathing
Infant botulismHuman-derived botulism immune globulin; supportive care; avoid aminoglycosides; no honey before age 1
ALSMultidisciplinary clinic; riluzole; noninvasive ventilation when FVC falls below about 50% or orthopnea appears; feeding gastrostomy before weight loss and respiratory decline progress; early advance care planning
Duchenne muscular dystrophyDystrophin gene deletion/duplication testing; glucocorticoids; cardiology (ACE inhibitor for cardiomyopathy) and pulmonary follow-up
Exam trap: a patient in neuromuscular respiratory failure can look comfortable with a normal pulse oximeter reading. Decide on the airway from the FVC and NIF trend, cough and secretions, not from the saturation.

sections.heading: Parkinson disease and other movement disorders: management
sections.html:
Diagnosing parkinsonism

Parkinsonism means bradykinesia plus rest tremor, rigidity or both. Parkinson disease is a clinical diagnosis: asymmetric onset, a clear response to levodopa and no red flags. A dopamine transporter scan can separate degenerative parkinsonism from essential tremor or drug-induced parkinsonism, but it does not tell Parkinson disease from atypical forms.

Red flagThink of
Falls in the first year, impaired downgaze, axial rigidityProgressive supranuclear palsy
Early severe autonomic failure (orthostatic hypotension, urinary retention) or cerebellar signsMultiple system atrophy
Markedly asymmetric rigidity, limb apraxia, "alien" limb, cortical sensory lossCorticobasal degeneration
Early dementia and hallucinationsDementia with Lewy bodies
Symmetric onset on a dopamine blocker (antipsychotic, metoclopramide)Drug-induced parkinsonism

Treating Parkinson disease

  • Start treatment when symptoms affect function or quality of life. Carbidopa-levodopa is the most effective first choice at any age and the preferred one in older adults. A dopamine agonist or MAO-B inhibitor is an option for younger patients with mild symptoms.
  • Wearing off (symptoms return before the next dose): shorten the interval between doses, or add a COMT inhibitor, MAO-B inhibitor or dopamine agonist. Peak-dose dyskinesia: smaller, more frequent doses or amantadine.
  • Deep brain stimulation (subthalamic nucleus or internal pallidum) helps levodopa-responsive patients with motor fluctuations, dyskinesia or drug-resistant tremor who do not have significant dementia.
  • Psychosis: check for infection or metabolic causes; then withdraw drugs in this order: anticholinergics, amantadine, MAO-B inhibitors, dopamine agonists, COMT inhibitors, and lower levodopa last. If an antipsychotic is still needed, use pimavanserin, low-dose quetiapine or clozapine (with blood count monitoring). Avoid haloperidol and risperidone.
  • Non-motor care: orthostatic hypotension, constipation, depression, sleep, physiotherapy for gait and falls. Never stop levodopa abruptly: it can cause a neuroleptic malignant-like syndrome.

Other movement disorders

DisorderFirst-line approach
Essential tremorPropranolol or primidone (primidone if asthma or bradycardia); topiramate second line; thalamic (VIM) deep brain stimulation or focused ultrasound if disabling
Huntington disease choreaA VMAT2 inhibitor (watch for depression and suicidality) or an antipsychotic; manage depression; genetic counseling for relatives, and pre-test counseling before predictive testing
Focal dystonia (neck, eyelids, writer's cramp)Botulinum toxin injections
Tourette syndromeEducation; behavioural therapy for tics (comprehensive behavioural intervention) first; alpha-2 agonists or antipsychotics if needed
Wilson diseaseChelation (penicillamine or trientine) or zinc; screen siblings

Movement disorders caused by dopamine blockers

SyndromeTimingTreatment
Acute dystoniaHours to daysAnticholinergic (benztropine) or diphenhydramine, IV or IM
AkathisiaDays to weeksLower the dose; propranolol; consider a benzodiazepine
Drug-induced parkinsonismWeeksLower or switch the drug; anticholinergic if needed
Tardive dyskinesiaMonths to yearsReview the need for the drug; VMAT2 inhibitor (valbenazine or deutetrabenazine); anticholinergics worsen it

sections.heading: Metabolic encephalopathies: hepatic, uremic, sodium and vitamin disorders
sections.html:
Hepatic encephalopathy

  • Diagnosis is clinical in a patient with cirrhosis or a portosystemic shunt: confusion, altered sleep, asterixis. A blood ammonia level does not grade severity and is not needed to diagnose or follow treatment; a normal level makes the diagnosis less likely.
  • Find the trigger: gastrointestinal bleeding, infection (do a diagnostic paracentesis for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis), dehydration or over-diuresis, hypokalemia, constipation, sedatives or opioids, a new TIPS.
  • Lactulose titrated to 2–3 soft stools a day is first line. Add rifaximin to prevent recurrence after a second episode. Do not restrict protein; aim for adequate protein and calories, with a late-evening snack. Protect the airway in deep coma.

Uremic encephalopathy

Confusion, asterixis, myoclonus or seizures in kidney failure are an indication for urgent dialysis, as are uremic pericarditis and bleeding.

Sodium disorders

  • Severe symptoms of hyponatremia (seizures, coma, vomiting with confusion): give a 100 mL bolus of 3% saline, repeated up to two more times if symptoms continue, to raise sodium by about 4–6 mEq/L, which is enough to reduce brain swelling.
  • Limit the rise in chronic hyponatremia: no more than about 8 mEq/L in 24 hours for patients at high risk of osmotic demyelination (sodium 105 mEq/L or less, alcohol use disorder, malnutrition, hypokalemia, advanced liver disease). Higher-risk patients can overshoot when the cause is removed (for example, stopping a thiazide or giving volume to a hypovolemic patient) and a water diuresis starts.
  • Overcorrection: stop the hypertonic or isotonic saline, give 5% dextrose in water and desmopressin to bring sodium back down.

Vitamin deficiencies

  • Suspected Wernicke encephalopathy: high-dose IV thiamine at once, before or with glucose; also correct magnesium. Do not wait for imaging or a level.
  • B12 deficiency with neurological signs: confirm with B12 plus methylmalonic acid; replace with intramuscular cobalamin, then look for the cause (autoimmune gastritis, metformin, acid suppression, gastric surgery, strict vegan diet, nitrous oxide). Giving folate alone can correct the anemia while the nerve damage progresses.
  • Copper deficiency (after bariatric surgery, or zinc excess from supplements or denture cream) produces the same myelopathy with cytopenias; check serum copper and ceruloplasmin, and remove the zinc source.

Inherited disorders that present in clinic

  • X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy is on many newborn screening panels. A boy with raised very-long-chain fatty acids needs regular adrenal testing and serial brain MRI, because haematopoietic stem cell transplant (or gene therapy) only helps when started at the earliest sign of cerebral disease. Steroid replacement treats adrenal insufficiency.
  • Mitochondrial disease: think of it when stroke-like episodes, seizures, hearing loss, diabetes and short stature cluster in a family through the mother. Lactate is often high; genetic testing confirms it.
Exam trap: a seizing patient with a sodium of 112 mEq/L needs hypertonic saline now, not fluid restriction. Once symptoms stop, slow down: the danger shifts to correcting too fast.

sections.heading: Seizures and epilepsy: mechanisms, classification and antiseizure drugs
sections.html:
A seizure is a transient burst of abnormal, excessive and synchronous neuronal firing. Epilepsy means an enduring tendency to unprovoked seizures: two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart, one unprovoked seizure with a high (about 60% or more) recurrence risk, or an epilepsy syndrome. A seizure caused by an acute insult (low sodium or glucose, alcohol withdrawal, a new stroke) is provoked and does not by itself mean epilepsy.

How seizures start and spread

  • Excitation outweighs inhibition: too much glutamate signalling (NMDA, AMPA receptors) or too little GABA-mediated inhibition.
  • Ion channel genes matter: for example, loss-of-function variants in the SCN1A sodium channel of inhibitory interneurons cause Dravet syndrome.
  • In absence seizures, T-type calcium channels in thalamic relay neurons drive rhythmic burst firing in thalamocortical loops, which gives the 3-per-second generalized spike-and-wave pattern on EEG.
  • Prolonged seizures injure neurons through excitotoxic calcium entry. The hippocampus is especially vulnerable: hippocampal (mesial temporal) sclerosis shows neuron loss and gliosis, most marked in the CA1 sector, and is the commonest lesion behind drug-resistant focal epilepsy in adults.

Classification (ILAE 2017 terms)

OnsetExamplesClinical clues
Focal, awareRising epigastric feeling, déjà vu, jerking of one handAwareness kept; what used to be called a simple partial seizure
Focal, impaired awarenessStaring with lip smacking and fumbling (temporal lobe)Lasts 1–2 minutes, followed by confusion
Focal to bilateral tonic-clonicFocal start, then generalized convulsionAn aura or a head turn before the convulsion points to a focal origin
Generalized, motorTonic-clonic, myoclonic, atonicMyoclonic jerks on waking: juvenile myoclonic epilepsy
Generalized, nonmotor (absence)Staring for 5–15 seconds, many times a dayNo aura or postictal state; hyperventilation provokes it

After a focal motor seizure, weakness of the involved limb may last hours (postictal or Todd paralysis).

Antiseizure drugs by mechanism

MechanismDrugs
Block voltage-gated Na+ channels (prolong inactivation)Phenytoin, fosphenytoin, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, lamotrigine; lacosamide enhances slow inactivation
Block T-type Ca2+ channels in the thalamusEthosuximide (absence only)
Bind synaptic vesicle protein SV2ALevetiracetam, brivaracetam
GABAA receptor: more frequent channel openingBenzodiazepines
GABAA receptor: longer channel openingPhenobarbital (barbiturates)
Irreversibly inhibit GABA transaminaseVigabatrin (infantile spasms)
Several: Na+ channels, T-type Ca2+, more GABAValproate (broad spectrum)
Several: Na+ channels, GABAA, AMPA/kainate block, carbonic anhydrase inhibitionTopiramate
Bind the α2δ subunit of voltage-gated Ca2+ channelsGabapentin, pregabalin (focal seizures, neuropathic pain)
Exam trap: sodium channel blockers such as carbamazepine and phenytoin can worsen absence and myoclonic seizures. For a generalized epilepsy, choose a broad-spectrum drug.
Pearl: benzodiazepines raise how often the GABAA chloride channel opens; barbiturates prolong how long it stays open, and at high doses open it directly. That is why barbiturates are more dangerous in overdose.

sections.heading: Headache: trigeminovascular mechanisms and the drugs that target them
sections.html:
The brain itself feels no pain. Headache comes from pain-sensitive structures: the meninges, the large intracranial vessels and venous sinuses, and extracranial tissues. Their sensory supply is mostly the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve above the tentorium and the upper cervical roots below it, which is why posterior fossa pain is often felt in the neck and occiput.

Migraine

  • Aura reflects cortical spreading depolarization: a slow wave of neuronal and glial depolarization moving across the cortex at a few millimetres per minute, followed by a period of suppressed activity. A visual aura that spreads across the visual field over 5–20 minutes and then fades matches this wave crossing the occipital cortex.
  • Pain comes from activation of trigeminal afferents around meningeal vessels. They release calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) and other neuropeptides, which cause vasodilation and sterile inflammation and sensitize central trigeminal neurons (scalp allodynia during an attack).
  • Risk factors: female sex after puberty, family history, hormonal fluctuation (attacks around menstruation).

Acute and preventive drugs by mechanism

Drug classMechanismKey cautions
Triptans (sumatriptan and others)5-HT1B agonism constricts cranial vessels; 5-HT1D agonism blocks neuropeptide release from trigeminal endingsAvoid in coronary, cerebrovascular or peripheral arterial disease and uncontrolled hypertension
Lasmiditan5-HT1F agonist; no vasoconstrictionDizziness and sedation; no driving for 8 hours after a dose
Gepants (ubrogepant, rimegepant, atogepant)Small-molecule CGRP receptor antagonistsNo vasoconstriction; CYP3A4 interactions
CGRP monoclonal antibodiesErenumab blocks the CGRP receptor; fremanezumab, galcanezumab and eptinezumab bind the CGRP ligandPrevention only; constipation and hypertension reported with erenumab
Ergot alkaloids (dihydroergotamine)Broad 5-HT, α-adrenergic and dopamine receptor actionsVasospasm; contraindicated in pregnancy and with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors
β-blockers, topiramate, amitriptyline, candesartanPreventive; mechanisms only partly understoodTopiramate: teratogenic, kidney stones, word-finding problems

Cluster headache

Cluster headache is a trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia. Functional imaging shows activation of the posterior hypothalamus, which explains the clockwork timing of attacks. Pain in the trigeminal territory triggers a reflex outflow from the superior salivatory nucleus through the facial nerve and the pterygopalatine ganglion. This gives same-side tearing and nasal congestion. Swelling around the carotid sympathetic plexus can add a partial Horner syndrome (ptosis and miosis without loss of sweating on the face).

Exam trap: CGRP-targeting drugs are not vasoconstrictors, so they are options when triptans are contraindicated by vascular disease. Lasmiditan is the non-vasoconstricting serotonin agonist (5-HT1F).

sections.heading: Sleep physiology, sleep stages and the neurobiology of sleep disorders
sections.html:
Sleep is generated by an active switch between wake-promoting and sleep-promoting neurons and is timed by a circadian clock.

The circuits

  • Wake: monoamine and acetylcholine nuclei (locus coeruleus norepinephrine, raphe serotonin, tuberomammillary histamine, basal forebrain and pontine acetylcholine) activate the thalamus and cortex. Orexin (hypocretin) neurons in the lateral hypothalamus stabilize wakefulness by exciting these nuclei.
  • Sleep: GABA neurons of the ventrolateral preoptic nucleus inhibit the arousal nuclei. Adenosine builds up during wakefulness and adds sleep pressure (caffeine blocks adenosine receptors).
  • Clock: light reaches the suprachiasmatic nucleus through melanopsin-containing retinal ganglion cells and the retinohypothalamic tract. The SCN drives melatonin release from the pineal gland at night through a sympathetic relay (spinal cord, superior cervical ganglion).
  • REM: pontine cholinergic neurons switch REM on while locus coeruleus and raphe neurons fall silent. Brainstem circuits inhibit spinal motor neurons, which causes atonia of the limb muscles; the diaphragm and eye muscles are spared.
[[figure:s23e-fig0601]]

Stages and their EEG

StateEEGNotes
Awake, eyes openLow-voltage, fast (beta)Alert, active thinking
Awake, eyes closed and relaxedAlpha rhythm over the occipital regionDisappears when the eyes open
N1Theta; vertex wavesLight sleep; sudden hypnic jerks
N2Sleep spindles and K complexesAbout half of total sleep; teeth grinding (bruxism) often occurs here
N3 (slow-wave)High-amplitude delta wavesDeepest sleep, hardest to wake; sleepwalking and sleep terrors; growth hormone release peaks
REMLow-voltage, mixed fast activity with sawtooth waves; rapid eye movementsVivid dreams, muscle atonia, variable pulse and blood pressure, penile and clitoral tumescence

Cycles of NREM and REM last about 90 minutes. N3 is concentrated early in the night and REM late. With age, N3 shrinks and awakenings increase. In major depression, REM starts sooner after sleep onset (short REM latency), REM increases and N3 falls.

Disorders explained by the circuits

  • Narcolepsy type 1: autoimmune-associated loss of orexin neurons (strong link to HLA-DQB1*06:02). Wake and REM become unstable: daytime sleep attacks, cataplexy (REM atonia breaking into wakefulness, set off by laughter or surprise), sleep paralysis and hypnagogic hallucinations.
  • REM sleep behavior disorder: the atonia of REM fails, so patients act out dreams. It is often the first sign of an α-synucleinopathy (Parkinson disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, multiple system atrophy).
  • Central sleep apnea with Cheyne-Stokes breathing in heart failure reflects an unstable ventilatory control loop: slow circulation delays feedback to the chemoreceptors, and the chemoreceptors are oversensitive to CO2.
  • Restless legs syndrome: linked to low iron in the brain and altered dopamine signalling; symptoms follow a circadian pattern and peak in the evening.

Drugs that act on sleep circuits

DrugMechanism
Suvorexant, lemborexant, daridorexantOrexin receptor antagonists (insomnia)
RamelteonMelatonin MT1/MT2 receptor agonist (sleep-onset insomnia)
Zolpidem, eszopicloneBind the benzodiazepine site of GABAA receptors containing α1 subunits
Modafinil, armodafinilWake promotion, mainly by blocking dopamine reuptake
SolriamfetolDopamine and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor
PitolisantHistamine H3 antagonist/inverse agonist, which increases histamine release
Sodium oxybateGABAB agonist (gamma-hydroxybutyrate); consolidates night sleep and reduces cataplexy
Pearl: NREM parasomnias (sleepwalking, sleep terrors) come out of N3 in the first third of the night, and the person remembers little. REM sleep behavior disorder happens in the second half of the night, and the person can often recall the dream.

sections.heading: How drugs injure the nervous system: mechanisms of neurotoxicity
sections.html:
Drug neurotoxicity follows a few patterns: too much of the intended effect (sedation, ataxia), interference with neurotransmitter systems (dopamine blockade, serotonin excess), damage to long axons (peripheral neuropathy) and immune-mediated reactions.

Antiseizure drugs

DrugToxicity and mechanism
PhenytoinZero-order (saturable) elimination in the usual dose range: a small dose increase can raise the level steeply. Toxicity in order of rising level: nystagmus, ataxia, slurred speech, confusion. Chronic use: gingival overgrowth, coarse facies, hirsutism, low folate, osteomalacia, cerebellar atrophy. Strong CYP inducer; teratogenic (fetal hydantoin effects). Highly protein bound, so low albumin raises the free fraction.
CarbamazepineHyponatremia (SIADH-like), aplastic anemia and agranulocytosis, liver injury, autoinduction of its own CYP3A4 metabolism, teratogenic. HLA-B*15:02 (common in people of Southeast and East Asian ancestry) greatly raises the risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis.
ValproateHepatotoxicity (highest in young children on several drugs or with mitochondrial disease), pancreatitis, thrombocytopenia, tremor, weight gain, hair loss, hyperammonemic encephalopathy (even with normal liver tests). Strongest teratogen among them: neural tube defects and lower childhood IQ. Inhibits drug metabolism, including glucuronidation of lamotrigine.
LamotrigineRash, including SJS/TEN; risk rises with fast titration and with valproate (which roughly doubles lamotrigine levels).
TopiramateCarbonic anhydrase inhibition gives a non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis and calcium phosphate kidney stones. Also word-finding problems, paresthesias, weight loss, acute angle-closure glaucoma, oral clefts.
LevetiracetamIrritability, depression and behaviour change.

Dopamine blockade and the movement spectrum

D2 antagonists (antipsychotics, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine) reduce dopamine signalling in the nigrostriatal pathway, which leaves striatal acetylcholine relatively unopposed.

  • Acute dystonia (hours to days) and parkinsonism (weeks) respond to antimuscarinic drugs (benztropine) or diphenhydramine.
  • Akathisia (days to weeks) is a subjective, driven restlessness.
  • Tardive dyskinesia (months to years) is thought to come from upregulated, supersensitive D2 receptors. Anticholinergics worsen it. VMAT2 inhibitors (valbenazine, deutetrabenazine) deplete presynaptic dopamine and reduce it.
  • Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is sudden, severe dopamine blockade in the hypothalamus and striatum: fever, lead-pipe rigidity, autonomic instability, altered mental status and a high creatine kinase.

Serotonin excess

Combining serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, tramadol, linezolid or other MAO inhibitors, triptans in high doses, dextromethorphan) overstimulates 5-HT2A receptors: agitation, tremor, clonus and hyperreflexia (worse in the legs), diaphoresis, mydriasis, diarrhoea and hyperthermia. Linezolid is a weak, nonselective MAO inhibitor.

Peripheral neuropathy and other targets

DrugMechanism or pattern
VincristineBinds tubulin and blocks microtubule assembly, impairing axonal transport: length-dependent sensorimotor neuropathy and autonomic neuropathy (constipation, ileus)
PaclitaxelStabilizes microtubules; also disrupts axonal transport
Cisplatin, oxaliplatinDamage dorsal root ganglion neurons (sensory neuronopathy); cisplatin is ototoxic; oxaliplatin causes acute cold-triggered dysesthesias
IsoniazidDepletes pyridoxine (vitamin B6), the cofactor for glutamate decarboxylase, so GABA synthesis falls: neuropathy with chronic use, seizures in overdose
MetronidazoleCerebellar dysfunction (with reversible lesions of the dentate nuclei on MRI) and neuropathy with long courses
Linezolid (long courses)Peripheral and optic neuropathy (mitochondrial toxicity)
Fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosidesCan unmask or worsen myasthenia gravis (neuromuscular transmission); fluoroquinolones also lower the seizure threshold and cause neuropathy
Calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, cyclosporine)Tremor and posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (endothelial injury and failed autoregulation)
Exam trap: rigidity with slow reflexes points to neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Clonus with brisk reflexes points to serotonin syndrome.

sections.heading: Seizures in practice: the first seizure, choosing a drug, febrile seizures and functional events
sections.html:
Is it a seizure?

FeatureGeneralized seizureSyncopeFunctional (psychogenic nonepileptic) event
TriggerOften none; sleep deprivation, alcoholStanding, pain, venipuncture, exertionEmotional stress; often in front of others
MovementsTonic then rhythmic, synchronous clonic jerksA few brief jerks are commonWaxing and waning, asynchronous, side-to-side head shaking, pelvic thrusting
EyesOpenOpenOften forcibly closed
Duration and recovery1–2 minutes; confusion afterwardSeconds; quick return to normalOften longer than 5 minutes; may recall events
Other cluesLateral tongue bite, incontinencePallor, sweating before the eventCrying during the event

The first seizure

  • Check glucose, sodium, calcium, magnesium, a pregnancy test where relevant, and a toxicology screen. Look for alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal.
  • Lumbar puncture only if infection or subarachnoid hemorrhage is suspected.
  • Emergency CT if there is a focal deficit, head trauma, anticoagulation or failure to recover. Otherwise an MRI of the brain and an EEG are the standard work-up of an unprovoked first seizure.
  • When to start a drug: usually after a second unprovoked seizure. Start after a first one if recurrence risk is high: an epileptiform EEG, a relevant brain lesion, prior brain injury or a seizure from sleep. Early treatment lowers the short-term recurrence risk but does not change long-term remission.

Choosing an antiseizure drug

SituationUsual choicesAvoid or caution
Focal epilepsyLamotrigine, levetiracetam; carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine are alternatives—
Generalized epilepsy (including juvenile myoclonic)Valproate is most effective; levetiracetam or lamotrigine when valproate is unsuitableCarbamazepine, oxcarbazepine and phenytoin can worsen absence and myoclonic seizures; lamotrigine can worsen myoclonus
Childhood absence epilepsyEthosuximideValproate works but has more side effects
Anyone who could become pregnantLamotrigine or levetiracetam, plus folic acid before conceptionAvoid valproate (malformations, lower IQ, autism) and topiramate if possible
Pregnancy on lamotrigineCheck levels: clearance rises markedly, so doses often need to go up—
Older adultsLamotrigine or levetiracetamEnzyme inducers interact with many drugs and thin bones

Enzyme-inducing drugs (carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, high-dose topiramate) reduce the effectiveness of hormonal contraceptives. An IUD avoids the problem.

Febrile seizures

  • Children aged 6 months to 5 years with fever and no CNS infection or prior afebrile seizure.
  • Simple: generalized, under 15 minutes, once in 24 hours. Complex: focal, prolonged or repeated.
  • For a simple febrile seizure in a well-appearing, vaccinated child, no EEG, imaging or blood tests are needed. Lumbar puncture is for meningeal signs or a child who still looks unwell, and should be considered in infants who are unimmunized or already on antibiotics.
  • About a third recur. Antipyretics make the child comfortable but do not prevent recurrence, and daily antiseizure drugs are not recommended.

Functional (psychogenic nonepileptic) seizures

Video-EEG monitoring that captures a typical event without EEG change is the diagnostic standard. Some patients have both epilepsy and functional events. Explain the diagnosis clearly and without blame; cognitive behavioural therapy is the main treatment. Taper antiseizure drugs if there is no coexisting epilepsy.

Exam trap: a teenager with morning jerks who drops a cup, plus an occasional convulsion, has juvenile myoclonic epilepsy. It usually needs lifelong treatment, and carbamazepine can make it worse.

sections.heading: Status epilepticus: emergency management
sections.html:
Convulsive status epilepticus is a seizure lasting 5 minutes or more, or repeated seizures without return to baseline between them. After about 30 minutes, lasting neuronal injury becomes likely, and benzodiazepines lose effect as GABAA receptors are internalized. Treat by the clock.

[[figure:s23e-fig0602]]

Step by step

  1. Stabilize: airway, oxygen, cardiac monitoring, IV access. Check fingerstick glucose. Give thiamine before glucose if the patient may be malnourished or alcohol-dependent.
  2. Benzodiazepine at 5 minutes: IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (up to 4 mg per dose), repeated once if needed. Without IV access, IM midazolam (10 mg in adults over 40 kg) works as well. Rectal or intranasal options suit prehospital and home care.
  3. Second-line drug if seizures continue after the benzodiazepine: IV levetiracetam, fosphenytoin or valproate. A large trial found them about equally effective, so choose by patient factors: avoid valproate in pregnancy and liver disease; fosphenytoin can cause hypotension and arrhythmias and needs cardiac monitoring.
  4. Refractory status (seizures continue after these drugs): intubate and start a continuous infusion of midazolam, propofol or pentobarbital, guided by continuous EEG.

Look for the cause in parallel

  • Low antiseizure drug levels (missed doses), hyponatremia, hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia, alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, drug toxicity (for example, isoniazid, bupropion, tricyclics), CNS infection, stroke, tumour, trauma, eclampsia.
  • Isoniazid overdose: seizures resist benzodiazepines; give IV pyridoxine.
  • Eclampsia: magnesium sulfate is the anticonvulsant of choice.

Nonconvulsive status

If the patient does not start to wake within about 20–30 minutes after the movements stop, or has subtle twitching of the face or eyes, suspect nonconvulsive status epilepticus and obtain an EEG. It is common in ICU patients with unexplained coma.

Exam trap: do not wait for a CT scan or a drug level before giving a benzodiazepine to a patient who is still seizing.

sections.heading: Headache in practice: red flags, migraine, cluster, tension-type and medication overuse
sections.html:
Find the dangerous headache first

Red flagThink ofFirst test
Thunderclap onset (peak within a minute)Subarachnoid hemorrhage, reversible cerebral vasoconstriction, arterial dissectionNoncontrast head CT; if negative and more than 6 hours from onset, lumbar puncture or CT angiography
Fever, neck stiffness, rashMeningitisBlood cultures, empirical antibiotics, lumbar puncture
New headache after age 50 with jaw claudication or scalp tendernessGiant cell arteritisESR and CRP; start glucocorticoids without waiting for the biopsy
Worse lying down, on waking, with Valsalva; papilledemaRaised intracranial pressure (mass, venous sinus thrombosis, idiopathic intracranial hypertension)MRI with venography, then lumbar puncture with opening pressure
Worse when upright, better lying flatLow CSF pressure (after lumbar puncture or a spontaneous leak)MRI with contrast
New focal deficit, seizure, confusion; cancer or immunosuppression; pregnancy or postpartumMass, abscess, venous thrombosis, preeclampsiaMRI (or CT first in an emergency)

Migraine

Recurrent attacks lasting 4–72 hours with at least two of unilateral, pulsating, moderate-severe and worse with activity, plus nausea or light and sound sensitivity. A third have aura. Neuroimaging is not needed when the pattern is typical and the examination is normal.

  • Acute, mild-moderate: an NSAID or acetaminophen, taken early.
  • Acute, moderate-severe: a triptan, often combined with an NSAID. If triptans fail or are contraindicated (vascular disease), use a gepant or lasmiditan.
  • Emergency department: IV fluids, an IV dopamine antagonist antiemetic (metoclopramide or prochlorperazine; add diphenhydramine to prevent akathisia), ketorolac, and dexamethasone to reduce early recurrence. Avoid opioids.
  • Prevention when attacks are frequent (for example, 4 or more headache days a month) or disabling: propranolol or metoprolol, topiramate, amitriptyline, candesartan, CGRP monoclonal antibodies or atogepant. OnabotulinumtoxinA is for chronic migraine (15 or more headache days a month).
  • Choose by comorbidity: a β-blocker for hypertension (not in asthma), amitriptyline for poor sleep or depression (sedating, weight gain), topiramate for obesity (not with kidney stones or pregnancy plans).
  • Migraine with aura: estrogen-containing contraceptives are contraindicated because of stroke risk. Use progestin-only methods or an IUD.
  • Pregnancy: acetaminophen first; metoclopramide for nausea. Avoid ergots, valproate and topiramate.

Cluster headache

Severe unilateral orbital or temporal pain for 15–180 minutes, up to several times a day, often at the same time each night, with same-side tearing, red eye, nasal congestion or ptosis. Patients are restless and pace. It is more common in men and smokers.

  • Acute: 100% oxygen at 12–15 L/min by non-rebreather mask, or subcutaneous sumatriptan.
  • Prevention during a cluster: verapamil, with ECG monitoring for heart block as the dose rises. A short course of oral glucocorticoids or an occipital nerve block can bridge until verapamil works.

Tension-type headache

Bilateral, pressing, mild-moderate, without nausea or worsening on activity. Treat with an NSAID or acetaminophen; amitriptyline prevents frequent episodes.

Medication-overuse headache

Headache on 15 or more days a month in someone with a primary headache who uses simple analgesics on 15 or more days a month, or triptans, opioids, butalbital or combination analgesics on 10 or more days a month, for over 3 months. Withdraw the overused drug (taper opioids and butalbital) and start a preventive drug.

Exam trap: a first or worst headache that peaks within a minute is a subarachnoid hemorrhage until proven otherwise, even if the patient has migraine.

sections.heading: Sleep disorders in practice: insomnia, hypersomnolence, sleep apnea, restless legs and parasomnias
sections.html:
Chronic insomnia

Difficulty starting or keeping sleep at least 3 nights a week for 3 months, with daytime impairment, despite adequate opportunity to sleep. Look for depression, anxiety, pain, sleep apnea, restless legs, alcohol, caffeine and drugs (corticosteroids, stimulants, some antidepressants).

  • First line: cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I): sleep restriction, stimulus control (bed only for sleep; get up if awake), a fixed wake time and work on unhelpful beliefs about sleep. It lasts longer than drugs.
  • Drugs, short term and at the lowest dose, if CBT-I is not enough: orexin receptor antagonists, nonbenzodiazepine hypnotics (zolpidem, eszopiclone), low-dose doxepin for sleep maintenance, ramelteon for sleep onset.
  • Older adults: avoid benzodiazepines, Z-drugs and sedating antihistamines (diphenhydramine). They cause falls, fractures, confusion and anticholinergic effects.

Narcolepsy

  • Chronic daytime sleepiness with sleep attacks; type 1 adds cataplexy (brief muscle weakness with laughter or surprise) or low CSF orexin.
  • Diagnosis: overnight polysomnography (to exclude other causes and ensure enough sleep) followed the next day by a multiple sleep latency test: mean sleep latency of 8 minutes or less and 2 or more sleep-onset REM periods. Stop REM-suppressing antidepressants beforehand if safe.
  • Treatment: scheduled naps and regular sleep; modafinil or armodafinil, solriamfetol, pitolisant or stimulants for sleepiness. Sodium oxybate (and pitolisant) also reduce cataplexy. Counsel on driving while sleepy.

Obstructive and central sleep apnea

  • OSA: snoring, witnessed apneas, daytime sleepiness, obesity, large neck, hypertension. Diagnose with polysomnography or a home sleep apnea test; the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) grades it (5–14 mild, 15–29 moderate, 30 or more severe).
  • Treatment: CPAP for symptomatic or moderate-severe OSA, weight loss (tirzepatide is approved for moderate-severe OSA with obesity), positional therapy, oral appliances, and hypoglossal nerve stimulation for selected patients who cannot use CPAP.
  • Central sleep apnea: heart failure (Cheyne-Stokes breathing), opioids, stroke, high altitude. Treat the cause first. Adaptive servo-ventilation is contraindicated in heart failure with an ejection fraction of 45% or less because it increased mortality.

Restless legs syndrome

  • An urge to move the legs with unpleasant sensations, at rest, worse in the evening, relieved by movement. Clinical diagnosis.
  • Check ferritin and transferrin saturation. Give iron if ferritin is 75 ng/mL or less or transferrin saturation is under 20%; IV iron works faster.
  • Drug of choice: an α2δ ligand (gabapentin enacarbil, gabapentin, pregabalin). Dopamine agonists are no longer preferred for routine use because of augmentation: symptoms start earlier, become more intense and spread to the arms.
  • Look for secondary causes: iron deficiency, pregnancy, kidney failure, neuropathy, and drugs (antihistamines, antidopaminergic antiemetics, many antidepressants).

Parasomnias

DisorderStage and timingManagement
Sleepwalking, sleep terrors (children)N3, first third of the night; little recallReassurance, safety, regular sleep; most children outgrow them
Nightmare disorderREM, late night; vivid recall, fully alert on wakingImagery rehearsal therapy; treat PTSD if present
REM sleep behavior disorder (older men)REM, second half of the night; acts out dreams, can be wokenPolysomnography (REM without atonia); bedroom safety; melatonin or clonazepam; counsel about later Parkinson disease or Lewy body dementia

Circadian rhythm disorders

  • Delayed sleep-wake phase (adolescents): falls asleep very late, cannot wake for school, sleeps normally on free days. Fixed wake time, bright light in the morning, low-dose melatonin in the early evening.
  • Advanced phase (older adults): sleepy early in the evening, wakes very early. Bright light in the evening.
  • Shift work disorder: bright light during the shift, dark sleeping room, planned naps; modafinil or armodafinil for sleepiness at work.

furtherReading.label: StatPearls: Circadian Rhythm Sleep-Wake Disorders (NCBI Bookshelf)

sections.heading: Neurologic adverse drug effects in practice: recognition and management
sections.html:
Hyperthermic drug syndromes

FeatureNeuroleptic malignant syndromeSerotonin syndromeAnticholinergic toxicity
CauseDopamine antagonist (or abrupt stop of levodopa)Two or more serotonergic drugs, or an overdoseAntihistamines, tricyclics, antimuscarinics
OnsetOver daysWithin hoursWithin hours
NeuromuscularLead-pipe rigidity, slow reflexesClonus, hyperreflexia, tremorNormal tone and reflexes
OtherMutism, high CK, leukocytosisDiarrhea, sweating, dilated pupilsDry hot skin, urinary retention, absent bowel sounds, dilated pupils
TreatmentStop the drug, cool, fluids, benzodiazepines; dantrolene or bromocriptine if severeStop the drugs, benzodiazepines, cool; cyproheptadine if not settlingStop the drug, supportive care; physostigmine in selected cases

Drug-induced movement disorders

  • Acute dystonia (torticollis, oculogyric crisis, tongue protrusion) within hours to days of an antipsychotic or antiemetic: IV or IM diphenhydramine or benztropine.
  • Akathisia: lower the dose or switch; propranolol helps.
  • Parkinsonism: lower the dose or switch to an antipsychotic with less D2 blockade; an antimuscarinic can help.
  • Tardive dyskinesia: stop metoclopramide; for patients who need an antipsychotic, keep the lowest effective dose and add a VMAT2 inhibitor (valbenazine or deutetrabenazine). Clozapine carries the lowest risk. Avoid anticholinergics.

Antiseizure drug toxicity

  • Phenytoin: nystagmus, ataxia, then confusion. Correct the total level for low albumin, or better, measure the free level. Hold doses until symptoms settle. Use fosphenytoin IV, which avoids the tissue injury of IV phenytoin.
  • Carbamazepine: screen for HLA-B*15:02 in patients of Asian ancestry before starting; check sodium and blood counts.
  • Valproate hyperammonemic encephalopathy: confusion with high ammonia and normal liver tests. Stop valproate; levocarnitine may help.
  • Lamotrigine rash: stop the drug at the first sign of a rash that could be serious; do not rechallenge after SJS.

Sedative toxicity and reversal

  • Opioids: miosis, respiratory depression, coma. Give naloxone, titrated to breathing rather than full wakefulness in opioid-dependent patients. Long-acting opioids may outlast it, so watch closely and repeat or infuse.
  • Benzodiazepines: usually supportive care (airway). Flumazenil can provoke seizures in chronic benzodiazepine users and after co-ingestion of proconvulsants such as tricyclics, so it is rarely the right answer outside reversal of procedural sedation.

Other patterns to recognize

  • Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome: headache, confusion, seizures and visual loss with posterior white matter edema on MRI. Causes include tacrolimus and cyclosporine, severe hypertension, eclampsia and some chemotherapy. Lower the blood pressure and stop or switch the drug.
  • Isoniazid: give pyridoxine with it to people at risk of neuropathy (diabetes, alcohol use, malnutrition, pregnancy, HIV, chronic kidney disease).
  • Chemotherapy neuropathy: dose reduction or delay is the main tool; duloxetine is the drug with evidence for painful neuropathy.
  • Anticholinergic burden in older adults: diphenhydramine, oxybutynin, tricyclics, first-generation antihistamines and some antipsychotics add up to confusion, falls, constipation and urinary retention. Review and deprescribe; prefer drugs with low anticholinergic activity.
  • Linezolid with an SSRI can cause serotonin syndrome; metronidazole can cause reversible cerebellar ataxia.
Exam trap: a confused older adult with new urinary retention and dry mouth often has drug-induced delirium. The answer is to stop the drug, not to add a sedative.
