title: Eye · Infection, tumours, glaucoma, lens, pupil and eye movements

sections.heading: Infections and inflammation of the eye and orbit
sections.html:
The eye is layered like an onion, and naming the layer that is inflamed predicts both the symptoms and the urgency. The conjunctiva covers the sclera and lines the lids; the cornea is the clear, avascular front window; the uvea (iris, ciliary body and choroid) is the vascular middle coat; the sclera is the tough outer coat with a thin episclera over it. The orbital septum, a fibrous sheet from the orbital rim into the lids, separates the superficial lid tissues from the orbit proper.

Conjunctivitis

TypeTypical organism or causeDistinguishing features
ViralAdenovirus (most common overall)Watery discharge, gritty feel, often starts in one eye and spreads to the other; tender preauricular node; very contagious
BacterialStaphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalisPurulent discharge, lids stuck together on waking
Hyperacute bacterialNeisseria gonorrhoeaeCopious pus that reaccumulates within minutes; can perforate the cornea
Inclusion (adult)Chlamydia trachomatis serotypes D–KChronic follicular conjunctivitis in a sexually active adult
AllergicIgE-mediated mast cell degranulationItching dominates; bilateral; stringy mucus; atopic history

Neonatal conjunctivitis is timed from birth. A chemical reaction to prophylactic drops appears in the first day. Gonococcal infection appears in roughly the first 2–5 days and is a medical emergency. Chlamydial infection appears later, around days 5–14, and the infant may go on to develop an afebrile pneumonia with a repetitive staccato cough. Herpes simplex can cause neonatal keratoconjunctivitis, often with skin vesicles. Erythromycin ointment at birth prevents gonococcal disease but does not reliably prevent chlamydial disease.

Keratitis

  • Bacterial: contact lens wear, especially overnight wear, is the main risk. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the classic culprit and can melt the cornea within a day.
  • Herpes simplex: branching dendritic ulcers that stain with fluorescein. The virus lies latent in the trigeminal ganglion and reactivates, so attacks recur and corneal scarring builds up. Corneal sensation is reduced.
  • Herpes zoster ophthalmicus: shingles of V1. Vesicles on the side or tip of the nose (supplied by the nasociliary branch) predict eye involvement.
  • Acanthamoeba and fungi: contact lenses rinsed in tap water, or trauma with plant matter. Pain is often out of proportion to the findings.

Uveitis, scleritis and episcleritis

Anterior uveitis (iritis) causes pain, photophobia, a red ring around the cornea (ciliary flush), a small pupil, and white cells and protein flare in the anterior chamber; pus may layer as a hypopyon. It is linked to the HLA-B27 spondyloarthropathies (ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, psoriatic arthritis), sarcoidosis, Behçet disease and juvenile idiopathic arthritis (often painless in children, hence screening). Posterior uveitis has more infectious causes, such as toxoplasmosis and CMV.

EpiscleritisScleritis
PainMild or noneSevere, deep and boring; wakes the patient; globe tender
ColourBright red, sectoralViolet-blue hue
Phenylephrine dropsVessels blanchDeep vessels do not blanch
AssociationsUsually noneRheumatoid arthritis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, other vasculitides
RiskSelf-limitedScleral thinning and perforation; vision loss

Preseptal versus orbital cellulitis

Infection in front of the orbital septum (preseptal) causes lid swelling and redness only. Infection behind it (orbital) adds pain with eye movement, restricted movement, proptosis, double vision and, at worst, loss of vision. In children it usually spreads from ethmoid sinusitis through the paper-thin medial orbital wall (lamina papyracea). The ophthalmic veins have no valves and drain into the cavernous sinus, so orbital infection can cause cavernous sinus thrombosis: bilateral eye signs, palsies of the nerves in the sinus (III, IV, V1, V2 and VI) and a very ill patient.

Dacryocystitis is infection of an obstructed lacrimal sac: a tender red swelling below the medial canthus, with pus expressed from the punctum on pressure.

Exam trap: itching points to allergy, pus to bacteria, and a watery eye with a tender preauricular node to adenovirus. Pain, photophobia and reduced vision are not features of simple conjunctivitis; they suggest keratitis, uveitis or glaucoma.
Pearl: topical corticosteroids worsen epithelial herpes keratitis and can let bacterial or fungal keratitis run riot. They are given only by an ophthalmologist after the diagnosis is secure.

sections.heading: Tumours of the eye, eyelid and orbit
sections.html:
Retinoblastoma

Retinoblastoma is the most common primary intraocular cancer of childhood. It arises from immature retinal cells that have lost both copies of the RB1 tumour suppressor gene on chromosome 13q14. The RB protein, when unphosphorylated, holds E2F transcription factors inactive and so blocks entry into S phase. Cyclin D–CDK4/6 phosphorylates RB in late G1 and releases E2F. Without RB, the G1 checkpoint is gone.

  • Heritable form (about 40%): one mutant allele is present in every cell (germline), so a single further somatic hit in any retinal cell starts a tumour. Tumours tend to be bilateral or multifocal and present earlier. Survivors carry a lifelong risk of second cancers, notably osteosarcoma and soft-tissue sarcomas, which radiation raises further.
  • Nonheritable form: both hits occur in the same retinal cell after conception. Tumours are unilateral and single.

This is Knudson's two-hit model. Inheritance of the heritable form is autosomal dominant at the level of the family, although each tumour is recessive at the level of the cell.

Presentation: a white pupillary reflex (leukocoria) instead of the red reflex, often noticed in a flash photograph, and strabismus because the affected eye cannot fixate. Histology shows small round blue cells forming rosettes around a central lumen (Flexner–Wintersteiner rosettes). Calcification within the mass is typical on imaging.

Adult intraocular tumours

TumourKey points
Metastasis to the choroidThe most common intraocular malignancy in adults overall. Breast cancer in women and lung cancer in both sexes are the usual primaries. Creamy yellow, often multiple or bilateral, choroidal lesions.
Uveal (choroidal) melanomaThe most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults. Arises from melanocytes of the choroid, ciliary body or iris. Risk factors: fair skin, light iris colour, ocular melanocytosis. Driver mutations differ from skin melanoma (GNAQ or GNA11 rather than BRAF), and BAP1 loss predicts metastasis. The globe has no lymphatics, so spread is through the blood, overwhelmingly to the liver.
Ocular adnexal lymphomaUsually extranodal marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma: slow, painless proptosis or a salmon-pink patch under the conjunctiva in an older adult.

Eyelid tumours

  • Basal cell carcinoma: by far the most common eyelid malignancy, usually on the lower lid or medial canthus. A pearly nodule with rolled edges, fine surface vessels and sometimes a central ulcer; lashes over it fall out. Histology: nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading. It invades locally and rarely metastasises.
  • Sebaceous gland carcinoma: arises from the meibomian glands, more often on the upper lid in older adults. It mimics a recurrent chalazion or a one-sided chronic blepharitis. Histology shows cells with foamy, vacuolated, lipid-rich cytoplasm. It can spread to regional lymph nodes and is more aggressive than basal cell carcinoma.
  • Squamous cell carcinoma and melanoma of the lid are less common.
Exam trap: a "chalazion" that keeps coming back in the same place in an older adult needs a biopsy, not another incision and curettage.
Pearl: any child with an absent or white red reflex, or a new squint, needs prompt examination by an ophthalmologist. Retinoblastoma is curable when found inside the eye.

sections.heading: Aqueous humour, glaucoma, the lens and refraction
sections.html:
Aqueous humour

The non-pigmented epithelium of the ciliary body secretes aqueous humour into the posterior chamber. This depends on carbonic anhydrase and is stimulated through β-adrenergic receptors. Aqueous flows through the pupil into the anterior chamber and leaves mainly through the trabecular meshwork into Schlemm's canal at the angle between iris and cornea. A smaller share leaves through the ciliary muscle (the uveoscleral route).

Glaucoma

Glaucoma is a progressive optic neuropathy: retinal ganglion cell axons are lost, the optic cup enlarges, and the visual field shrinks from the periphery inward. Raised intraocular pressure is the main modifiable risk factor, but glaucoma can occur at normal pressure.

Primary open-angleAcute angle-closure
MechanismAngle open; outflow through the meshwork gradually reducedPeripheral iris pushed against the meshwork, blocking outflow; pressure rises within hours
Risk factorsAge, African ancestry, family history, myopia, high pressure, thin corneaHyperopia (short eye, shallow chamber), older age, East Asian ancestry, female sex, a lens that thickens with age
SymptomsNone until late; peripheral field lossSevere eye pain, headache, nausea and vomiting, halos around lights, blurred vision
SignsIncreased cup-to-disc ratio, notched rimRed eye, hazy cornea, fixed mid-dilated pupil, eye hard to palpation

Angle closure is triggered by anything that dilates the pupil (a mid-dilated pupil lets the iris bunch into the angle): a dark room, emotional stress, anticholinergic or sympathomimetic drugs. Some drugs, notably topiramate and sulfonamide-related compounds, cause bilateral angle closure by swelling the ciliary body and pushing the lens–iris forward, often with a sudden myopic shift.

Drugs that lower intraocular pressure

Class (example)MechanismNotable adverse effects
Prostaglandin F2α analogue (latanoprost)Increases uveoscleral outflowDarker iris (more melanin), longer lashes, periorbital fat loss
β-Blocker (timolol)Decreases aqueous productionSystemic absorption: bradycardia, bronchospasm
α2-Agonist (brimonidine, apraclonidine)Decreases production; brimonidine also adds uveoscleral outflowAllergic conjunctivitis; brimonidine can cause apnoea and sedation in infants
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (dorzolamide drops, acetazolamide orally or IV)Decreases productionSystemic: paraesthesia, metabolic acidosis, kidney stones
Muscarinic agonist (pilocarpine)Contracts the ciliary muscle and iris sphincter, opening the meshwork and pulling the iris out of the angleBrow ache, dim vision, myopic shift

The lens

For near vision, parasympathetic fibres (via M3 receptors) contract the ring-shaped ciliary muscle. This slackens the zonular fibres, and the elastic lens rounds up and gains focusing power (accommodation). With age the lens stiffens, so near focus fails from the mid-40s onward: presbyopia.

Cataract is opacity of the lens. Causes include age (nuclear sclerosis), diabetes (sorbitol made by aldose reductase draws water into the lens), long-term corticosteroids (typically posterior subcapsular, causing glare and poor near vision), radiation, trauma, congenital rubella, and galactosaemia or galactokinase deficiency (galactitol accumulates in the lens).

Marfan syndromeHomocystinuria (cystathionine β-synthase deficiency)
DefectFibrillin-1 (FBN1), autosomal dominantEnzyme defect, autosomal recessive; plasma homocysteine and methionine high
Lens displacementUsually upward and outwardUsually downward and inward
Other cluesAortic root dilation, normal intellectIntellectual disability, venous and arterial thrombosis, osteoporosis

Refractive errors

  • Myopia: the eye is too long (or too powerful) and distant images focus in front of the retina; corrected with a diverging (concave, minus) lens.
  • Hyperopia: the eye is too short and images focus behind the retina; corrected with a converging (convex, plus) lens.
  • Astigmatism: unequal corneal curvature in different meridians; corrected with a cylindrical lens.

Lids and tear film

A hordeolum (stye) is an acute, painful staphylococcal infection of a lash follicle or gland. A chalazion is a painless, firm lump from a blocked meibomian gland with lipogranulomatous inflammation. Entropion (lid turning in) makes lashes scratch the cornea; ectropion (lid turning out) causes watering and exposure. Dry eye results from too little tear production (for example, Sjögren syndrome) or too much evaporation (meibomian gland dysfunction).

Exam trap: anticholinergic drugs (including some antihistamines and antidepressants) are a classic trigger of angle closure in a patient with a narrow angle. They do not cause angle closure in open-angle glaucoma.

sections.heading: The visual pathway and the pupil
sections.html:
Localising a visual field defect

Each retina sends its nasal fibres (which see the temporal field) across the midline at the optic chiasm, while temporal fibres stay on the same side. So, from the chiasm backward, each side of the brain handles the opposite half of the visual world from both eyes.

[[figure:s23e-fig0701]]
LesionDefectTypical cause
Optic nerveLoss of vision in that eye; relative afferent pupillary defectOptic neuritis, ischaemic optic neuropathy, compression
Optic chiasm (crossing fibres)Bitemporal hemianopiaPituitary adenoma (from below; upper fields go first), craniopharyngioma (from above; lower fields first)
Optic tractContralateral homonymous hemianopia, often incongruousTumour, stroke, demyelination
Meyer loop (temporal lobe)Contralateral upper quadrantanopiaMiddle cerebral artery stroke, temporal lobe surgery or tumour
Parietal radiationContralateral lower quadrantanopiaMiddle cerebral artery stroke, tumour
Occipital cortexContralateral homonymous hemianopia, congruous, often sparing the maculaPosterior cerebral artery stroke (the occipital pole also has middle cerebral supply)

Fibres from the lower retina (upper field) loop forward into the temporal lobe, which is why the upper quadrant is lost with temporal lesions. Pupillary fibres leave the optic tract before the lateral geniculate nucleus, so lesions behind the tract do not affect the light reflex.

Pupillary pathways

[[figure:s23e-fig0702]]

The light reflex runs from the retina to the pretectal nucleus of the midbrain, which projects to both Edinger–Westphal nuclei. Parasympathetic fibres travel on the outside of the oculomotor nerve to the ciliary ganglion, then through the short ciliary nerves to the iris sphincter. Light in one eye therefore constricts both pupils.

A relative afferent pupillary defect (Marcus Gunn pupil) is found with the swinging-flashlight test. When the light swings from the healthy eye to the eye with optic nerve damage, both pupils dilate, because less light signal reaches the midbrain. It points to optic nerve (or severe retinal) disease, not to cataract or refractive error.

Abnormal pupils

PupilFindingsLesion and causes
Horner syndromeMild ptosis, small pupil, anisocoria greater in the dark; facial anhidrosis with central or preganglionic lesionsInterrupted oculosympathetic chain: lateral medulla or cord (1st order), lung apex or neck (2nd order), internal carotid wall or cavernous sinus (3rd order)
Oculomotor nerve palsyEye down and out, ptosis; dilated, unreactive pupil if the parasympathetic fibres are involvedCompression (posterior communicating artery aneurysm, uncal herniation) affects the pupil early; microvascular ischaemia (diabetes) typically spares it
Tonic (Adie) pupilLarge pupil, poor light reaction, slow sustained constriction to near effort; often reduced tendon reflexesDamage to the ciliary ganglion or short ciliary nerves; the denervated sphincter becomes supersensitive to dilute pilocarpine
Argyll Robertson pupilSmall, irregular pupils in both eyes that constrict to near effort but not to light (light–near dissociation)Dorsal midbrain near the pretectal area; classic cause is tertiary syphilis
Exam trap: in Horner syndrome the ptosis is mild (the superior tarsal, or Müller, muscle is sympathetic). Complete ptosis means the levator palpebrae, and so the oculomotor nerve.
Pearl: a Pancoast tumour at the lung apex can produce Horner syndrome, shoulder and arm pain, and hand weakness by also involving the lower trunk of the brachial plexus.

furtherReading.label: StatPearls: Neuroanatomy, Pupillary Light Reflexes and Pathway (NCBI Bookshelf)

sections.heading: Eye movements: cranial nerves III, IV and VI, gaze centres and the orbit
sections.html:
Which nerve moves which muscle

The lateral rectus is supplied by the abducens nerve (VI), the superior oblique by the trochlear nerve (IV), and every other extraocular muscle, plus the levator palpebrae and the pupillary sphincter, by the oculomotor nerve (III).

PalsyResting eye positionDouble vision and compensation
Oculomotor (III)Down and out; ptosis; pupil may be dilatedDiplopia in most directions (unless ptosis covers the eye)
Trochlear (IV)Affected eye slightly higherVertical diplopia, worst looking down and in (reading, going downstairs); head tilted away from the affected side
Abducens (VI)Affected eye turned inHorizontal diplopia, worst looking toward the affected side; head turned toward that side

The abducens nerve has a long course along the clivus, so it is often the first nerve affected by raised intracranial pressure, a false-localising sign. The trochlear nerve is the only cranial nerve to leave the dorsal brainstem and it crosses, so a trochlear nucleus lesion affects the opposite superior oblique. It is easily torn in head trauma.

Horizontal gaze and the MLF

To look right, the right paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF) drives the right abducens nucleus. That nucleus sends one set of axons to the right lateral rectus and, through the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF), another to the left oculomotor subnucleus for the left medial rectus.

  • Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO): an MLF lesion. On gaze to the opposite side, the eye on the side of the lesion fails to adduct and the abducting eye shows nystagmus. Convergence is preserved, because it does not use the MLF. In a young adult, especially when both sides are affected, think multiple sclerosis; in an older adult, think brainstem stroke.
  • Abducens nucleus or PPRF lesion: neither eye can look toward the side of the lesion (a gaze palsy).
  • One-and-a-half syndrome: one lesion takes out the abducens nucleus (or PPRF) and the adjacent MLF. The only horizontal movement left is abduction of the opposite eye.

Thyroid eye disease

Autoantibodies, chiefly against the TSH receptor, activate orbital fibroblasts (with signalling through the IGF-1 receptor). The fibroblasts make glycosaminoglycans, which draw in water, and some become fat cells. The extraocular muscles swell (sparing their tendons) and orbital fat expands. The results are proptosis, lid retraction, restricted eye movement with double vision (the inferior and medial recti are hit most often), exposure of the cornea and, in severe cases, compression of the optic nerve at the orbital apex. Smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor. The disease can occur when the patient is hyperthyroid, euthyroid or hypothyroid.

Childhood strabismus and amblyopia

Amblyopia is reduced vision in an eye whose image the developing brain has suppressed: from a squint, unequal refractive error (anisometropia), or a blocked visual axis (congenital cataract, ptosis covering the pupil). It is reversible only while the visual system is still plastic, roughly the first 7–8 years. Esotropia (eye turned in) is the most common childhood squint. The corneal light reflex test and the cover test detect a true squint; a broad nasal bridge with epicanthal folds can make straight eyes look crossed (pseudostrabismus).

Nystagmus is a rhythmic eye oscillation. In jerk nystagmus, the slow phase is the abnormal drift and the fast phase is the correction, and the direction is named by the fast phase.

Exam trap: in an INO the medial rectus works when the patient converges, so the nerve and the muscle are intact. The problem is the connection between the abducens nucleus and the opposite oculomotor nucleus.

furtherReading.label: StatPearls: Cranial Nerve III Palsy (Oculomotor Palsy) (NCBI Bookshelf)

title: Ophthalmology · Red eye, tumours, glaucoma, cataract, pupils and squint

sections.heading: The red eye: triage and management
sections.html:
Most red eyes are conjunctivitis and settle with simple care. The task is to spot the few that threaten sight. Red flags: moderate to severe pain, photophobia, reduced visual acuity, a corneal opacity or staining defect, a fixed or irregular pupil, contact lens wear, recent eye surgery or trauma, a newborn, and an immunocompromised patient. Any red flag means same-day ophthalmology.

Conjunctivitis

  • Viral: supportive care (cool compresses, lubricants), hand hygiene and avoiding shared towels. Antibiotics do not help.
  • Bacterial: often self-limited; a topical antibiotic shortens the illness and allows earlier return to school or work. In contact lens wearers, choose drops that cover Pseudomonas (a fluoroquinolone) and stop lens wear.
  • Allergic: avoid the allergen; topical antihistamine with mast cell–stabilising action.
  • Hyperacute (gonococcal): systemic ceftriaxone plus saline irrigation, same-day ophthalmology, and treatment for chlamydia unless it has been excluded; test and treat sexual partners.
  • Adult chlamydial: systemic treatment (azithromycin or doxycycline), with testing of the patient and partners for other sexually transmitted infections.

Neonatal conjunctivitis

Take a Gram stain and culture plus a chlamydial test from the conjunctiva. Gonococcal disease needs hospital admission, a single parenteral dose of ceftriaxone (use another third-generation cephalosporin in a jaundiced or premature infant), eye irrigation and a search for disseminated infection. Chlamydial disease needs a systemic macrolide, because topical treatment does not clear the nasopharynx and does not prevent pneumonia; erythromycin in the first weeks of life carries a small risk of infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. Treat the mother and her partners in both cases.

Keratitis

Fluorescein staining with a cobalt-blue light shows epithelial defects. A white corneal infiltrate in a contact lens wearer is presumed bacterial: no patching, remove the lenses, start intensive topical antibiotics, and get same-day ophthalmology for corneal scrapings. Herpes simplex dendritic keratitis is treated with a topical antiviral (such as ganciclovir gel or trifluridine) or an oral antiviral (acyclovir or valacyclovir). Topical steroids are avoided in epithelial disease. Herpes zoster ophthalmicus needs an oral antiviral within 72 hours of the rash and prompt eye examination, especially if the nose is involved.

Uveitis, scleritis, episcleritis and endophthalmitis

ConditionKey featuresManagement
Anterior uveitisPhotophobia, ciliary flush, small pupil, cells in the anterior chamberSame-day ophthalmology; topical corticosteroid plus a cycloplegic (relieves ciliary spasm and stops the iris sticking to the lens); look for an associated systemic disease
EpiscleritisMild ache, sectoral redness that blanchesReassurance, lubricants; oral NSAID if troublesome
ScleritisSevere boring pain, tender globe, violet hueUrgent ophthalmology; systemic NSAID, then systemic corticosteroid or immunosuppression; screen for rheumatoid arthritis and vasculitis
EndophthalmitisPain and falling vision days after surgery or an injection; hypopyonEmergency: vitreous sampling and intravitreal antibiotics (for example, vancomycin plus ceftazidime); vitrectomy if vision is very poor

Preseptal versus orbital cellulitis

Preseptal cellulitis with normal vision, eye movements and pupils can be treated with oral antibiotics covering staphylococci and streptococci, with close review. Pain on eye movement, restricted movement, proptosis, reduced vision or a relative afferent pupillary defect means orbital cellulitis: admit, give intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics, obtain CT of the orbits and sinuses with contrast, and involve ophthalmology and ENT. Drain a subperiosteal or orbital abscess if it is large or vision is threatened. A child who cannot be examined properly is treated as having orbital cellulitis until proven otherwise.

Exam trap: never patch an eye with a suspected contact lens–related ulcer, and never start a steroid–antibiotic combination drop for an undiagnosed red eye in primary care.

sections.heading: Leukocoria, intraocular tumours and suspicious eyelid lesions
sections.html:
Red reflex screening and leukocoria

The red reflex is checked at every newborn and infant examination. An absent, dull, white or asymmetric reflex needs an urgent referral to an ophthalmologist for a dilated fundus examination. The differential diagnosis includes retinoblastoma, congenital cataract, persistent fetal vasculature, Coats disease, retinopathy of prematurity and toxocariasis. Parents' photographs that show a white pupil should be taken seriously.

Retinoblastoma

  • Diagnosis: examination under anaesthesia with ocular ultrasound. MRI of the brain and orbits stages the tumour (optic nerve invasion, a pineal tumour). CT is avoided because ionising radiation raises the risk of second cancers in children with germline RB1 mutations.
  • Treatment aims first at life, then the eye, then vision: chemotherapy (intravenous or intra-arterial), local therapies (laser, cryotherapy, plaque radiotherapy), and enucleation for advanced disease. Biopsy through the eye wall is avoided because it can seed the tumour.
  • Genetics: offer germline RB1 testing to every affected child. Siblings and offspring of a carrier need regular dilated examinations from birth, and testing for the family's mutation when it is known. Survivors with a germline mutation need lifelong vigilance for second cancers, such as osteosarcoma.

Uveal melanoma

It is usually found on routine examination or causes painless blurred vision or field loss. A pigmented (sometimes amelanotic), dome- or mushroom-shaped choroidal mass is confirmed with ultrasound, which typically shows low internal reflectivity. Treatment for most tumours is radiotherapy (plaque brachytherapy or proton beam), which saves the eye; large tumours need enucleation. Because metastasis goes almost always to the liver, staging and surveillance focus on liver imaging. A small, flat, stable pigmented choroidal lesion is usually a benign nevus and is photographed and followed.

Choroidal metastasis and adnexal lymphoma

New visual symptoms in someone with breast or lung cancer suggest choroidal metastasis; treatment is that of the systemic cancer, with local radiotherapy if needed. A painless, slowly growing orbital mass or a salmon-coloured conjunctival patch in an older adult needs a biopsy for lymphoma, followed by systemic staging. Localised marginal zone lymphoma usually responds well to low-dose radiotherapy.

Eyelid lesions

Features that suggest cancer: a lesion that grows, ulcerates or bleeds; lash loss over it; distortion of the lid margin; pearly edges with surface vessels; and recurrence of a "chalazion" in the same spot. These need a biopsy. Basal cell carcinoma near the eye is removed with margin control (Mohs micrographic surgery or frozen-section excision) to clear the tumour while saving lid tissue. A recurrent chalazion in an older adult needs a full-thickness biopsy to exclude sebaceous carcinoma.

Exam trap: do not "wait and repeat the red reflex" in an infant with leukocoria, and do not order CT as the first imaging test for suspected retinoblastoma.

sections.heading: Glaucoma, cataract, lids and the dry eye: clinical management
sections.html:
Acute angle-closure glaucoma: an emergency

Typical patient: an older, long-sighted adult with sudden severe eye pain, frontal headache, nausea and vomiting, halos around lights and blurred vision, often after time in a dark room or a new anticholinergic or sympathomimetic drug. The eye is red, the cornea hazy, the pupil fixed and mid-dilated, and the globe hard. Vomiting and headache can mislead toward migraine or an intracranial cause.

  1. Lower the pressure now: topical β-blocker, α2-agonist and, once the pressure starts to fall, pilocarpine; plus acetazolamide by mouth or IV. Add an IV hyperosmotic agent (mannitol) if the pressure does not respond. Treat pain and vomiting. Get emergency ophthalmology.
  2. Definitive treatment: laser peripheral iridotomy makes a small hole in the peripheral iris so aqueous can bypass the pupil. Lens extraction is an alternative in suitable patients.
  3. Protect the other eye: its angle is usually just as narrow, so it gets a prophylactic iridotomy.

Avoid mydriatics and anticholinergic drugs until the angle has been opened. Drug-induced angle closure from topiramate is usually bilateral; stop the drug and treat with aqueous suppressants and cycloplegia (pilocarpine and iridotomy do not help because the mechanism is not pupillary block).

Primary open-angle glaucoma

It is painless and silent until advanced, so it is found by examination: an enlarged or asymmetric optic cup, raised pressure and characteristic field loss. Refer people at higher risk (older age, African ancestry, family history, high myopia, long-term steroid use) for a comprehensive eye examination. First-line treatment is a prostaglandin analogue drop at night, or selective laser trabeculoplasty. Other drops are added if the target pressure is not reached, and surgery (trabeculectomy, tube shunts) follows if disease progresses.

Cataract

Gradual, painless blurring, glare and halos when driving at night, faded colours, and frequent spectacle changes (nuclear cataract makes the eye more myopic). The red reflex is dimmed. There is no medical treatment. Surgery (phacoemulsification with an artificial intraocular lens) is offered when the cataract limits daily activities such as driving or reading. Months to years later, the capsule behind the implant may cloud (posterior capsule opacification); this is cleared with a YAG laser capsulotomy.

Lids

  • Hordeolum and chalazion: warm compresses and lid massage several times a day. A chalazion that persists for weeks to months can be injected with a corticosteroid or removed by incision and curettage. Systemic antibiotics are kept for spreading cellulitis.
  • Blepharitis: chronic lid-margin inflammation; lid hygiene and warm compresses; associated with rosacea and seborrhoeic dermatitis.
  • Ptosis: most acquired ptosis in older adults is aponeurotic (the levator tendon stretches) with good levator function. New ptosis with a pupil change, double vision or variable weakness that worsens through the day needs evaluation for oculomotor palsy, Horner syndrome or myasthenia gravis.
  • Entropion and ectropion: lubricate and protect the cornea; surgical repair is definitive.

Dry eye

Gritty, burning eyes that are worse with screens, wind and dry air, and paradoxical watering. Treat with artificial tears, lid hygiene for meibomian gland dysfunction, and anti-inflammatory drops (such as cyclosporine) for persistent disease. Dry eyes with a dry mouth suggest Sjögren syndrome: test for anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB antibodies. Review drugs that dry the eye, such as anticholinergics and antihistamines.

Exam trap: a vomiting patient with a headache and a red eye with a mid-dilated pupil does not need a head CT first. Measure the pressure and treat the glaucoma.

sections.heading: Anisocoria, double vision and the child with a squint
sections.html:
Anisocoria: which pupil is abnormal?

Compare the pupils in bright light and in dim light. If the difference is greater in the dark, the small pupil fails to dilate: think Horner syndrome (or simple physiological anisocoria). If the difference is greater in bright light, the large pupil fails to constrict: think oculomotor palsy, a tonic pupil or a drug (an anticholinergic patch or drops).

Oculomotor nerve palsy

PatternLikely causeAction
Pupil dilated, with or without headacheCompression, classically a posterior communicating artery aneurysmEmergency CT angiography (or MR angiography); if negative and suspicion stays high, catheter angiography
Pupil spared, motor palsy complete, older patient with vascular risk factorsMicrovascular ischaemia of the nerveControl vascular risk factors and follow closely; image if the pupil becomes involved, other signs appear, or there is no recovery within about 3 months
Palsy with a decreased level of consciousnessUncal herniationEmergency neuroimaging and measures to lower intracranial pressure

Horner syndrome

Confirm with eye drops when the diagnosis is uncertain: apraclonidine dilates a Horner pupil (denervated dilator muscle is supersensitive) and reverses the anisocoria; cocaine drops fail to dilate it. Hydroxyamphetamine releases noradrenaline from an intact third-order neuron, so a pupil that does not dilate localises the lesion to the postganglionic neuron. Investigate by site:

  • Acute and painful (neck, face or head pain): carotid artery dissection until proven otherwise. Emergency CT angiography or MR angiography of the head and neck.
  • With shoulder or arm pain in a smoker: chest imaging for an apical lung tumour.
  • With brainstem signs: MRI of the brain (lateral medullary infarct).
  • In a child without birth trauma: imaging of the chest, neck and abdomen and urine catecholamines for neuroblastoma.

Internuclear ophthalmoplegia and other gaze problems

A young adult with an INO, especially a bilateral one, needs MRI of the brain and spinal cord with contrast for demyelination. An older adult with a sudden INO is managed as having a brainstem stroke. Double vision that varies through the day, with ptosis that worsens with sustained upgaze and normal pupils, suggests myasthenia gravis.

Thyroid eye disease

  • All patients: stop smoking, restore and keep a normal thyroid state, and lubricate the eyes. Selenium can help mild, active disease.
  • Moderate-to-severe active disease (inflammation, progressing proptosis or double vision): intravenous methylprednisolone pulses are a standard first line; teprotumumab (an IGF-1 receptor antibody) and other immunotherapy are alternatives. Teprotumumab can cause hearing loss and high blood glucose.
  • Sight-threatening disease (compressive optic neuropathy, corneal breakdown): urgent high-dose IV corticosteroid, then orbital decompression if vision does not recover promptly.
  • Radioactive iodine can worsen active eye disease; when it is used in a patient with mild active disease or risk factors, oral corticosteroid cover is given.
  • Strabismus surgery and lid surgery are done only after the disease has been inactive and stable.

Strabismus and amblyopia in children

  • Intermittent misalignment in the first months of life is common. A constant squint at any age, or any squint after about 4–6 months, needs referral to a paediatric ophthalmologist.
  • A symmetric corneal light reflex and a normal cover test with a broad nasal bridge mean pseudostrabismus: reassure.
  • Amblyopia: correct the cause (spectacles for refractive error, surgery for cataract or ptosis), then penalise the stronger eye with patching or atropine drops so the brain must use the weaker eye. Results are best the younger the child.
Exam trap: a painful Horner syndrome after a neck injury, chiropractic manipulation or a coughing fit is a carotid dissection. It needs vascular imaging, not reassurance.

sections.heading: Retina and optic disc: vascular, degenerative and developmental disease
sections.html:
The inner two-thirds of the neural retina (ganglion cells, inner nuclear layer) is fed by the central retinal artery, an end artery and usually the first branch of the ophthalmic artery. The outer retina, including the photoreceptors, depends on the choroid (ciliary arteries). The fovea has no inner retinal layers and no retinal vessels, so it lives entirely off the choroid. These two facts explain most of the fundus signs below.

[[figure:s23e-fig0801]]

Diabetic retinopathy

Chronic hyperglycaemia injures retinal capillaries: pericytes are lost early, the basement membrane thickens, and capillaries become leaky and then close. Contributing mechanisms include polyol (sorbitol) accumulation through aldose reductase, advanced glycation end products and oxidative stress.

  • Non-proliferative: microaneurysms (the earliest visible sign), dot-blot haemorrhages in the inner nuclear and outer plexiform layers, hard exudates (lipid leaked from capillaries), cotton-wool spots (swollen axons in infarcted nerve-fibre layer), venous beading.
  • Proliferative: ischaemic retina releases VEGF, and fragile new vessels grow on the disc, the retina or the iris. They bleed into the vitreous, pull the retina off (tractional detachment) and can block the drainage angle (neovascular glaucoma).
  • Macular oedema can occur at any stage and is the commonest cause of visual loss in diabetes.

Hypertensive retinopathy

Chronic hypertension thickens arteriolar walls: generalised and focal narrowing, a widened light reflex, and arteriovenous nicking where a stiff arteriole compresses a vein at a crossing. Severe or abrupt elevation adds flame haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, hard exudates arranged around the fovea and, in a hypertensive emergency, optic disc swelling.

Retinal vascular occlusions

FeatureCentral retinal artery occlusionCentral retinal vein occlusion
Usual causeEmbolus (carotid plaque, heart) or giant cell arteritisThrombosis at the lamina cribrosa in older patients with hypertension, diabetes or glaucoma
OnsetSudden, painless, profound monocular lossSudden or subacute painless blurring, often milder
FundusPale, opaque inner retina; cherry-red spot at the fovea; thin arteries, sometimes a visible embolusDilated tortuous veins, haemorrhages in all four quadrants, cotton-wool spots, disc swelling
Why it looks that wayIschaemic inner retina turns white; the thin fovea lets the intact choroid show throughVenous outflow is blocked, so blood and fluid back up into every quadrant

A cilioretinal artery (a choroidal branch present in some people) can keep a strip of retina between disc and fovea alive in arterial occlusion and preserve central vision.

Retinal detachment

The neural retina separates from the retinal pigment epithelium. Rhegmatogenous detachment starts with a break, often when the vitreous pulls away with age; risk rises with high myopia, cataract surgery and trauma. Tractional detachment follows fibrovascular scarring (proliferative diabetic retinopathy). Exudative detachment is fluid under an intact retina (severe hypertension, tumours, inflammation). Symptoms: photopsia (flashes, from traction on photoreceptors), a shower of new floaters, then a shadow spreading across the field.

Age-related macular degeneration

  • Dry (atrophic), the majority: drusen (deposits between the retinal pigment epithelium and Bruch membrane), pigment changes and finally geographic atrophy. Slow loss of central vision.
  • Wet (neovascular): choroidal new vessels, driven by VEGF, break through Bruch membrane and leak or bleed under the macula. Rapid distortion (straight lines look bent) and a central scotoma.
  • Risks: age, smoking (the strongest modifiable risk), family history and complement pathway variants such as CFH.

Inherited and developmental retinopathies

  • Retinitis pigmentosa: a group of inherited rod-then-cone dystrophies. Night blindness comes first, then a slowly shrinking peripheral field. Fundus: dark bone-spicule pigment in the mid-periphery, narrowed arterioles and a waxy pale disc. It appears with hearing loss in Usher syndrome and is a feature of abetalipoproteinaemia and Refsum disease.
  • Retinopathy of prematurity: the retina of a preterm infant is not yet fully vascularised. High oxygen exposure suppresses vessel growth, and the later relative hypoxia drives VEGF-mediated abnormal growth at the vascular border that can cause fibrosis and detachment.
  • Cytomegalovirus retinitis: in advanced HIV with a CD4 count below 50/mm3, a necrotising retinitis spreads along vessels as white granular areas mixed with haemorrhage. It is painless, causes floaters and field loss, and can lead to detachment.

The swollen or pale optic disc

ConditionMechanismHallmarks
PapilloedemaRaised intracranial pressure transmitted along the optic nerve sheath stops axoplasmic flowBilateral disc swelling; acuity normal early; enlarged blind spot; brief visual obscurations
Optic neuritisInflammatory demyelination of the optic nerveYoung adult; pain on eye movement; reduced acuity and colour vision; relative afferent pupillary defect; disc often normal
Non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathyHypoperfusion of the short posterior ciliary arteries in a crowded small discOlder patient with vascular risk factors; painless loss noticed on waking; altitudinal field defect; sectoral disc swelling
Arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathyGiant cell arteritis occludes the posterior ciliary arteriesOver 50; headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness; high ESR/CRP; pale swollen disc; high risk to the other eye
Exam trap: a cherry-red spot is not specific to arterial occlusion. It also appears in lysosomal storage diseases (Tay-Sachs, Niemann-Pick), where lipid-laden ganglion cells whiten the retina around the fovea, which has no ganglion cells.
Pearl: anti-VEGF drugs injected into the vitreous treat three of the diseases above (diabetic macular oedema, wet macular degeneration, macular oedema from vein occlusion) because all three are driven by the same ischaemia-to-VEGF signal.

sections.heading: Eye trauma: chemical, blunt and penetrating injury
sections.html:
Chemical injury

Alkalis (lime, lye, ammonia, cement, drain cleaner) are usually worse than acids. They saponify cell-membrane lipids, cause liquefactive necrosis and keep penetrating into the anterior chamber, where they damage the trabecular meshwork, lens and ciliary body. Acids denature surface proteins and cause coagulative necrosis, which forms a barrier and limits deeper spread (hydrofluoric acid is an exception). Ischaemic whitening of the limbus marks loss of limbal stem cells and a poor prognosis.

Corneal abrasion and foreign body

The corneal epithelium is richly innervated by the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, so a small defect causes intense pain, tearing and photophobia. Fluorescein pools in the epithelial defect and glows green under cobalt-blue light. Vertical linear streaks suggest a foreign body under the upper lid. An iron foreign body left in place leaves a rust ring.

Open globe

A full-thickness wound of the cornea or sclera, from a laceration or a blunt rupture (typically at the limbus or behind the muscle insertions, where the sclera is thinnest). Signs: a peaked or teardrop pupil pointing at the wound, a shallow or flat anterior chamber, extensive subconjunctival haemorrhage, uveal tissue in the wound, low intraocular pressure and a positive Seidel sign (fluorescein diluted by leaking aqueous).

Hyphema

Blood in the anterior chamber, usually from a torn iris root or ciliary body vessel after blunt trauma. Red cells can clog the trabecular meshwork and raise intraocular pressure. In sickle cell disease or trait, red cells sickle in the low-oxygen, acidic aqueous and obstruct outflow even more readily.

Orbital floor (blow-out) fracture

A blow from an object larger than the orbital rim (a fist, a ball) raises orbital pressure, and the thin floor (the roof of the maxillary sinus) gives way. Orbital fat and the inferior rectus may herniate and become trapped.

  • Limited upgaze and vertical double vision.
  • Numb cheek, side of the nose and upper lip (infraorbital nerve, a branch of V2, runs in the floor).
  • Enophthalmos once swelling settles; subcutaneous emphysema after nose blowing.
  • Traction on a trapped muscle can trigger the oculocardiac reflex (trigeminal afferent, vagal efferent): bradycardia, nausea and syncope.

Retrobulbar haemorrhage

Bleeding behind the globe in a closed orbit (bounded by bone and the orbital septum) causes an orbital compartment syndrome. Rising pressure compresses the optic nerve and its blood supply: proptosis, a tense eyelid, restricted eye movements, falling vision and a relative afferent pupillary defect.

InjuryKey signKey danger
Alkali splashWhite, ischaemic limbusDeep penetration, corneal scarring, glaucoma
Corneal abrasionFluorescein-staining defectBacterial keratitis, especially in contact lens wearers
Open globeTeardrop pupil, Seidel positiveExtrusion of contents, endophthalmitis
HyphemaLayered blood in the anterior chamberRaised pressure, rebleeding, corneal blood staining
Orbital floor fractureRestricted upgaze, numb cheekMuscle entrapment
Retrobulbar haemorrhageTense proptosis with visual lossOptic nerve ischaemia within hours
Exam trap: numbness of the cheek and upper lip after orbital trauma localises to the infraorbital nerve (V2), not to the facial nerve, which is motor to the face.

sections.heading: Drugs that harm the eye: mechanisms
sections.html:
Drug toxicity can strike every layer of the eye. Grouping the drugs by the structure they damage makes them easier to recall.

StructureDrugEffect and mechanism
LensGlucocorticoids (any route, including inhaled at high dose)Posterior subcapsular cataract
Trabecular outflowGlucocorticoids, especially eye dropsRaised intraocular pressure and open-angle glaucoma in susceptible people (reduced outflow through the trabecular meshwork)
Drainage angle (pupillary block)Antimuscarinics (topical cycloplegics, scopolamine, tricyclics, first-generation antihistamines, nebulised ipratropium), sympathomimeticsMid-dilated pupil pushes the peripheral iris against the trabecular meshwork in an eye with a narrow angle: acute angle closure
Drainage angle (no pupillary block)Topiramate and some other sulfonamide-derived drugsCiliochoroidal effusion rotates the lens-iris diaphragm forward: bilateral angle closure with a sudden myopic shift, usually in the first weeks of treatment
Iris dilator muscleTamsulosin (alpha-1A antagonist)Floppy iris that billows and constricts during cataract surgery; the effect persists after the drug is stopped
CorneaAmiodaroneWhorl-shaped epithelial deposits in most long-term users, usually harmless; occasional haloes
CorneaRepeated topical anaestheticBlocks epithelial healing and blink protection: toxic keratopathy, ulceration and melting
Macula / retinal pigment epitheliumHydroxychloroquine, chloroquineDose-dependent, irreversible maculopathy (bull's-eye pattern late)
MaculaFingolimodMacular oedema, mostly in the first months
PhotoreceptorsSildenafil and other PDE5 inhibitorsCross-inhibition of retinal PDE6 alters phototransduction: a blue tint and light sensitivity
Photoreceptors / conesDigoxin (toxic levels)Yellow-green tinted vision and haloes
Retina (peripheral)Vigabatrin (irreversible GABA transaminase inhibitor)Permanent concentric constriction of the visual field
Optic nerveEthambutol (also isoniazid, linezolid)Optic neuropathy: falling acuity, red-green colour loss, central scotoma; dose-related and worse with renal impairment
Optic nerveAmiodarone (rare)Insidious, often bilateral optic neuropathy with disc swelling
Uvea and scleraBisphosphonates (especially intravenous)Anterior uveitis, scleritis

Eye drops with effects beyond the eye

  • Timolol (non-selective beta-blocker) is absorbed through the nasolacrimal mucosa without first-pass metabolism: bradycardia, heart block and bronchospasm in asthma or COPD.
  • Prostaglandin analogues (latanoprost): permanent darkening of the iris, longer eyelashes and periorbital skin darkening.
  • Brimonidine (alpha-2 agonist): can cause apnoea and lethargy in infants, because it crosses their blood-brain barrier.
  • Atropine drops: flushing, fever, tachycardia and delirium, especially in children and the elderly.
Exam trap: topiramate-induced angle closure is not pupillary block, so laser iridotomy does not help. Stopping the drug and treating the pressure does.
Pearl: PDE5 inhibitors tint vision blue, digoxin tints it yellow. Ethambutol takes away the red-green distinction.

title: Ophthalmology · Retina, eye injuries and drug toxicity

sections.heading: Retinal and optic nerve disease: diagnosis and management
sections.html:
Sudden painless monocular visual loss: triage

DiagnosisCluesImmediate action
Central retinal artery occlusionProfound loss; relative afferent pupillary defect; pale retina with cherry-red spotTreat as a stroke: same-day transfer to a stroke centre; in patients over 50 check ESR and CRP for giant cell arteritis
Giant cell arteritisHeadache, jaw claudication, polymyalgia symptoms, high ESR/CRPHigh-dose glucocorticoid at once (intravenous if vision is already lost), then temporal artery biopsy or ultrasound
Central retinal vein occlusionHaemorrhages in all quadrants, dilated veinsOphthalmology within days; control vascular risk factors; anti-VEGF for macular oedema
Retinal detachmentFlashes, new floaters, a spreading curtainSame-day ophthalmology for surgical repair
Vitreous haemorrhageSudden floaters or loss in proliferative diabetic retinopathy; red reflex dimOphthalmology; ultrasound if the retina cannot be seen

Central retinal artery occlusion is an ocular stroke. After it, look for the source as for a TIA or ischaemic stroke: carotid imaging, ECG with rhythm monitoring and echocardiography, glucose and lipids. Ocular massage and anterior chamber paracentesis have no proven benefit; reperfusion therapy is being studied and is offered only within research or stroke-centre protocols.

Diabetic retinopathy

  • Screening: in type 2 diabetes at diagnosis; in type 1 diabetes within 5 years of onset; then yearly (every 1–2 years if no retinopathy and glycaemia is well controlled). In pregnancy, examine before conception or in the first trimester and follow closely, because retinopathy can worsen.
  • Control glucose, blood pressure and lipids in every patient.
  • Centre-involving macular oedema with reduced vision: intravitreal anti-VEGF injections are first line.
  • Proliferative disease: panretinal laser photocoagulation (destroys ischaemic peripheral retina so it stops making VEGF) or anti-VEGF injections. Laser costs peripheral and night vision.
  • Non-clearing vitreous haemorrhage or tractional detachment: vitrectomy.

Macular degeneration

  • Stop smoking in all patients.
  • Intermediate dry AMD, or advanced AMD in one eye: an AREDS2-type supplement (vitamins C and E, zinc, copper, lutein and zeaxanthin). The newer formula left out beta-carotene, which raised lung cancer risk in smokers.
  • Self-monitoring with an Amsler grid: new distortion means urgent review.
  • Wet AMD: repeated intravitreal anti-VEGF injections (for example aflibercept, ranibizumab, bevacizumab, faricimab). Started promptly, they preserve and often improve vision.

Other retinal conditions

  • Hypertensive retinopathy with disc swelling, haemorrhages and exudates means a hypertensive emergency: admit and lower blood pressure in a controlled way with an intravenous agent, by no more than about a quarter in the first hour.
  • Retinopathy of prematurity: screen infants born at 30 weeks' gestation or earlier or weighing 1,500 g or less, and selected larger infants with an unstable course. Severe disease is treated with laser to the avascular retina or intravitreal anti-VEGF.
  • CMV retinitis (CD4 below 50/mm3): oral valganciclovir, with intravitreal ganciclovir or foscarnet added for lesions threatening the fovea or optic nerve, and start antiretroviral therapy. Screen patients with very low CD4 counts with dilated eye examinations.
  • Retinitis pigmentosa: diagnosis by fundus appearance, visual fields and electroretinography (reduced rod responses). Genetic counselling. Gene therapy exists for RPE65-related disease.

Swollen optic discs

  • Bilateral disc swelling = papilloedema until proved otherwise: urgent brain imaging (MRI with venography) before lumbar puncture. If imaging is normal, measure opening pressure; idiopathic intracranial hypertension is treated with weight loss and acetazolamide, with surgery when vision is threatened.
  • Optic neuritis: MRI of the brain and orbits with gadolinium to assess multiple sclerosis risk. High-dose intravenous methylprednisolone speeds recovery but does not change final acuity; oral prednisone at standard doses alone is avoided because it was linked to more recurrences.
  • Non-arteritic ischaemic optic neuropathy: no proven treatment; manage vascular risk factors and screen for sleep apnoea. Always exclude giant cell arteritis in older patients.
Exam trap: in suspected giant cell arteritis, never wait for the biopsy to start glucocorticoids. The biopsy stays diagnostic for a couple of weeks after treatment starts.
Pearl: after a central retinal vein occlusion, new vessels can grow on the iris over the following months and close the angle (neovascular glaucoma). Scheduled follow-up looks for this.

sections.heading: Eye injuries in the emergency department
sections.html:
Chemical injury: irrigate first

  1. Start copious irrigation at once, before taking a history, measuring visual acuity or examining. Tap water is acceptable at the scene; in hospital use normal saline or lactated Ringer solution, with a topical anaesthetic drop and a lid speculum or irrigating lens to keep the eye open.
  2. Sweep the fornices for retained particles (lime, cement).
  3. Check the tear-film pH with a strip a few minutes after stopping. Continue until it is neutral (about 7.0–7.5).
  4. Then examine (acuity, fluorescein, pressure) and refer urgently to ophthalmology.

Corneal abrasion

  • Fluorescein examination; evert the upper lid to look for a foreign body.
  • Topical antibiotic: erythromycin ointment or a similar agent; for contact lens wearers, an anti-pseudomonal fluoroquinolone drop, no lens wear until healed, and no patching.
  • Oral analgesia or topical NSAID. Never send the patient home with a topical anaesthetic.
  • Re-examine in 24–48 hours if large, central or in a lens wearer.

Corneal foreign body: remove a superficial one under topical anaesthesia with a needle or burr at the slit lamp. A high-velocity injury (hammering metal on metal, grinding) can drive a particle into the globe: get CT of the orbits and avoid MRI until a metallic foreign body is excluded.

Open globe

  • Place a rigid shield that rests on the bony orbit; no pressure on the eye, no pressure measurement, no topical drops or ointment.
  • Keep the patient nil by mouth, give analgesia and an antiemetic (vomiting and straining raise eye pressure), update tetanus and start systemic antibiotics against endophthalmitis.
  • CT of the orbits; emergency ophthalmology for surgical repair. Do not remove a protruding object.

Hyphema

  • Rigid shield, head of the bed raised about 30–45°, rest, and avoidance of NSAIDs and antiplatelet drugs.
  • Ophthalmology manages topical steroid and cycloplegic drops and checks pressure; rebleeding is most likely in the first days.
  • Screen patients at risk (for example, of African ancestry) for sickle cell disease or trait; in these patients, avoid carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and osmotic agents, which can promote sickling or hypovolaemia.

Orbital floor fracture

  • CT of the orbits with thin cuts. Advise no nose blowing.
  • Urgent surgery for entrapment with an oculocardiac reflex (bradycardia, nausea, syncope) — classic in children, whose flexible floor can snap back and trap the muscle while the eye looks only mildly injured.
  • Otherwise repair is often elective, within about 2 weeks, for persistent diplopia, large defects or enophthalmos.

Retrobulbar haemorrhage

Proptosis, a tense orbit, falling vision, a relative afferent pupillary defect and high intraocular pressure after trauma (or orbital or sinus surgery) need lateral canthotomy with inferior cantholysis at the bedside. It is a clinical diagnosis; do not delay decompression for imaging.

Exam trap: the first step for a chemical splash is irrigation, even before visual acuity. For an open globe it is a shield, and nothing that presses on the eye or enters it.

sections.heading: Ocular adverse drug effects: monitoring and management
sections.html:
Monitoring that prevents permanent loss

DrugWhat to do
HydroxychloroquineKeep the daily dose at or below 5 mg/kg of actual body weight. Baseline examination early in treatment, then yearly screening from 5 years of use (sooner with renal impairment, tamoxifen use, higher doses or macular disease), with optical coherence tomography and automated visual fields. Toxicity is irreversible and can progress after stopping, so the aim is to stop before symptoms.
EthambutolBaseline acuity and colour vision; ask about vision at every visit and retest regularly, more often with renal impairment or higher doses. Stop the drug at the first sign of toxicity and refer.
VigabatrinBaseline and periodic visual field testing; field loss is permanent.
FingolimodFundus examination including the macula before starting and again 3–4 months after, and at any visual change; diabetes and uveitis raise the risk of macular oedema.
Long-term glucocorticoidsPeriodic eye pressure checks and cataract surveillance, especially with steroid eye drops.

Drug-triggered acute angle closure

  • Pupillary-block type (antimuscarinics, adrenergic mydriatics in a narrow-angle eye): a painful red eye, blurred vision with haloes, headache and vomiting, a fixed mid-dilated pupil and a hazy cornea. Lower the pressure at once (topical beta-blocker, alpha-2 agonist and miotic drops, systemic acetazolamide or mannitol), then laser peripheral iridotomy in both eyes.
  • Topiramate type (bilateral, myopic shift, first weeks of treatment): stop topiramate, use aqueous suppressants and cycloplegic drops to deepen the chamber; avoid pilocarpine and iridotomy, which do not work and may worsen it.

Other effects to recognise

  • Tamsulosin: tell the cataract surgeon before surgery; stopping it beforehand does not reliably prevent floppy iris.
  • Amiodarone: corneal deposits need no action. New visual loss with disc swelling raises optic neuropathy: involve cardiology before stopping the drug.
  • Sildenafil: blue-tinged vision is dose-related and reversible. Sudden painless visual loss needs urgent review for ischaemic optic neuropathy.
  • Digoxin: coloured vision suggests toxicity; check the level, potassium, magnesium and renal function.
  • Bisphosphonates: a painful red eye after an infusion may be uveitis or scleritis and needs ophthalmology review.
  • Topical anaesthetic misuse: a non-healing epithelial defect or ring infiltrate in a patient who has been using "numbing drops" at home; stop them and refer.
  • Eye drops with systemic effects: consider timolol in a patient with new bradycardia or wheeze; teach punctal occlusion (pressing the inner corner of the eye after each drop) to reduce absorption.
Exam trap: a patient with a known narrow angle who needs an anticholinergic drug can usually receive it safely after laser iridotomy. Open-angle glaucoma is not a contraindication to anticholinergics.
