sections.heading: Ear infections and inflammation: anatomy, organisms and pathogenesis
sections.html:
The middle ear is an air-filled space ventilated through the eustachian (auditory) tube, which runs from the anterior wall of the middle ear to the lateral nasopharynx. The tube opens during swallowing and yawning, mainly through contraction of the tensor veli palatini. In young children the tube is shorter, more horizontal and less rigid, so it drains poorly and lets nasopharyngeal secretions reach the middle ear. This is why middle-ear infection peaks between 6 and 24 months of age, often right after a viral upper respiratory infection.

Acute otitis media (AOM)

A viral infection inflames the tube mucosa. The tube then blocks, air in the middle ear is absorbed, negative pressure draws in fluid, and bacteria from the nasopharynx multiply in that fluid. The usual bacteria are:

  • Streptococcus pneumoniae: reduced penicillin susceptibility comes from altered penicillin-binding proteins. Higher amoxicillin doses overcome it, while a beta-lactamase inhibitor does not help against this mechanism.
  • Nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae (unencapsulated, so the Hib vaccine does not prevent it): often produces beta-lactamase. It is the typical cause when otitis comes with purulent conjunctivitis.
  • Moraxella catarrhalis: a gram-negative diplococcus; nearly all strains produce beta-lactamase.

On otoscopy, a bulging tympanic membrane is the most specific sign. Redness alone is not, because crying also reddens the drum. Otitis media with effusion (OME) is fluid without acute inflammation. It commonly follows AOM and causes a mild conductive hearing loss.

Otitis externa

Cerumen keeps the external canal acidic and water-repellent. Repeated wetting (swimming), scratching and cotton swabs strip it, so the skin macerates and becomes infected. Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus cause most cases. The hallmark is pain when the tragus is pressed or the pinna is pulled, because the inflamed canal skin is moved.

Necrotizing (malignant) otitis externa is an invasive Pseudomonas infection, usually in older people with diabetes or other immune compromise. It spreads from the canal floor at the bony-cartilaginous junction into the temporal bone and skull base. Granulation tissue in the canal, pain out of proportion to the findings and facial nerve palsy are warning signs.

Mastoiditis and intracranial spread

The mastoid air cells connect with the middle ear, so AOM can spread into them and erode their bony walls. Pus can track outwards (a postauricular abscess that pushes the auricle forwards and down) or inwards. Inward spread can cause thrombosis of the sigmoid sinus, which lies directly behind the mastoid, as well as meningitis, epidural or brain abscess, and facial nerve palsy.

Cholesteatoma

A cholesteatoma is not a tumour and contains no cholesterol. It is a sac of keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium that keeps shedding keratin into the middle ear or mastoid. Most are acquired, from a retraction pocket of the pars flaccida in a poorly ventilated ear. The sac grows and releases enzymes that erode bone: the ossicles (conductive loss), the lateral semicircular canal (a fistula with vertigo), the facial canal and the tegmen (intracranial infection). The typical clue is painless, foul-smelling discharge that keeps coming back, with white debris on otoscopy.

LesionWhat it is made of
CholesteatomaKeratinizing squamous epithelium and keratin debris
Cholesterol granulomaCholesterol crystals surrounded by foreign-body giant cells and old blood
Granulation tissue (chronic otitis)Capillaries, fibroblasts and inflammatory cells

Herpes zoster oticus (Ramsay Hunt syndrome)

Varicella-zoster virus reactivates in the geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve. The result is severe ear pain, vesicles on the concha, canal or palate, and a lower motor neuron facial palsy. The virus can spread to the nearby vestibulocochlear nerve and cause hearing loss and vertigo. Recovery of facial function is worse than in Bell palsy.

Exam trap: "cholesteatoma" and "cholesterol granuloma" sound alike but differ. The first is skin (keratin) in the wrong place, the second a reaction to old blood.
Pearl: an older person with diabetes, severe ear pain and granulation tissue on the canal floor has an invasive Pseudomonas infection of the skull base until proven otherwise.

sections.heading: Tumours of the ear and cerebellopontine angle
sections.html:
Vestibular schwannoma

A benign tumour of Schwann cells, usually arising from the vestibular division of cranial nerve VIII inside the internal auditory canal. It grows slowly and extends into the cerebellopontine angle. Histology shows cellular areas with nuclear palisading around pink fibrillar zones (Antoni A, with Verocay bodies) next to loose, myxoid areas (Antoni B). The cells are S-100 positive.

  • Early: slowly progressive one-sided sensorineural hearing loss, often with tinnitus. Imbalance is usually mild because the brain compensates as the vestibular nerve is slowly lost.
  • Larger tumours press on the trigeminal nerve (facial numbness, a reduced corneal reflex), the cerebellum (limb ataxia) and finally the fourth ventricle (hydrocephalus). The facial nerve tolerates stretching well, so facial weakness is a late finding.

Bilateral vestibular schwannomas define NF2-related schwannomatosis (formerly neurofibromatosis type 2). It is autosomal dominant, caused by loss of the NF2 tumour suppressor on chromosome 22, which encodes merlin, a protein linking the cytoskeleton to the cell membrane. Other features are meningiomas, ependymomas and juvenile posterior subcapsular cataracts.

Paraganglioma (glomus tumour)

A tumour of paraganglion chief cells, which derive from the neural crest. Nests of chief cells (chromogranin positive) are surrounded by S-100-positive sustentacular cells in a richly vascular stroma. In the ear it arises on the promontory (glomus tympanicum) or at the jugular bulb (glomus jugulare). Typical features:

  • Pulsatile tinnitus in time with the heartbeat, and conductive hearing loss;
  • a red-purple mass seen behind an intact eardrum;
  • with jugular foramen spread, palsies of cranial nerves IX, X and XI.

Up to about a third of head and neck paragangliomas are hereditary, most often from germline variants in a succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) subunit gene. SDH is complex II of the electron transport chain and also a citric acid cycle enzyme. Its loss lets succinate build up, which stabilises hypoxia-inducible factor. Never biopsy a suspected glomus tumour through the eardrum, because it bleeds briskly.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma and the adult with a one-sided effusion

A carcinoma in the lateral nasopharynx (the fossa of Rosenmüller) can block the eustachian tube opening. It then shows up as one-sided otitis media with effusion in an adult, sometimes with a neck node or nasal bleeding. The common non-keratinizing (undifferentiated) type is strongly linked to Epstein-Barr virus and is most frequent in southern China, Southeast Asia and North Africa.

Skin cancers of the auricle

The helix gets heavy sun exposure. Squamous cell carcinoma (keratin pearls; it can spread to the parotid and neck nodes) and basal cell carcinoma are both common. Ultraviolet B light creates pyrimidine (thymine) dimers, which are repaired by nucleotide excision repair. Xeroderma pigmentosum, a defect in that repair, causes skin cancers in childhood.

TumourKey clueCell or cause
Vestibular schwannomaOne-sided sensorineural loss and tinnitusSchwann cell; NF2 (merlin)
ParagangliomaPulsatile tinnitus, red mass behind the drumNeural crest chief cell; SDH genes
Nasopharyngeal carcinomaAdult with one-sided effusion, neck nodeEpithelial; Epstein-Barr virus
Auricular squamous cell carcinomaUlcerated helix lesion in sun-exposed older adultUltraviolet damage
Exam trap: in vestibular schwannoma the facial nerve sits right next to the tumour, yet a reduced corneal reflex usually comes before facial weakness.

sections.heading: Hearing: how sound is transduced, and conductive versus sensorineural loss
sections.html:
From air to nerve

  • Middle ear: the eardrum and ossicles match the low impedance of air to the high impedance of inner-ear fluid. The large drum drives the small stapes footplate, which concentrates force and lever action. Without this, most sound energy would bounce off the fluid.
  • Cochlea: the basilar membrane is narrow and stiff at the base and wide and floppy at the apex. High frequencies peak near the base and low frequencies near the apex (tonotopy). Noise, ageing and ototoxic drugs damage the basal hair cells first, so high tones go first.
  • Hair cells sit in endolymph, which is rich in potassium. The stria vascularis keeps it about +80 mV positive (the endocochlear potential). Bending the stereocilia opens mechanotransduction channels, and K+ flowing in depolarises the cell. Inner hair cells send signals to the brain. Outer hair cells change length (through the motor protein prestin) to amplify the signal; they generate otoacoustic emissions.
  • Supporting cells recycle K+ back to the stria through gap junctions made of connexins.

Conductive versus sensorineural

Conductive loss is a problem in the canal, drum or ossicles. Sensorineural loss is a problem in the cochlea, the cochlear nerve or the central pathways. The tuning-fork tests and the audiogram tell them apart.

[[figure:s23e-fig0902]][[figure:s23e-fig0901]]
CauseTypeDistinguishing feature
Cerumen, otitis media with effusionConductiveAbnormal otoscopy
OtosclerosisConductiveNormal drum; young adult, often female; abnormal bone remodelling fixes the stapes footplate in the oval window; worsens in pregnancy
PresbycusisSensorineuralBoth ears, high tones first; trouble following speech in noise
NoiseSensorineuralNotch near 4 kHz
Vestibular schwannomaSensorineural (retrocochlear)One-sided; speech understanding worse than the tone thresholds predict

Congenital and genetic hearing loss

  • Congenital cytomegalovirus is the most common non-genetic cause. The loss may be absent at birth and appear or worsen later. Look for periventricular calcifications, microcephaly and petechiae.
  • GJB2 (connexin 26) variants are the most common genetic cause of non-syndromic sensorineural loss. They are autosomal recessive, so the parents usually hear normally.
  • Pendred syndrome (autosomal recessive, SLC26A4, pendrin): sensorineural loss with an enlarged vestibular aqueduct, plus goitre. Pendrin moves iodide across the apical membrane of thyroid cells into the follicle, so organification is impaired.
  • Alport syndrome (usually X-linked, type IV collagen alpha-5 chain): haematuria that progresses to kidney failure, high-frequency sensorineural loss and anterior lenticonus.
  • Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome (autosomal recessive potassium-channel variants): congenital deafness with a long QT interval and a risk of sudden death.
  • Waardenburg syndrome (for example PAX3): deafness, a white forelock, heterochromia of the irises and widely spaced inner canthi, from a neural crest melanocyte defect.
Exam trap: in one-sided sensorineural loss, the Weber goes to the good ear and the Rinne stays positive (air louder than bone) on the bad side, just softer.

sections.heading: Balance: vestibular physiology and peripheral vestibular disorders
sections.html:
Each labyrinth has three semicircular canals set at right angles. Their cristae sense angular acceleration, that is, head rotation. The two otolith organs, the utricle and the saccule, have maculae topped by calcium carbonate crystals (otoconia). They sense linear acceleration and head tilt relative to gravity. At rest both vestibular nerves fire tonically at equal rates. The brain reads a difference between the two sides as movement.

[[figure:s23e-fig0903]]

The vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR)

When the head turns right, the right horizontal canal is excited and the eyes move left by the same amount, so gaze stays on target. If one labyrinth or vestibular nerve stops working:

  • The healthy side's tonic firing is unopposed, so the brain senses rotation towards the healthy side. The eyes drift slowly towards the damaged side, and quick corrective jerks beat away from the lesion. This is spontaneous horizontal-torsional nystagmus that fixation dampens.
  • The head impulse test is abnormal when the head is turned quickly towards the damaged side: the eyes move with the head, then make a catch-up saccade back to the target.
  • The patient tends to veer or fall towards the damaged side.

Peripheral disorders

DisorderMechanismTime courseHearing
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV)Otoconia loosened from the utricle drift into a canal, most often the posterior canal (canalithiasis). They move with gravity when the head moves.Seconds, triggered by changes in head positionNormal
Vestibular neuritisInflammation of the vestibular nerve, probably viralContinuous vertigo for days, slow recoveryNormal
LabyrinthitisInflammation of the whole labyrinthContinuous for daysSensorineural loss
Ménière diseaseToo much endolymph (endolymphatic hydrops), linked to poor resorption in the endolymphatic sacAttacks lasting 20 minutes to 12 hoursFluctuating low-frequency sensorineural loss, tinnitus, fullness

Central causes to keep in mind

A stroke of the cerebellum or brainstem can look like vestibular neuritis. Occlusion of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA), which usually supplies the labyrinthine artery, can cause sudden vertigo with one-sided deafness, facial weakness and limb ataxia on the same side. Nystagmus that changes direction with gaze, vertical or purely torsional nystagmus, and a vertical misalignment of the eyes (skew deviation) all point to a central cause.

Motion sickness and its drugs

Motion sickness comes from a conflict between vestibular, visual and body-position signals. Scopolamine, a muscarinic antagonist given as a patch behind the ear, and first-generation H1 antihistamines such as meclizine and dimenhydrinate act on vestibular and brainstem pathways. Scopolamine side effects are anticholinergic: dry mouth, drowsiness, confusion in older adults, urinary retention and dilated pupils. Dilated pupils can trigger angle-closure glaucoma in eyes with narrow angles.

Pearl: in a peripheral lesion the fast phase beats away from the bad ear, and a quick head turn towards the bad ear shows the catch-up saccade.

furtherReading.label: StatPearls: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (NCBI Bookshelf)

sections.heading: Ear trauma: auricle, eardrum, temporal bone and pressure injury
sections.html:
Auricular haematoma

Auricular cartilage has no blood vessels of its own. It is fed by diffusion from the overlying perichondrium. A shearing blow (wrestling, boxing, rugby) bleeds into the space between cartilage and perichondrium. The cartilage loses its blood supply and dies, and the perichondrium lays down new, disorganised fibrocartilage. The result is a permanently thickened, crumpled ear ("cauliflower ear") unless the blood is drained early.

Tympanic membrane perforation

Causes include a slap or blast (a sudden pressure wave), cotton swabs or other objects, and AOM that ruptures. The eardrum is the structure most easily injured by a primary blast wave, because air-filled organs are the most vulnerable. Small traumatic perforations usually heal on their own. Vertigo or sensorineural loss after the injury suggests the inner ear was damaged as well.

Temporal bone fracture

These follow major head trauma. Signs of a fracture of the skull base include bruising over the mastoid (Battle sign), blood behind the eardrum (haemotympanum), and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) otorrhoea, or rhinorrhoea when the drum is intact and fluid drains down the eustachian tube. Beta-2 transferrin in the fluid confirms CSF, because this form of transferrin is made within the central nervous system.

PatternTypical result
Fracture that spares the otic capsule (most cases; older term: longitudinal, from a blow to the side of the head)Torn drum, haemotympanum, ossicular disruption: conductive loss. Facial nerve injury is less common.
Fracture that crosses the otic capsule (older term: transverse, from a blow to the front or back of the head)Sensorineural loss and vertigo from labyrinth damage. Facial nerve injury is more common.

Barotrauma

By Boyle's law, gas volume falls as pressure rises. During descent in an aircraft or a dive, the middle ear must be filled with air through the eustachian tube. If the tube stays shut (for example, with a cold), the relative vacuum pulls the eardrum inwards and causes pain, fluid or bleeding in the middle ear. The tube is opened by the tensor veli palatini, supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve. Forceful Valsalva against a blocked tube can rupture the round or oval window. The resulting perilymph fistula causes sudden sensorineural loss and vertigo.

Foreign bodies

Button batteries are an emergency. Current flowing through moist tissue makes hydroxide ions at the negative pole, and this causes alkaline liquefactive necrosis within hours, even with a "dead" battery. Vegetable matter swells when wet, so it should not be irrigated.

Exam trap: clear fluid from the ear after head trauma is CSF until proven otherwise. Test for beta-2 transferrin; glucose testing is unreliable.

sections.heading: Ototoxic drugs: mechanisms and patterns
sections.html:
Ototoxic drugs damage the cochlea, the vestibular system or both. Cochlear damage usually starts with the outer hair cells in the basal turn, so high frequencies go first. Patients often do not notice until the loss reaches speech frequencies. Vestibular damage is usually bilateral and symmetric, so it causes imbalance and blurred vision with head movement (oscillopsia), not spinning vertigo.

DrugMain targetMechanismReversible?
AminoglycosidesGentamicin and streptomycin mostly vestibular; amikacin, neomycin and kanamycin mostly cochlearTaken up into hair cells through mechanotransduction channels, form reactive oxygen species, trigger apoptosis; build up in inner-ear fluidsNo (permanent)
CisplatinCochlea (outer hair cells, stria vascularis)Reactive oxygen species and DNA damage; dose-related; children at highest riskNo
Loop diuretics (furosemide, ethacrynic acid)CochleaBlock the Na+-K+-2Cl− cotransporter (NKCC1) in the stria vascularis, so the endocochlear potential collapses; worst with fast high-dose IV doses and kidney failureUsually
Salicylates (high dose)CochleaInterfere with outer hair cell electromotility (prestin); tinnitus and mild lossYes, within days of stopping
Quinine, chloroquine, hydroxychloroquineCochleaCinchonism: tinnitus, hearing loss, headache, blurred vision, nauseaOften, but not always

Aminoglycosides in more depth

The risk rises with total dose and duration, high trough levels, kidney impairment, older age, and loop diuretics or other ototoxins given at the same time. A maternally inherited variant in the mitochondrial 12S ribosomal RNA gene (MT-RNR1, m.1555A>G) makes the mitochondrial ribosome look more like a bacterial one. In carriers, even a single standard dose can cause profound, permanent deafness. Because the variant is mitochondrial, it passes from a mother to all her children, and affected relatives are on the mother's side.

Pearl: aminoglycoside ototoxicity can begin or progress after the drug is stopped, because the drug stays in inner-ear fluids for a long time.
Exam trap: a patient on gentamicin who complains that the world bounces while walking has bilateral vestibular loss. There may be no vertigo and normal hearing.

title: Otolaryngology · Ear disorders: diagnosis and management

sections.heading: Otitis media, otitis externa and their complications: management
sections.html:
Acute otitis media: diagnosis

Diagnose AOM when the eardrum is moderately or severely bulging, or there is new ear discharge not caused by otitis externa. Mild bulging counts if there is recent ear pain (in a non-verbal child: holding, tugging or rubbing the ear) or intense redness of the drum. Do not diagnose AOM without middle-ear fluid; pneumatic otoscopy shows reduced drum movement.

Antibiotics or observation (children aged 6 months and older)

PresentationApproach
Severe signs (moderate or severe pain, pain for 48 hours or more, or temperature 39°C (102.2°F) or higher), or ear dischargeAntibiotics at any age
Age 6 to 23 months, both ears, not severeAntibiotics
Age 6 to 23 months, one ear, not severeAntibiotics or observation, decided with the family
Age 2 years or older, not severeAntibiotics or observation, decided with the family

Observation means pain relief now and a reliable plan to start antibiotics if the child is not better, or is worse, by 48 to 72 hours. Treat the pain in every case (acetaminophen or ibuprofen).

  • First line: high-dose amoxicillin.
  • Amoxicillin-clavulanate instead if amoxicillin was taken in the past 30 days, if there is purulent conjunctivitis too (suggesting beta-lactamase-producing H. influenzae), or if amoxicillin has failed.
  • Penicillin allergy that is not immediate-type: an oral cephalosporin such as cefdinir, cefuroxime or cefpodoxime. Intramuscular ceftriaxone is used when oral treatment fails or is not possible.
  • Reassess at 48 to 72 hours if symptoms persist. Consider tympanostomy tubes for recurrent AOM (3 episodes in 6 months, or 4 in a year with 1 in the past 6 months) when middle-ear fluid is present at the assessment.

Otitis media with effusion (OME)

Fluid without signs of acute infection. Most cases clear within 3 months, so watch and wait, and recheck every 3 to 6 months. Antibiotics, corticosteroids, antihistamines and decongestants do not help. Test hearing if the fluid lasts 3 months or more. Offer tympanostomy tubes for fluid in both ears for 3 months or more with documented hearing loss, or sooner in children at risk of speech or learning delay. For discharge through a tube, use topical antibiotic drops (a fluoroquinolone) rather than oral antibiotics.

Otitis externa

  • Uncomplicated: topical antibiotic drops, with or without a corticosteroid, for about 7 days. Insert a wick if the canal is too swollen for drops to get in. Keep the ear dry and give pain relief. Oral antibiotics are not needed.
  • If the drum is perforated, or a tube is in place, use a non-ototoxic fluoroquinolone drop, not an aminoglycoside drop.
  • Give systemic antibiotics only if infection spreads beyond the canal, or in diabetes or immune compromise.

Necrotizing otitis externa (an older adult with diabetes, severe pain, granulation tissue on the canal floor, a raised ESR, and sometimes facial palsy): image the temporal bone (CT shows bone erosion; MRI shows soft-tissue and intracranial spread). Send a culture, start IV antipseudomonal antibiotics for weeks, control the glucose, and involve ENT.

Complications

  • Acute mastoiditis: swelling, redness and tenderness behind the ear, with the auricle pushed forwards. Give IV antibiotics. Order contrast CT of the temporal bones for an abscess or intracranial spread. Myringotomy, with or without a tube, drains the middle ear; mastoidectomy is for abscess or failed treatment.
  • Cholesteatoma: painless, foul discharge that keeps coming back, a retraction pocket with white debris, and conductive loss. Treatment is surgical removal. Drops only calm the infection on top.
  • Ramsay Hunt syndrome: facial palsy plus vesicles in the ear. Give an oral corticosteroid plus an antiviral (valacyclovir or acyclovir) early, and protect the eye.
Exam trap: fluid behind the drum weeks after AOM, in a well child, is OME. It does not need another course of antibiotics.

furtherReading.label: StatPearls: Otitis Media With Effusion (NCBI Bookshelf)

sections.heading: Ear and skull-base tumours: when to image, scope or biopsy
sections.html:
Asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss or one-sided tinnitus

A meaningful difference in sensorineural loss between the ears, or one-sided tinnitus, needs a look for a retrocochlear lesion. The test of choice is gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the internal auditory canals. CT can miss small intracanalicular tumours.

Vestibular schwannoma: choosing treatment

OptionBest for
Observation with serial MRISmall, slow-growing tumours, especially in older patients or those with other illnesses (many never grow)
Stereotactic radiosurgerySmall to medium tumours that are growing
Microsurgical removalLarge tumours compressing the brainstem, or younger patients choosing removal

Bilateral tumours, or a tumour in a young person, prompt evaluation for NF2-related schwannomatosis. That means an eye exam for juvenile cataract, spinal imaging, genetic counselling and screening of relatives.

Pulsatile tinnitus

Rhythmic, pulse-synchronous tinnitus needs otoscopy and vascular imaging. A red mass behind an intact drum suggests a paraganglioma: image with CT of the temporal bone and MRI. Do not biopsy through the eardrum. Before surgery, check plasma free metanephrines, because a few of these tumours secrete catecholamines. Other causes include idiopathic intracranial hypertension, dural arteriovenous fistula, arterial stenosis or dissection, and a high-output state such as anaemia or thyrotoxicosis.

The adult with one-sided otitis media with effusion

OME is common in children but unusual in adults. New, persistent fluid on one side, especially with a neck mass, nosebleeds or nasal blockage, or in someone from a high-incidence region, needs endoscopic examination of the nasopharynx, with biopsy of any mass, to exclude nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is treated mainly with radiotherapy, with chemotherapy for advanced stages.

Lesions of the auricle

A non-healing, crusted or ulcerated lesion on the helix of an older, sun-exposed patient needs a biopsy before any destructive treatment. Excise squamous and basal cell carcinomas with clear margins (Mohs surgery spares cartilage). Examine the parotid and neck nodes.

Exam trap: do not treat an adult's one-sided effusion with antibiotics or a tube alone. Look at the nasopharynx first.

sections.heading: Hearing loss in practice: newborns to older adults, and sudden loss
sections.html:
Newborns

Every newborn is screened, with otoacoustic emissions or automated auditory brainstem response (ABR). The 1-3-6 timeline: screen by 1 month, confirm a loss with a full diagnostic audiological evaluation (diagnostic ABR) by 3 months, and start intervention (hearing aids, early intervention services) by 6 months. Babies in the neonatal intensive care unit are screened with ABR, because emissions miss auditory neuropathy. A failed screen is never "probably fluid" without a diagnostic follow-up.

Congenital cytomegalovirus: test saliva or urine by PCR within the first 3 weeks of life (later positives may reflect postnatal infection). Newborns with symptomatic disease are treated with oral valganciclovir for 6 months, which improves hearing and developmental outcomes. They need repeated hearing tests, because the loss can be delayed or progressive.

Children

Test hearing in any child with speech delay, school difficulties or persistent effusion. Cochlear implants are an option for severe to profound sensorineural loss from about 9 to 12 months of age. Earlier implantation gives better language outcomes.

Adults: a stepwise approach

  1. Otoscopy: cerumen, effusion, perforation, cholesteatoma.
  2. Tuning forks (Weber, Rinne) to separate conductive from sensorineural loss.
  3. Formal audiometry.
  4. MRI of the internal auditory canals if the sensorineural loss is asymmetric.
ConditionManagement
Cerumen impactionSoftening drops, irrigation (only if the drum is known to be intact), or manual removal
PresbycusisAudiology referral and hearing aids (over-the-counter aids are an option for mild to moderate loss); cochlear implant when aids no longer help. Treating hearing loss may lower the risk of cognitive decline.
Noise-induced lossPrevention: hearing protection and less exposure. In the workplace, an average of 85 dBA over 8 hours triggers a hearing conservation program.
OtosclerosisHearing aid, or surgery (stapedotomy or stapedectomy)

Sudden sensorineural hearing loss: an otologic urgency

A sensorineural loss of 30 dB or more at 3 neighbouring frequencies, developing within 72 hours, usually in one ear. Most cases have no cause found. A patient who "wakes up deaf in one ear" is often wrongly told it is wax or fluid.

  • First separate it from a conductive loss: tuning forks in the room, then audiometry promptly.
  • Do not order routine blood tests or CT.
  • Offer a corticosteroid (oral, or intratympanic injection) as early as possible, ideally within 2 weeks. Intratympanic steroid is a salvage option if recovery is incomplete. Hyperbaric oxygen can be added within 3 months.
  • Get an MRI of the internal auditory canals (or ABR if MRI is not possible) to look for a retrocochlear lesion such as vestibular schwannoma.
  • Sudden loss with vertigo and other brainstem signs can be an AICA stroke. Send the patient straight to emergency stroke imaging.
Exam trap: antivirals, antibiotics and "watch for a week" are wrong answers for sudden sensorineural loss. Confirm it with an audiogram and start steroids early.

furtherReading.label: StatPearls: Noise Exposure and Hearing Loss (NCBI Bookshelf)

sections.heading: The dizzy patient: positional, acute continuous and episodic vertigo
sections.html:
Sort vertigo by timing and trigger more than by how the patient describes it.

PatternCommon peripheral causeDangerous mimic
Brief (seconds to under a minute), set off by changes in head positionBPPVCentral positional nystagmus (posterior fossa lesion)
Acute and continuous for a day or more, with nausea, nystagmus and unsteady gait (acute vestibular syndrome)Vestibular neuritis; labyrinthitis if hearing is lostCerebellar or brainstem stroke
Spontaneous attacks lasting minutes to hoursMénière disease; vestibular migraineTransient ischaemic attack of the posterior circulation

BPPV

The Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre brings on vertigo and torsional upbeating nystagmus towards the lower ear, after a short delay. It lasts under a minute and lessens with repeated tests. Treat with canalith repositioning (the Epley manoeuvre) on the affected side. No imaging, no lab tests and no routine vestibular suppressants are needed, and there is no need to restrict posture after the manoeuvre. If BPPV is suspected but the Dix-Hallpike is negative, test the horizontal canal with a supine roll test. BPPV is common in older adults and raises their risk of falls, so ask about it.

Acute vestibular syndrome: peripheral or stroke?

In a patient with ongoing vertigo and nystagmus, a three-part bedside exam (head impulse, nystagmus, test of skew) is more sensitive for stroke than early CT, or even early diffusion MRI.

  • Reassuring (peripheral): an abnormal head impulse test (a catch-up saccade), nystagmus in one direction only, and no skew deviation.
  • Dangerous (central): a normal head impulse test in a patient who has nystagmus, nystagmus that changes direction with gaze, or skew deviation. New hearing loss also raises concern for an AICA infarct.
  • Central signs, severe imbalance (cannot stand or walk unaided), or vascular risk factors with a new headache: get an MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging, and repeat it if the first is negative but suspicion remains. Noncontrast CT misses most posterior fossa infarcts.

Vestibular neuritis: a short course of a vestibular suppressant (meclizine, or a benzodiazepine) for the first days only, antiemetics, then early mobilisation and vestibular rehabilitation. Long-term suppressants slow the brain's compensation.

Ménière disease

The diagnosis needs 2 or more attacks of vertigo, each lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours, with low- to mid-frequency sensorineural loss documented on audiometry in that ear, and fluctuating hearing, tinnitus or fullness in it. Rule out a vestibular schwannoma with MRI.

  • Maintenance: education, less dietary salt, and limiting caffeine and alcohol; a diuretic can be added.
  • Attacks: a short-term vestibular suppressant or antiemetic.
  • Persistent attacks: intratympanic corticosteroid. Then destructive options for the vertigo, which may cost hearing: intratympanic gentamicin, surgery to the endolymphatic sac, labyrinthectomy or vestibular nerve section.

Vestibular migraine

Recurrent vestibular attacks lasting 5 minutes to 72 hours in someone with migraine, with migraine features (headache, light or sound sensitivity, aura) during at least half of the attacks. Hearing is normal between attacks. Manage it as migraine: identify triggers, treat attacks, and use preventives for frequent episodes.

Motion sickness

Prevent it with a transdermal scopolamine patch applied behind the ear several hours before travel, or with a first-generation antihistamine (meclizine, dimenhydrinate). Avoid scopolamine in narrow-angle glaucoma, urinary retention and, where possible, in frail older adults (it can cause delirium). Behavioural measures help too: look at the horizon, and sit where motion is least.

Exam trap: a normal head impulse test is reassuring in a patient who is not dizzy. In a patient with acute, continuous vertigo and nystagmus, it suggests stroke.

sections.heading: Ear injuries and foreign bodies: emergency management
sections.html:
Auricular haematoma

A tense, fluctuant, purple swelling on the front of the auricle after a blow. Treat promptly by incision and drainage (or needle aspiration if it is small and fresh), then a bolster or compressive dressing to stop it filling again. Review within a day or so, because it often recurs. Leaving it causes cartilage necrosis and cauliflower ear. Advise protective headgear for contact sports.

Traumatic tympanic membrane perforation

  • Most heal on their own within weeks. Keep water out of the ear and avoid ototoxic (aminoglycoside) drops. Antibiotic drops (a fluoroquinolone) are used only for contamination or infection. Check healing and hearing with audiometry at follow-up.
  • Refer for repair (tympanoplasty) if it has not healed after about 2 to 3 months.
  • Refer urgently for vertigo, sensorineural hearing loss or facial weakness after the injury, which point to inner-ear injury or a perilymph fistula.

Temporal bone fracture

Assess the patient first as a head-injury patient (airway, cervical spine, CT of the head). High-resolution CT of the temporal bones defines the fracture. Check facial nerve function as early as possible, because the timing of a palsy matters:

  • Delayed-onset or incomplete facial weakness (swelling in the canal): an excellent prognosis. Give an oral corticosteroid and observe.
  • Immediate, complete paralysis (nerve cut or crushed): electrodiagnostic testing and surgical decompression or exploration are considered.

CSF otorrhoea: most leaks stop with conservative care. Keep the head of the bed up, tell the patient not to strain or blow the nose, and give stool softeners. Prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended. Persistent leaks need a lumbar drain or surgical repair. Do not pack the canal, and do not put drops in an ear that is leaking CSF.

Barotrauma

Middle-ear barotrauma (ear pain after flying or diving, a retracted or bruised drum, mild conductive loss) is managed with pain relief and decongestants, and no flying or diving until the ear is normal. Advise against diving with a cold, and suggest equalising early and often. Vertigo or sensorineural loss after a dive needs urgent evaluation. It may be inner-ear barotrauma, which needs rest and no further diving, or inner-ear decompression sickness, which needs hyperbaric oxygen.

Foreign bodies in the ear

ObjectApproach
Button batteryRemove immediately, under direct vision or a microscope. Do not irrigate. Check the canal and drum afterwards for burns.
Live insectKill it first with mineral oil or lidocaine drops, then remove it
Food or plant matterDo not irrigate (it swells). Remove with forceps or suction.
Small, smooth inert objectIrrigation or instruments, if the drum is intact and the child is still. Refer to ENT if removal fails or the child cannot cooperate.
Exam trap: a button battery in the ear or nose is not a clinic appointment. It is a same-hour removal, like one in the oesophagus.

sections.heading: Preventing and recognising drug ototoxicity
sections.html:
Before treatment

  • Ask about personal or family hearing loss, especially deafness after an aminoglycoside in a maternal relative. This suggests the mitochondrial MT-RNR1 m.1555A>G variant. In known carriers, avoid aminoglycosides unless no adequate alternative exists for a life-threatening infection.
  • Get a baseline audiogram (including high frequencies) before long courses of aminoglycosides, for example for drug-resistant tuberculosis or nontuberculous mycobacteria, and before cisplatin.
  • Adjust the dose for kidney function, use extended-interval dosing where it fits, and monitor drug levels.
  • Avoid giving other ototoxins at the same time where possible: loop diuretics and vancomycin with aminoglycosides.

During treatment

  • Repeat audiometry during prolonged courses, and ask about tinnitus, fullness, unsteadiness and oscillopsia.
  • New ototoxic symptoms on an aminoglycoside: stop the drug if an effective alternative exists, check levels and kidney function, and arrange audiological and vestibular testing. Damage is usually permanent, so early detection is what saves hearing.
DrugPractical point
Cisplatin in childrenMonitor hearing at each cycle. Sodium thiosulfate, given about 6 hours after cisplatin, lowers the risk of hearing loss in children with localised, non-metastatic solid tumours.
IV furosemideThe risk rises with high peak levels. Give large doses as a slow infusion (often quoted as no faster than about 4 mg/min), especially in kidney failure.
Aspirin and other salicylatesTinnitus at high doses: check a salicylate level and lower or stop the dose. Hearing recovers.
QuinineNot recommended for leg cramps. It can cause cinchonism and serious blood toxicity (thrombocytopenia, haemolytic-uraemic syndrome).
HydroxychloroquineHearing symptoms are uncommon. Retinal screening is the main monitoring.

Recognising vestibulotoxicity

Bilateral vestibular loss causes unsteadiness that is worse in the dark or on uneven ground, and oscillopsia on walking. The head impulse test is abnormal in both directions, and the Romberg test is positive. Patients need vestibular rehabilitation and fall-prevention measures.

Pearl: deafness after a single dose of gentamicin, with similar stories in the mother's relatives, points to a mitochondrial susceptibility variant. Record it as a lifelong drug alert.
